title: Quantum III
subtitle: Approximation, transitions and scattering
prerequisites: Quantum II and the Mathematical toolkit. Explicit local bridges cover approximation order, Airy/delta/gauge/solid angle, continuum rates, Green/Legendre functions and Kraus maps before use. Each lesson links its precise prior preparation.
coverage: A bounded introduction to open systems
Choose, test and report an approximation

lessons.title: Start with a model you can solve
lessons.idea: A small correction should be measured against the feature it might disturb.
body: Imagine two energy levels separated by a clear gap. A weak coupling can move the levels and mix their states. We start with H₀, a Hamiltonian whose states and energies we already know, and write the changed Hamiltonian as H(λ)=H₀+λV. Here V has energy units, while λ is a unit-free control number.

Writing λ as a small number is not enough. The matrix elements of λV must be compared with the relevant energy gaps. A coupling of 0.1 eV is small beside a 10 eV gap but large beside a 0.001 eV gap. The dimensionless ratio makes that comparison explicit.

In this lesson take H₀=diag(0,Δ) and V=[[0,v],[v,0]], where Δ>0 and v are real energies. The lower exact eigenvalue is [Δ−√(Δ²+4λ²v²)]/2. For |λv|/Δ much less than one, it is approximately −λ²v²/Δ. The symbol ≈ means an approximation, not equality. Higher powers of the small ratio were left out.
lessons.terms: H,H₀,V: Changed Hamiltonian, reference Hamiltonian and perturbing operator (energy; eV in this example). A Hamiltonian is the operator used to calculate energy and time evolution. λ,η: Control parameter and coupling-to-gap ratio (no unit). The vertical bars take the size without the sign. The approximation requires η much smaller than one. Δ,v,E₋: Positive reference gap, real coupling matrix element and lower exact energy (eV). The reference lower energy is zero; this energy zero is a choice, not a claim of zero absolute energy. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Add a scaled energy correction to a solvable model. Compare its coupling size with the old energy gap. In this two-state example a weak off-diagonal coupling lowers the lower energy by an amount proportional to the coupling squared.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Choose Δ=4 eV, v=1 eV and λ=0.20. The actual coupling is λv=0.20 eV and η=0.05.
The exact lower level is [4−√(16+0.16)]/2 eV≈−0.00997512 eV.
The small-ratio estimate is −(0.20 eV)²/(4 eV)=−0.0100 eV. Its error is about 0.00002488 eV, much smaller than this predicted shift.

visual.caption: Two-state energy bookkeeping, not a drawing of a particle moving between spatial locations.

check.prompt: Keep the actual coupling at 0.20 eV, but shrink the reference gap to 0.40 eV. What is η?
explanations: Correct. Divide 0.20 eV by 0.40 eV; the ratio is 0.50, no longer very small.
That used the old 4 eV gap.
Shrinking the gap makes the ratio larger, not smaller.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Could choosing λ=0.001 guarantee a good approximation for any V?
apply.answer: No. If V has enormous matrix elements or the reference gap is tiny, λV can still mix states strongly. State the actual energy scale and gap before trusting a label such as weak.

lessons.limits: Finite Hermitian two-state example with a positive nonzero gap. The approximation describes a local small-coupling limit, not a general proof that every perturbation series converges.

glossary.definition: A specified change added to a model whose solution is already known.
A comparison in which matching units cancel, such as one energy divided by another.

lessons.title: The first energy shift is an average
lessons.idea: A known state can tell us the first effect of a weak added energy operator.
body: Let |n⟩ be a normalized, isolated eigenstate of H₀ with energy Eₙ⁽⁰⁾. Isolated means that no other state has exactly this energy and that the relevant gaps do not close. Expand the changed energy as Eₙ=Eₙ⁽⁰⁾+λEₙ⁽¹⁾+O(λ²). The superscript (1) labels a coefficient; it is not a power.

The notation O(λ²) says the omitted terms begin at quadratic order as λ tends to zero, under this expansion. It does not give a numerical error bound by itself. Substitute a corresponding state expansion into H|ψ⟩=E|ψ⟩ and keep the terms proportional to λ. Taking the overlap with ⟨n| cancels the unknown first state correction because ⟨n|H₀=Eₙ⁽⁰⁾⟨n|.

The result is Eₙ⁽¹⁾=⟨n|V|n⟩. Read this as: calculate the average of the added energy operator in the old state. Then multiply by λ to obtain the first shift. The coefficient and the shift are different when λ is not one.
lessons.terms: |n⟩,n: Normalized reference eigenstate and its label (no unit). The state is nondegenerate; its label is not a power or a particle count. Eₙ,Eₙ⁽⁰⁾,Eₙ⁽¹⁾,V: Changed energy, reference energy, first coefficient and added operator (eV here). The coefficient Eₙ⁽¹⁾ is not yet multiplied by λ. λ,O(λ²),⟨n|V|n⟩: Control, omitted-order notation and reference expectation (λ has no unit; expectation has eV). The order notation tracks powers near λ=0, not a guaranteed error bar. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: The first energy coefficient is the expectation of V in the unchanged reference state. Multiplying it by the control parameter gives the first-order change in energy.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Take H₀=diag(1,5) eV and V=[[0.6,0.2],[0.2,−0.4]] eV, in the two reference eigenvectors. Prepare the reference first state |0⟩=(1,0)ᵀ.
Its first coefficient is the first diagonal element: E₀⁽¹⁾=0.6 eV. At λ=0.10, the first shift is 0.060 eV.
The first-order predicted energy is 1.060 eV. The off-diagonal 0.2 eV element can affect higher orders even though it did not enter this first expectation.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: The diagonal is taken in the reference energy basis; an arbitrary matrix diagonal is not automatically an energy correction.

items.label: Coefficient
items.value: Average of V in old state

check.prompt: For the second reference state of the same matrices at λ=0.20, what is the first-order energy?
explanations: Its coefficient is negative, so the first shift is downward.
Correct. Add (0.20)(−0.4 eV)=−0.08 eV to 5 eV.
That is only the shift, not the final predicted energy.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If V is diagonal in the complete reference basis, why can this prediction be exact rather than approximate?
apply.answer: Then H₀ and V share those eigenvectors and the displayed diagonal entries add directly. In that special case the energy is exactly Eₙ⁽⁰⁾+λVₙₙ. Do not infer exactness when off-diagonal couplings are present.

lessons.limits: An isolated nondegenerate level with a sufficiently regular small-parameter expansion. Degenerate states require a projected-block treatment; singular/unbounded perturbations need domain and convergence care.

lessons.title: A weak coupling adds small pieces of other states
lessons.idea: The size of a new piece depends on both the coupling and the energy gap.
body: A change can rotate an energy eigenvector even when its first energy shift is zero. Write the changed state as |ψₙ⟩=|n⟩+λ|n⁽¹⁾⟩+O(λ²). Choose its phase and scale so that ⟨n|n⁽¹⁾⟩=0. This convenient intermediate convention keeps the old component equal to one to first order; exact normalization is handled separately.

Project the first-order eigenvalue equation onto a different reference state |m⟩. The coefficient along that direction is ⟨m|V|n⟩ divided by Eₙ⁽⁰⁾−Eₘ⁽⁰⁾. The denominator is a signed gap. Changing its sign changes the admixture phase, not a probability into a negative number.

The reference basis must be complete for the stated finite model. An amplitude of −0.04 has probability weight 0.0016 before the small normalization correction, not −0.04. If a denominator is zero or too small, this formula is not the right approximation.
lessons.terms: |n⁽¹⁾⟩,|m⟩,|n⟩: First state coefficient and reference basis states (no unit in finite coordinates). The superscript (1) marks expansion order. The corrected state includes λ|n⁽¹⁾⟩. Vₘₙ,Eₙ⁽⁰⁾,Eₘ⁽⁰⁾: Connecting matrix element and two reference energies (eV). Their quotient is unit-free, as a state amplitude must be. Σ_(m≠n),λ: Sum over all other reference states and small control (no unit). The excluded original component is fixed by the chosen phase/scale convention. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: For each different reference state, divide the connecting energy matrix element by the signed energy gap. Add those state pieces, then multiply this first correction by λ when constructing the changed state.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Let H₀=diag(0,5) eV and V=[[0,1],[1,0]] eV. For n=0, the first correction is [1 eV/(0−5 eV)]|1⟩=−0.20|1⟩.
At λ=0.20 the unnormalized first-order state is |0⟩−0.04|1⟩.
The small second-basis weight is 0.04²=0.0016 before normalization. The norm squared is 1.0016, so exact normalization of this approximate vector gives a weight 0.0016/1.0016≈0.00159744.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: The two reference states are mathematical basis outcomes, not spatial paths followed by one particle.

check.prompt: Use the same reference gap and λ, but change V₁₀ to −1 eV. What happens to the leading |1⟩ amplitude?
explanations: The numerator changed sign while the denominator did not.
Probability is a magnitude square; it remains nonnegative.
Correct. The coefficient becomes +0.20, and multiplying by λ=0.20 gives +0.04.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would a 0.01 eV gap justify the same calculation with a 0.20 eV actual coupling?
apply.answer: No. The predicted admixture would have magnitude 20, not a small addition. That warns us to retain and diagonalize the strongly mixed block rather than trust this nondegenerate expression.

lessons.limits: Finite complete orthonormal reference basis, nonzero separated gaps, small mixing and the declared intermediate normalization. Renormalizing a first-order vector is useful but does not create all missing second-order state components.

lessons.title: The next energy shift comes from mixing
lessons.idea: Coupling to higher levels pushes a nondegenerate ground level down at second order.
body: The first energy correction used a diagonal expectation. The second coefficient accounts for a trip from the old state into another reference direction and back. For a Hermitian V, the product VₙₘVₘₙ is |Vₘₙ|², a nonnegative energy squared.

Divide that product by the signed reference gap and sum over other states. If n is the nondegenerate ground state, every denominator is negative, so the second coefficient is nonpositive. An excited state can receive terms of either sign because some reference energies lie below it and others above.

The actual second-order contribution is λ²Eₙ⁽²⁾. Neither this coefficient nor the first coefficient includes its own λ factor. This is still an approximation near λ=0, not a formula to use unchanged at strong mixing.
lessons.terms: Eₙ⁽²⁾,Eₙ⁽¹⁾,Eₙ⁽⁰⁾: Second coefficient, first coefficient and reference energy (eV). The expansion order is shown in parentheses; it is not an ordinary exponent. Vₘₙ,|Vₘₙ|²: Coupling and its magnitude square (eV and eV²). Hermiticity gives a magnitude square even for complex couplings. m,n,Σ,λ: Reference labels, sum and control parameter (no unit). The sum excludes n; all denominator gaps must be nonzero. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Square each connecting matrix element’s magnitude, divide by its signed gap and add. Multiplying the result by λ squared gives the second energy contribution.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Take reference energies 0, 3 and 8 eV. Let the ground state couple to them through V₁₀=0.6 eV and V₂₀=0.8i eV; take V₀₀=0.
The second coefficient is (0.6 eV)²/(−3 eV)+|0.8i eV|²/(−8 eV)=−0.12 eV−0.08 eV=−0.20 eV.
At λ=0.25, the second contribution is (0.25)²(−0.20 eV)=−0.0125 eV. Both terms lower this reference ground level.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: The sign statement is about a nondegenerate ground level under this perturbative expansion, not every excited level.

check.prompt: A reference level at 3 eV couples only to a lower level at 0 eV with matrix element 0.6 eV. What is its second coefficient?
explanations: Correct. (0.6 eV)²/(3 eV)=+0.12 eV.
That is the numerical squared coupling before division, with different units.
This denominator is positive: 3 eV−0 eV.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does a zero diagonal element prove that the energy is unchanged?
apply.answer: No. It makes the first coefficient zero, but nonzero off-diagonal elements can give a second-order shift. Check the relevant couplings and gaps instead of stopping at the diagonal.

lessons.limits: Nondegenerate stationary perturbation theory for a Hermitian perturbation and a well-defined isolated level. Infinite sums additionally need convergence and operator-domain control; the worked example is finite.

lessons.title: Normalize without pretending the missing terms are known
lessons.idea: A first-order state can be normalized exactly and still be only an approximation.
body: Suppose the first state correction is orthogonal to the reference vector. Write |χ⟩=|n⟩+λ|a⟩ with ⟨n|a⟩=0 and ⟨n|n⟩=1. Its norm squared is 1+λ²⟨a|a⟩. The absence of a linear norm change follows from the zero overlap, not from ignoring normalization.

Dividing by √(1+λ²⟨a|a⟩) makes this chosen truncated vector exactly normalized. If expanding instead, the original component receives the factor 1−λ²⟨a|a⟩/2 through second order. This uses the local small-u relation (1+u)^(−1/2)=1−u/2+O(u²), with u=λ²⟨a|a⟩.

Normalization fixes the part of the second-order correction parallel to the original vector in a fixed phase convention. It does not determine other second-order components. A normalized approximate state is not automatically the exact energy eigenstate.
lessons.terms: |ψ_tr⟩,|n⟩,|a⟩: Normalized truncated vector, reference vector and first coefficient (no unit). The subscript tr labels truncation, not an exact state. The stated orthogonality is essential. λ,N,u: Control, normalization factor and local expansion variable (no unit). u=λ²⟨a|a⟩ must be small for the displayed approximation to N. ⟨a|a⟩,O(u²): Squared size and omitted-order notation (no unit). The squared size is nonnegative. Order notation does not provide a numerical error bound by itself. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Divide the approximate column by its own norm. The small correction to its overall scale begins at second order because the added first-order component is orthogonal to the original state.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: The exact normalization factor for this truncated vector is 1/√1.0036≈0.99820485. Its second-order estimate is 1−0.0036/2=0.9982.
The normalized second-state probability is 0.0036/1.0036≈0.00358709. The two normalized weights add to one, but other omitted eigenvector corrections are still unknown.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: This is an approximation-order check. Making the norm one does not prove that the eigenvalue equation is satisfied.

check.prompt: Keep |a⟩=−0.30|1⟩ but double λ to 0.40. What is the norm excess u?
explanations: Doubling λ multiplies λ² by four, not two.
That was the old value.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: How could you check whether the normalized approximate state is close to an eigenstate?
apply.answer: Evaluate the residual H|ψ_tr⟩−E_tr|ψ_tr⟩ and its norm, using the proposed approximate energy E_tr. Normalization tests probability bookkeeping; a small residual tests a different part of the eigenstate claim and still needs gap information for a strong accuracy conclusion.

lessons.limits: The orthogonal-first-correction convention and a regular small-parameter expansion. Exact normalization here refers only to the explicitly constructed truncated vector, not to the full perturbative eigenstate.

lessons.title: Check the approximation against a solvable neighbor
lessons.idea: A measured error in one model is more informative than an unexplained claim that a coupling is small.
body: Use the same two-level model as the opening step: reference energies 0 and Δ>0, with real off-diagonal actual coupling g=λv. The lower exact energy is known, so it gives a clean reference against which to test the second-order estimate −g²/Δ.

Define an absolute error as the size of the difference between the approximate and exact energies. Here define relative shift error by dividing that difference by |E₋|, the nonzero exact shift. This denominator is a choice; it must be stated. At g=0 the relative shift error is undefined because both shifts are zero, although the absolute error is zero.

For this particular model the leading omitted energy term is +g⁴/Δ³. When g/Δ is already small, halving g therefore reduces the absolute error by about sixteen and the relative shift error by about four. This model-specific scaling is a check, not a convergence proof for unrelated Hamiltonians.
lessons.terms: g,Δ,E₂,E₋: Actual coupling, positive gap, second-order estimate and exact lower energy (eV). Here E₂ labels an approximation, not the second basis level or a squared energy. ε_abs,ε_rel: Absolute energy error and relative shift error (eV and no unit). The relative error defined here is only used when the exact shift is nonzero. g⁴/Δ³: Leading omitted term for this specific two-level model (eV). It follows by a small-ratio expansion of the exact square root, not a general bound. example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Choose Δ=2 eV and g=0.20 eV. The exact lower energy is (2−√4.16)/2 eV≈−0.01980390 eV, while E₂=−0.02000000 eV.
The absolute error is about 0.00019610 eV and the relative shift error is about 0.00990195, or 0.9902%.
Halve g to 0.10 eV. The exact shift is approximately −0.00498756 eV and the estimate is −0.00500000 eV. The absolute error is about 0.00001244 eV, smaller by a factor near 15.8.

visual.title: Compare the approximation with an exact two-state model
visual.caption: Separate finite model H=[[0,g],[g,Δ]] with positive reference gap Δ and real coupling g. The controls show energies in eV; the plot uses the unit-free ratios |g|/Δ and E/Δ. The solid curve is the exact lower eigenvalue, and the dashed curve is −g²/Δ divided by Δ. The marker follows the exact value for the selected controls. At large coupling/gap ratio the dashed approximation is deliberately not accurate. Relative shift error is |E₂−E₋|/|E₋|; it is undefined when g=0 because the exact shift is zero, although absolute error is then zero. This model-specific comparison does not prove convergence for other Hamiltonians.

check.prompt: At Δ=2 eV and g=0, what should you report for the relative shift error as defined here?
options: It is an infinite physical energy
Zero divided by zero is undefined
explanations: No energy diverges; only the chosen ratio is undefined.
Both shifts vanish, so this particular relative ratio cannot be evaluated.
Correct. The absolute error is zero, but this relative ratio has a zero denominator.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would the same absolute error always be acceptable in two applications?
apply.answer: No. Compare it with the precision and energy differences relevant to the question. A small error relative to a huge baseline energy can still spoil a tiny transition splitting. Record which physical prediction is being approximated.

lessons.limits: Exact reference available for this Hermitian two-level model; g and Δ are real, Δ>0. The series comparison is local in |g|/Δ. Finite-order agreement does not establish convergence for other potentials.

practice.prompt: Use reference gap Δ=3 eV and actual real coupling g=0.30 eV. The first diagonal shift vanishes.

parts.label: Leading admixture amplitude of the upper reference state
Exactly normalized upper-state weight of that first-order vector
parts.feedback: Normalize (1,−0.10) before taking its second weight.

practice.reasoning: Explain why the normalized trial weight is not claimed to be the exact eigenstate weight. Enter decimal or scientific-notation numbers, not fractions or expressions. Entry tolerances allow rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: First look inside the tied energy space
lessons.idea: When reference energies tie, the weak change chooses which combinations split.
body: If two different reference states have the same energy E₀, dividing by their energy difference would mean dividing by zero. Instead, keep their whole degenerate subspace. A subspace is the set of all combinations of a chosen group of basis states. The projector P keeps that part of a vector.

For a normalized vector |u⟩ inside this subspace, the first-order eigenvalue equation becomes PVP|u⟩=ε|u⟩. Thus diagonalize V restricted to the tied space. Its eigenvalues ε are first energy coefficients, and its eigenvectors supply the combinations that behave simply under the weak change.

PVP can be displayed as a matrix on the full space, with zeros outside P, but those extra zero eigenvalues are not additional states in the tied group. Work in a basis for the projected subspace itself. Coupling to separated outside states is not lost forever; it enters later corrections.
lessons.terms: P,|u⟩: Orthogonal projector and normalized state in its range (no unit). P²=P means projecting twice has the same effect as once. V,ε,E₀,E: Perturbing energy operator, projected eigenvalue, tied reference energy and predicted energy (eV). ε is a first coefficient, not yet multiplied by λ. λ,PVP: Unit-free control and projected perturbation (no unit; PVP has eV). Only the restriction to the tied subspace is diagonalized for these first coefficients. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Keep the entire group of states sharing one reference energy. Inside that group, find the eigenvectors and energy eigenvalues of the added operator. Add λ times each such eigenvalue to the shared reference energy.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Let H₀=diag(2,2,7) eV. The tied subspace consists of the first two reference states, so P=diag(1,1,0).
Choose V=[[0.3,0.4,0.5],[0.4,−0.3,0],[0.5,0,0.2]] eV. Its restricted block is [[0.3,0.4],[0.4,−0.3]] eV, with eigenvalues ±0.5 eV.
At λ=0.10 the two first-order energies are 2.05 eV and 1.95 eV. The coupling to the 7 eV reference state does not enter these first coefficients.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: A block in state space, not a spatial region. Outside-state couplings are deferred to higher-order calculations, not assumed absent.

check.prompt: If the tied reference energy changes to 4 eV but the same projected V and λ remain, what are the first-order energies?
explanations: Correct. The shifts remain ±0.05 eV; only the shared reference changes.
The projected eigenvalues still need multiplication by λ=0.10.
Those used the old reference energy.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can you use the two original diagonal elements 0.3 and −0.3 eV as the first coefficients without diagonalizing?
apply.answer: Not here. The 0.4 eV off-diagonal entries mix those tied reference vectors at the same order. The correct first coefficients are the eigenvalues of the full restricted block.

lessons.limits: A finite degenerate reference eigenspace separated by nonzero gaps from other reference levels, with a regular perturbation. If the projected perturbation itself remains degenerate, higher-order or additional symmetry analysis may be needed.

lessons.title: The correct combinations may have complex phases
lessons.idea: Diagonalizing the small block finds both the shifts and their state directions.
body: A projected Hermitian matrix can contain imaginary off-diagonal entries. They must be conjugates of each other. Diagonalize the block using its full complex entries rather than replacing them with their sizes.

For B=[[a,ic],[−ic,a]], with real energies a and c, the normalized columns (i,1)ᵀ/√2 and (−i,1)ᵀ/√2 are eigenvectors with eigenvalues a+c and a−c. Their phase difference is part of the basis choice selected by this perturbation.

We are finding energy eigenstates of the changed model to leading order within the formerly tied space. That does not say every preparation instantly jumps into one of them. A different initial preparation can remain a superposition and evolve according to the Hamiltonian.
lessons.terms: B,a,c: Projected Hermitian matrix and real coefficients (meV in this example). The lower-left entry is the conjugate of the upper-right entry. |u_+⟩,|u_-⟩,i: Normalized columns (i,1)ᵀ/√2 and (−i,1)ᵀ/√2; imaginary unit (no unit). i²=−1. Labels + and − follow the formulas, not necessarily energy order if c is negative. E₀,E_±,λ: Tied reference energy, first-order energies and control (meV; λ has no unit). A matrix eigenvector is a state direction, not a forced measurement result. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: The imaginary couplings combine with the relative state phases. The two orthonormal eigenvectors separate the block into two real energy coefficients, which become physical first shifts only after multiplication by λ.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Choose a=1 meV, c=2 meV and E₀=10 meV. Acting on (i,1)ᵀ/√2 gives 3 meV times that column.
The orthogonal column (−i,1)ᵀ/√2 has coefficient −1 meV. Their inner product is zero and both norms are one.
At λ=0.20, the first-order levels are 10.6 meV and 9.8 meV, with a separation of 0.8 meV.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: Relative phases belong to the chosen state coordinates. A common phase on either eigenvector changes no energy prediction.

check.prompt: Keep a=1 meV and λ=0.20 but change c to 3 meV. What is the first-order level separation?
explanations: The separation uses 2|c| before multiplying by λ.
Correct. λ×2|c|=0.20×6 meV=1.2 meV.
That is the separation of coefficients, not the physical first shifts.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: What remains true if you multiply the first eigenvector by −i?
apply.answer: Its norm, energy eigenvalue and every measurement probability remain unchanged. Only its overall phase changes. The relative phase between its components is retained.

lessons.limits: The complete projected two-state block is Hermitian with real a,c. This solves the block exactly, but its use as a first-order approximation to a larger system still requires the outside-state separation assumptions.

lessons.title: Keep a small splitting inside the block
lessons.idea: Near a crossing, solve the strongly mixed part instead of expanding across a tiny denominator.
body: Two levels need not tie exactly for the ordinary nondegenerate series to become poor. If their splitting is comparable with their coupling, retain both inside a small block and diagonalize it. Other well-separated states can still be treated approximately if their own gap tests pass.

Write the real two-state block using an average energy Ē, an uncoupled splitting δ and a coupling g. Its eigenvalues lie equally above and below the average by d=√[(δ/2)²+g²]. Even when δ reaches zero, a nonzero g leaves a gap 2|g|. This is an avoided crossing.

This exact block calculation does not prove that a chosen two-state truncation is accurate. Check coupling to omitted states and the physical model separately. It only avoids the bad expansion across the small internal gap.
lessons.terms: H_block,Ē,δ,g,d,E_±: Hamiltonian block, average, uncoupled splitting, real coupling, positive spectral distance and energies (eV). δ may have either sign; d is nonnegative. The block basis is the two chosen uncoupled states. ±,|g|: Two eigenvalue branches and coupling magnitude (no unit; |g| has eV). At δ=0 their separation is 2|g|, not zero unless g also vanishes. equationGuide.meaning: Keep the small energy difference and the connecting matrix element on equal footing. Diagonalizing gives two energies centered on the old average, separated by twice d.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: The exact block energies are approximately 4.81972244 eV and 5.18027756 eV.
An ordinary second-order estimate from the lower reference energy 4.9 eV would give 4.9−0.15²/0.20=4.7875 eV, using values in eV. The coupling/gap ratio 0.75 warns that this expansion is not small.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: The curve describes eigenvalues as model parameters change, not the time trajectory of a prepared state through those levels.

check.prompt: At δ=0, change g to −0.40 eV. What is the block energy gap?
explanations: A gap is a nonnegative difference; the sign of g affects state phases.
The splitting is twice the coupling magnitude.
Correct. 2|g|=0.80 eV.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does following an eigenvalue curve while changing δ automatically describe the actual state evolution?
apply.answer: No. The prepared state follows the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. Remaining near one instantaneous eigenstate requires a separate slow-change analysis and a nonzero gap, introduced later.

lessons.limits: Exact finite real two-state block. Its use as an effective truncation needs control of omitted-state couplings. It is not an automatic adiabatic theorem or a general multilevel solution.

lessons.title: A symmetry can forbid a coupling without protecting a tie
lessons.idea: Knowing which entries vanish is different from knowing two energies stay equal.
body: Parity Π reverses spatial coordinates. A parity eigenstate has eigenvalue +1 (even) or −1 (odd). If V is even, ΠVΠ=V. Then the matrix element between an even and an odd state must be zero: changing parity leaves V unchanged but changes the sign of that overlap.

If V is odd, ΠVΠ=−V, every diagonal expectation in a definite-parity state is zero. Opposite-parity off-diagonal elements may be nonzero. An odd perturbation can therefore split an even/odd degenerate pair at first order even though both old diagonal expectations vanish.

Conversely, an even perturbation can give different diagonal shifts to the two parity states. Parity stops their mixing but does not force their energies to stay tied. A protected degeneracy requires more information than this one symmetry alone.
lessons.terms: Π,|even⟩,|odd⟩,|±⟩: Parity operator and normalized parity eigenstates (no unit). Here ± labels parity eigenvalues, not energy ordering or spin. V,⟨u|V|v⟩: Perturbation and its matrix element (eV). Even means unchanged under inversion; odd means its sign reverses. ⇒: Logical implication (no unit). The zero follows from the stated symmetry and parity of the states, not from all perturbations. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: An even perturbation cannot connect opposite parity states. An odd perturbation has zero expectation in each definite-parity state, but can connect an even state to an odd one.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Take a tied even/odd pair with an even perturbation block diag(0.2,−0.1) eV. At λ=0.50 the two shifts are +0.10 eV and −0.05 eV: there is no mixing, but a 0.15 eV separation.
For a separate odd perturbation block [[0,0.3],[0.3,0]] eV, the old diagonal expectations are both zero.
That odd block has eigenvalues ±0.3 eV. At λ=0.50 it produces shifts ±0.15 eV and a 0.30 eV separation, in even/odd superpositions.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: These are selection rules within stated parity eigenstates. They do not say that every energy correction vanishes.

items.label: Degeneracy
items.value: Needs more than one zero entry

check.prompt: An isolated even reference state has an odd perturbation. Which statement is justified without further calculation?
options: Its first energy coefficient is zero
explanations: Correct. Its diagonal odd-operator expectation vanishes by parity.
Coupling to odd states can change higher-order energies.
Opposite-parity couplings can contribute to second order.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why should you inspect the whole degenerate block even when symmetry makes both old diagonal entries zero?
apply.answer: The allowed off-diagonal entries may be the leading effect. Diagonalizing those entries can reveal a first-order splitting that a list of old expectations would miss.

lessons.limits: An inversion-invariant reference problem and states with definite parity. Other symmetries, external fields or boundary conditions can change the selection rules; this is not a general degeneracy-protection theorem.

practice.prompt: A tied even/odd pair has reference energy 6 meV. Use odd perturbation block [[0,2i],[−2i,0]] meV and λ=0.10.
practice.reasoning: Explain why zero old diagonal entries do not mean zero first-order splitting. Enter decimal or scientific-notation numbers, not fractions or expressions. Entry tolerances allow rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: A trial state gives an upper energy bound
lessons.idea: A weighted average cannot fall below the smallest value being averaged.
body: A trial state is a normalized candidate chosen to make a calculation manageable. For a Hamiltonian with a ground energy E₀, its energy expectation cannot be lower than E₀. This is an upper bound on the unknown ground energy: the ground lies at or below the trial result.

For a discrete orthonormal energy basis, write the trial state as a sum of amplitudes cₙ. Its energy is the weighted average Σₙ|cₙ|²Eₙ. The weights are nonnegative and add to one. Since every Eₙ is at least E₀, the average is at least E₀.

The trial state must be allowed by the Hamiltonian’s boundary and domain conditions and have finite energy. More generally a finite-energy state in the associated energy quadratic-form domain can be used. An arbitrary discontinuous function is not automatically a valid trial state for a kinetic-energy operator. The bound is useful even if the chosen family cannot reach the exact ground state.
lessons.terms: H, E_trial,Eₙ,E₀: Hamiltonian, trial expectation, exact energy levels and ground energy (eV in the worked case). The inequality bounds the ground from above; it does not say the trial state is an exact eigenstate. |ψ⟩,cₙ: Normalized trial vector and its exact-energy-basis amplitudes (no unit in this discrete example). Weights |cₙ|² sum to one. The spectral expansion explains the bound even when the exact basis is not available for practical calculation. ≥,Σₙ: At least as large as, and sum over the complete basis (no unit). A Hamiltonian bounded below and valid finite energy are essential assumptions. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Calculate the energy average of an allowed normalized trial state. It lies above or at the true ground energy because it averages energies that are all at least that ground value.

symbols.unit: no unit in this discrete example

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For a simple exact spectrum 1, 3 and 7 eV, choose a trial vector with energy-basis weights 0.50, 0.25 and 0.25.
Its energy expectation is (0.50)(1 eV)+(0.25)(3 eV)+(0.25)(7 eV)=3.00 eV.
This supplies E₀≤3.00 eV. Here we happen to know E₀=1 eV, so the bound is valid but loose; the average 3 eV does not identify the trial as the 3 eV eigenstate.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: An inequality for energy expectations, not a measurement guarantee that every energy outcome equals the average.

check.prompt: For the same spectrum, use weights 0.80, 0.20 and 0. What is the trial bound?
explanations: That reverses the variational inequality.
Correct. The average is 0.8×1+0.2×3=1.4 eV, an upper bound.
An arbitrary trial family need not contain the exact ground state.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If one valid trial gives 4 eV and another gives 3 eV, which is the tighter ground-energy upper bound?
apply.answer: The 3 eV result is tighter. It rules out more possible ground energies above it. Neither result alone supplies a matching lower bound or proves that the associated state has every property of the true ground state.

lessons.limits: A self-adjoint Hamiltonian bounded below and normalized finite-energy trial states satisfying the applicable boundary/form-domain conditions. The displayed sum uses a discrete spectrum; general spectral measures need corresponding care.

lessons.title: Choose a width and calculate its energy cost
lessons.idea: A narrow wave costs kinetic energy; a wide wave can cost potential energy.
body: Consider a particle of mass m on the full line in the confining potential V(x)=E_s(x/a)⁴. The positive length a sets the spatial scale, and E_s=ℏ²/(ma²) sets the energy scale. Choose the normalized trial wave ψ_b(x)=(πb²)^(−1/4)exp[−x²/(2b²)], with a positive width b. The wave has units of inverse square-root length.

This Gaussian has ⟨x²⟩=b²/2 and ⟨x⁴⟩=3b⁴/4. One way to obtain the latter is integration by parts: for I₂ₙ=∫x²ⁿexp(−x²/b²)dx over the full line, I₂ₙ=(2n−1)b²I₂ₙ₋₂/2. Boundary terms vanish because the Gaussian decays. The fourth moment is I₄/I₀, not the square of the second moment.

The kinetic expectation is ℏ²/(4mb²), using the integral of |dψ_b/dx|² times ℏ²/(2m). The potential expectation is 3E_sb⁴/(4a⁴). Write β=b/a to express their sum in dimensionless form. This is a trial energy for a quartic potential, not the harmonic-oscillator energy formula.
lessons.terms: x,a,b,β: Position, fixed length scale, Gaussian width and width ratio (x,a,b in m; β has no unit). The Gaussian probability variance is b²/2; b is not its standard deviation. m,ℏ,E_s,E_trial: Particle mass, reduced Planck constant, energy scale and trial expectation (kg, J·s, J and J). The same formulas can use any consistently converted energy unit. I₂ₙ,n,ψ_b: Full-line even Gaussian integral, nonnegative integer index and normalized trial wave (I₂ₙ has length^(2n+1); ψ_b has m^(-1/2)). The integration-by-parts recurrence is used for n≥1; π is the usual circle constant. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Divide the trial width by the fixed length scale. The first term is kinetic energy, which grows when the width shrinks; the second is quartic potential energy, which grows when the width expands. Their sum times E_s is the trial energy.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Choose a physical mass/length pair giving E_s=0.20 eV. At β=1, the kinetic contribution is 0.25E_s=0.050 eV.
The quartic potential contribution is 0.75E_s=0.150 eV, so E_trial=0.200 eV.
At β=0.50, the kinetic contribution is 1E_s and the potential contribution is 0.046875E_s. The total rises to 1.046875E_s=0.209375 eV: making this trial narrower did not lower its energy.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: A mathematical probability-wave width. The energy contributions are expectations, not separate classical paths or orbit energies.

check.prompt: At β=2 in the same quartic model, what is E_trial/E_s?
explanations: That was the β=1 value.
The potential term uses β to the fourth power.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would b itself be the position standard deviation of this normalized state?
apply.answer: No. Its variance is b²/2, so the standard deviation is b/√2. Stating the precise Gaussian convention prevents a factor-of-√2 mistake when comparing different width definitions.

lessons.limits: Full-line one-dimensional positive quartic potential and a Gaussian finite-energy trial family. E_s and a are linked to the chosen mass; they cannot all be picked independently. The Gaussian is not claimed to solve the quartic eigenvalue equation exactly.

lessons.title: Find the best width within the chosen family
lessons.idea: Optimizing a trial family improves a bound, not the range of shapes in that family.
body: For the quartic model, let F(β)=E_trial/E_s=1/(4β²)+3β⁴/4 for β>0. We can vary β while keeping the physical potential, mass and scale a fixed. Setting the derivative to zero finds a candidate minimum.

The derivative is F′(β)=−1/(2β³)+3β³. Its zero gives β⁶=1/6. The energy grows without bound as β approaches zero or grows without bound, and F″(β)=3/(2β⁴)+9β² is positive for β>0. Thus this stationary point is the global minimum within this one-width family.

The optimized result remains an upper bound on the exact ground energy. It is not an exact answer unless the trial family contains the exact ground state. Another valid family with more adjustable shapes might lower the bound further.
lessons.terms: β,β_*,F: Width ratio, optimizing ratio and energy divided by E_s (no unit). The star marks an optimum, not complex conjugation in this notation. F′,F″: First and second derivatives with respect to β (no unit). The first derivative tests a stationary value; the second and endpoint behavior establish the minimum here. E_min,trial,E_s: Minimum Gaussian trial energy and fixed energy scale (eV or J consistently). Minimum refers to this family, not an assertion that the exact ground energy has been found. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Choose the positive width where the rate of energy change with width is zero. Substitute that width back into the trial energy to obtain the best upper bound in this Gaussian family.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: The positive solution is β_*=6^(−1/6)≈0.74183638.
The minimum energy ratio is (3/8)6^(1/3)≈0.68142022. Its kinetic contribution is about 0.45428015E_s and its potential contribution about 0.22714007E_s.
At E_s=0.20 eV, the upper bound is E₀≤0.13628404 eV. The kinetic contribution is twice the potential contribution at this variational optimum.

visual.title: Find the best width within a Gaussian family
visual.caption: Fixed one-dimensional positive quartic model V(x)=Eₛ(x/a)⁴, with Eₛ=ℏ²/(ma²)=0.20 eV in this illustration. The slider changes only β=b/a for the normalized trial ψ_b=(πb²)^(−1/4) exp[−x²/(2b²)]. The plot shows kinetic ratio 1/(4β²), potential ratio 3β⁴/4 and their total, all divided by Eₛ. The optimum β=6^(−1/6) gives an upper bound, not an exact quartic ground energy. The position standard deviation is b/√2, not b. All plotted widths and energy ratios are unit-free; readout energies are eV. This is a mathematical trial-state comparison, not a time evolution or a physical squeezing process.

check.prompt: Keep this dimensionless model but choose a mass/length pair with E_s=0.40 eV. What happens to the optimized energy bound?
explanations: Correct. The ratio is unchanged, so doubling E_s doubles the energy bound.
The dimensionless ratio stays fixed, but its energy scale doubles.
Both kinetic and positive quartic potential expectations remain nonnegative.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Could you lower the bound by changing E_s while claiming the same physical Hamiltonian?
apply.answer: Not without changing other physical parameters consistently. E_s=ℏ²/(ma²), and the potential coefficient is tied to that scale here. Variational optimization changes the trial state, not the specified mass or potential.

lessons.limits: Positive width, fixed quartic Hamiltonian and the single Gaussian family. The numerical optimum is not a lower bound and does not quantify the unknown gap between trial and exact ground energies.

lessons.title: Let several trial shapes work together
lessons.idea: A small matrix can find the best combination inside a chosen trial space.
body: Choose linearly independent allowed trial shapes and make an orthonormal basis |χ_j⟩ for their span. The span means every linear combination of them. Form the small matrix Hᵣ with entries ⟨χ_j|H|χ_k⟩. Its eigenvectors choose combinations of the trial shapes, and its lowest eigenvalue is the smallest energy expectation in that trial subspace.

This is the Rayleigh–Ritz method. If you enlarge the trial space while keeping every old trial vector available, the smallest trial energy cannot increase: the old best choice is still allowed. Numerical roundoff or an inconsistent Hamiltonian may break that observed trend, but not the exact variational reasoning.

For a self-adjoint Hamiltonian bounded below with the relevant discrete eigenvalues, the ordered finite-subspace eigenvalues provide corresponding upper bounds under the min–max principle. We use that theorem here rather than claiming to prove its full infinite-dimensional form. The lowest-state bound also follows directly from the previous weighted-average argument.
lessons.terms: H,Hᵣ,|χ_j⟩: Full Hamiltonian, trial-space matrix and orthonormal trial basis (Hamiltonians in eV; finite coefficients have no unit). The subscript r labels restriction to the trial space, not a radial coordinate. j,k,c,c†: Trial-basis indices, coefficient column and conjugate-transpose row (no unit). ||c||²=c†c=1 uses the orthonormal-basis convention. E_Ritz,0,E₀,min: Lowest trial-matrix eigenvalue, true ground energy and minimum over normalized coefficients (eV; min is an operation). The matrix is exact for this chosen subspace, not necessarily for the full system. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Calculate the energy matrix among the allowed orthonormal trial shapes. Its lowest eigenvector chooses the combination with the smallest energy expectation in that subspace, giving a ground-energy upper bound.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Suppose two orthonormal trial functions give Hᵣ=[[2,−0.3],[−0.3,5]] eV.
Its eigenvalues are [7±√(9+0.36)]/2 eV, so the lower is approximately 1.97029415 eV.
The single first trial function gave an energy of 2 eV. Allowing its mixture with the second improves the upper bound by about 0.02970585 eV. The exact ground could still lie lower.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: Basis size is an approximation choice, not a physical number of particles or a measured energy resolution.

check.prompt: You enlarge this trial subspace by one new allowed basis function. What must happen to the exact lowest Ritz value?
options: It must become the exact ground energy
explanations: Every old normalized vector is still an available choice.
Correct. The minimum over a larger set is no higher than the old minimum.
A larger finite space still need not contain the exact ground state.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can you use c†c=1 unchanged for nonorthogonal trial shapes?
apply.answer: No. Their overlap matrix S has entries ⟨χ_j|χ_k⟩, so normalization is c†Sc=1 and the matrix equation becomes Hᵣc=ESc. This course’s worked Ritz calculation uses an orthonormal trial basis to keep that distinction explicit.

lessons.limits: Allowed finite-energy orthonormal trial subspace, Hermitian matrix elements and a Hamiltonian bounded below. Ordered excited-state bounds additionally require the stated discrete-spectrum/min–max setting; continuum thresholds and inconsistent basis truncation need care.

lessons.title: An excited-state bound must exclude lower states
lessons.idea: A small ground-state component can pull an average below the excited energy you want.
body: The ground-energy variational bound allows every normalized state. To bound the first excited energy E₁ by a trial expectation, restrict the trial state to be exactly orthogonal to the true ground state. Then the remaining spectral weights involve energies E₁ and above.

For a higher discrete energy E_k, impose orthogonality to all lower exact eigenspaces, not just one chosen vector if a lower energy is degenerate. The energy average then cannot fall below E_k. Knowing only approximate lower states does not automatically give this exact bound.

A parity restriction can provide exact orthogonality when the lower state’s parity is known, but merely drawing a node in a trial function is not sufficient. The condition is an inner product, not the visual appearance of the graph.
lessons.equation: ⟨n|ψ_trial⟩=0 for all lower states n<k ⇒ E_trial≥E_k
lessons.terms: |n⟩,|ψ_trial⟩,n,k: Exact lower energy eigenstates, normalized trial state and ordered labels (no unit in this finite example). All vectors in a lower degenerate eigenspace must be excluded, not just one representative. E_trial,E_k,⟨n|ψ_trial⟩: Trial expectation, desired exact energy and overlap amplitude (energies in eV; overlap has no unit). Zero overlap is exact orthogonality. An approximate lower state needs separate error analysis. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Remove every exact lower-energy component before using a trial energy as an upper bound on the chosen excited level. Then its weighted average only includes that level and higher ones.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Use a finite exact spectrum 0, 2 and 6 eV with basis states |0⟩, |1⟩ and |2⟩. Choose ψ=√0.75|1⟩+0.50|2⟩, which is normalized and orthogonal to |0⟩.
Its energy is (0.75)(2 eV)+(0.25)(6 eV)=3 eV, a valid upper bound on E₁=2 eV.
For contrast, √0.60|0⟩+√0.40|1⟩ has energy 0.80 eV. It cannot bound E₁ from above because it contains a ground-state component.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: Orthogonality is a state-space overlap condition. It is not inferred from a sketch alone.

check.prompt: In that three-level example, a normalized trial is exactly orthogonal to both |0⟩ and |1⟩. What energy must it have?
explanations: The ground component was excluded.
The first excited component was excluded as well.
Correct. Only the final basis direction remains in this complete three-state model.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can a very accurate approximate ground vector automatically be used in place of the exact one for a rigorous excited-state upper bound?
apply.answer: Not automatically. A trial orthogonal to the approximate vector can retain overlap with the true ground state. You need additional certified error information or an appropriate finite-subspace min–max construction, not just an accuracy impression.

lessons.limits: Discrete ordered energies and exact orthogonality to all lower eigenspaces. The worked example is a complete finite model; more general spectral or approximate-orthogonality bounds require extra analysis.

practice.prompt: For exact energies 1,4,9 eV, use a normalized trial orthogonal to the first state, with weights 0.80 and 0.20 on the other two. Separately use the quartic Gaussian optimum at E_s=0.10 eV.

parts.label: Gap between that trial bound and the exact first excited energy
Separate Gaussian quartic upper bound
parts.feedback: Multiply the optimized dimensionless ratio by the stated E_s.

practice.reasoning: State which lower eigenspace was excluded and why the separate Gaussian result is not claimed exact. Enter decimal or scientific-notation numbers, not fractions or expressions. Entry tolerances allow rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: A smooth potential changes the local wavelength
lessons.idea: Where the remaining kinetic energy is smaller, a stationary wave bends more slowly.
body: For a one-dimensional stationary state of energy E, the local kinetic-energy difference is E−V(x). In a classically allowed region this is positive. Define the positive local momentum magnitude p(x)=√[2m(E−V(x))] and the local wave number k(x)=p(x)/ℏ.

A wave number measures phase change per distance, not probability. A locally sinusoidal wave has wavelength λ_w=2π/k. If k changes slowly over a wavelength, adding up k dx gives its leading accumulated phase. The subscript w distinguishes this wavelength from the perturbation control λ used earlier.

The letters WKB name this slowly varying wave approximation. It is not exact for an arbitrary potential. At a turning point E=V, k reaches zero and the usual local-wave formulas need a separate connection treatment.
lessons.terms: x,m,E,V,p,k: Position, mass, fixed energy, potential energy, local momentum magnitude and wave number (m, kg, J, J, kg·m/s and m⁻¹). p is positive in this definition; propagation direction will be carried by the phase sign. ℏ,λ_w,phase: Reduced Planck constant, local wavelength and accumulated phase (J·s, m and rad). Radian is dimensionless in products such as k dx. The integral needs an explicitly chosen reference point for an absolute phase. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Subtract potential energy from the state’s fixed energy, then convert the positive remainder into a local momentum magnitude and wave number. Integrating wave number over distance counts the leading phase change in radians.

symbols.name: Position, mass, fixed energy, potential energy, local momentum magnitude and wave number
symbols.unit: m, kg, J, J, kg·m/s and m⁻¹

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For a convenient scale define E_L=ℏ²/(2ma²), so k=a⁻¹√[(E−V)/E_L]. Choose a consistent mass/length pair with a=2 nm and E_L=0.10 eV.
At E−V=0.40 eV, k=√4/(2 nm)=1 nm⁻¹, giving a local wavelength 2π nm≈6.28319 nm.
If E−V falls to 0.10 eV while the same scales remain, k=0.50 nm⁻¹ and the local wavelength doubles to about 12.5664 nm.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: Local wavelength describes a stationary probability amplitude, not a particle following a wavy path.

check.prompt: At fixed mass, the positive difference E−V is multiplied by nine. How does k change?
explanations: Correct. √9=3.
The momentum and wave number use a square root.
A larger allowed kinetic-energy difference increases the wave number.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can the same real oscillatory k formula be used in a region where V exceeds E?
apply.answer: Not as a real oscillatory wave number. That region has exponential leading solutions, described with a separate positive decay scale. Matching across the boundary matters; it is not correct to discard the wave simply because classical motion is forbidden.

lessons.limits: One-dimensional nonrelativistic stationary scalar potential, positive allowed-region energy difference and smooth slow variation for the WKB phase interpretation. The exact Schrödinger equation remains the reference.

lessons.title: Check whether one wavelength is short enough
lessons.idea: A local-wave approximation needs the medium to change little over the wave’s own scale.
body: The wave number k(x) may be well defined yet change too quickly for a slowly varying approximation. A useful local diagnostic is ε_WKB=|k′(x)|/k(x)². The prime is a derivative with respect to x. This ratio is unit-free: k′ has inverse-length-squared units, as does k².

When the ratio is much less than one over the region of interest, the leading slow-change idea is plausible. It is a local diagnostic, not a universal error theorem. Higher derivatives, boundaries and accumulated effects can also matter.

For a linear potential V=E_L ξ, use ξ=x/a and energy E=4E_L. Then k=√(4−ξ)/a on ξ<4. Differentiation gives ε_WKB=1/[2(4−ξ)^(3/2)]. The ratio grows without bound near ξ=4, exactly where the ordinary WKB amplitude would become singular.
lessons.terms: ε_WKB,k,k′: Slow-variation diagnostic, local wave number and its position derivative (no unit, m⁻¹ and m⁻²). The symbol ≪ means much smaller than, not a strict numerical threshold valid for every problem. ξ,a,E_L: Scaled position x/a, positive length scale and ℏ²/(2ma²) (no unit, m and J). The example potential is linear locally; no bound-state spectrum is being claimed for this whole-line potential. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Compare the change of wave number over distance with the square of the wave number itself. A small ratio means the leading oscillatory description changes slowly on its local scale; a large ratio warns against it.

symbols.description: The symbol ≪ means much smaller than, not a strict numerical threshold valid for every problem.

symbols.name: Scaled position x/a, positive length scale and ℏ²/(2ma²)
symbols.description: The example potential is linear locally; no bound-state spectrum is being claimed for this whole-line potential.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: At ξ=3, it rises to 1/2=0.50, which is not much less than one.
At ξ=3.9 it is about 15.8114. Using the ordinary WKB form arbitrarily close to the turning point would ignore its own warning test.

visual.caption: These samples illustrate a diagnostic in one smooth linear-potential model, not a universal accuracy percentage.

check.prompt: At ξ=2 in this same example, what is ε_WKB approximately?
explanations: That is not the derivative-to-wave-number-squared ratio.
That was the ξ=0 value.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would sampling this diagnostic only at the middle of a barrier justify the approximation everywhere?
apply.answer: No. Inspect the whole relevant region and especially its boundaries and turning points. A locally small value at one point does not control a region containing a failure point.

lessons.limits: A useful leading local criterion for a smooth nonzero wave number. It is not a sufficient general convergence bound; ordinary WKB fails at a simple turning point and needs connection formulas.

lessons.title: A slower wave needs a larger local density to carry the same flux
lessons.idea: The leading amplitude is fixed by current conservation, not chosen independently at every point.
body: Write a one-direction allowed-region WKB wave with positive momentum magnitude p(x). Its phase is plus or minus the integral of p dx divided by ℏ. At leading order a constant stationary current requires the amplitude magnitude to vary as 1/√p.

A simple way to express this without hiding units is to compare with a reference point x₀: A(x)=A(x₀)√[p(x₀)/p(x)]. Here A is the amplitude magnitude and A² is local probability density. The current for the positive-phase branch is j=pA²/m; the negative-phase branch has the opposite sign.

Thus decreasing p by a factor of four increases the amplitude by two and the density by four. The local speed p/m decreases by four, leaving the flux unchanged. A superposition of both directions needs coherent amplitudes; do not add their pointwise densities as if all interference had vanished.
lessons.terms: x,x₀,s,p,m: Position, reference point, integration variable, positive local momentum and mass (positions in m; p in kg·m/s; m in kg). s is a dummy position coordinate inside this integral, not the unit second. A,ψ_±,j_±: Amplitude magnitude, leading wave and signed one-dimensional current (m^(-1/2), m^(-1/2) and s⁻¹). A² is density per length. These stationary local amplitudes need not by themselves form a normalizable full-line scattering state. ℏ,i,exp: Reduced Planck constant, imaginary unit and exponential (J·s; i and phase factor have no unit). The exponent is dimensionless, and the two signs label opposite propagation branches. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Keep the product of local speed and local density fixed for a one-direction stationary branch. The amplitude scales with the square root of the inverse momentum, while the phase sign selects current direction.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Suppose p(x₀)=4p_ref for a positive momentum scale p_ref, while p(x)=p_ref. Let the reference density be A(x₀)²=0.10 nm⁻¹.
The amplitude ratio is √4=2, so the new density is 4×0.10 nm⁻¹=0.40 nm⁻¹.
The products pA² are equal: 4p_ref×0.10 nm⁻¹ and p_ref×0.40 nm⁻¹. Dividing either by the same mass gives the same positive branch current.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: Current is probability flow in a stationary wave description, not a literal collection of slowing particle trajectories.

check.prompt: If the positive momentum instead rises by a factor of nine, how does the leading amplitude magnitude change?
explanations: That reverses the constant-current scaling.
That is the density factor, not the amplitude factor.
Correct. A scales as p^(−1/2), so the factor is 1/√9.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why does the ordinary expression become a problem as p tends to zero?
apply.answer: It predicts an unbounded amplitude while the slow-variation condition also fails. The true local Schrödinger solution at a simple smooth turning point stays finite; a separate turning-point solution connects the branches.

lessons.limits: Leading one-direction WKB current in a smooth allowed region with nonzero p. Relative phases and boundary conditions must be retained for superpositions; the formula is not uniformly valid at turning points.

lessons.title: An exponential is controlled by an accumulated decay scale
lessons.idea: A short forbidden interval and a long forbidden interval need not suppress a wave by the same amount.
body: Where V(x)>E, define a positive forbidden-region momentum scale χ(x)=√[2m(V(x)−E)]. It is a decay scale, not a real classical momentum in that forbidden region. The leading decaying WKB solution includes exp[−S(x)/ℏ], where S is the integral of χ over distance.

The full leading expression also contains the prefactor 1/√χ. If χ changes between two endpoints, include the square-root prefactor ratio rather than using only the exponential. The accumulated S has units of action, J·s; S/ℏ is dimensionless.

A decaying density ratio is not automatically the transmission probability through a complete barrier. Incident/reflected branches, both boundaries and current normalization must be matched. This lesson first isolates what happens within one forbidden segment.
lessons.equation: χ=√[2m(V−E)];  S=∫χ dx;  ψ_dec(x₂)/ψ_dec(x₁)≈√[χ(x₁)/χ(x₂)] exp[−∫_(x₁)^(x₂)χ dx/ℏ]
lessons.terms: χ,V,E,m: Positive forbidden decay momentum, potential, fixed energy and mass (kg·m/s, J, J and kg). χ is real and positive where V exceeds E; it is not a measured imaginary momentum. S,ℏ,x₁,x₂: Accumulated action, Planck scale and ordered segment endpoints (J·s, J·s and m). The ratio formula follows one decaying branch between endpoints with χ>0. ψ_dec,exp: Decaying leading amplitude and exponential (m^(-1/2) and a unit-free operation). The density ratio is the magnitude square of the amplitude ratio, not automatically a flux transmission. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Add up the positive decay momentum along the forbidden segment and divide by ℏ. Its negative exponential suppresses the amplitude, with a square-root prefactor if the decay scale varies.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Inside a constant forbidden segment, let κ=χ/ℏ=2 nm⁻¹ and x₂−x₁=1 nm. The prefactor ratio is one and S/ℏ=2.
The amplitude ratio is e⁻²≈0.135335; the density ratio is e⁻⁴≈0.0183156.
For a 2 nm segment at the same κ, the amplitude ratio becomes e⁻⁴≈0.0183156 and the density ratio e⁻⁸≈0.000335463. Matching the complete barrier is still a separate calculation.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: The constant-segment exponential is exact inside that segment. Abrupt external interfaces do not satisfy smooth-turning WKB assumptions.

check.prompt: For a constant forbidden segment with κL=3, what is the decaying density ratio?
explanations: Correct. Squaring e⁻³ gives e⁻⁶≈0.00247875.
That is the amplitude ratio.
An accumulated decay exponent is not itself a probability ratio.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: May you report e^(−2S/ℏ) as an exact transmission for any barrier shape?
apply.answer: No. That expression describes a leading opaque-barrier estimate only under further matching and smoothness conditions. Exact rectangular-barrier transmission includes interface factors; near a barrier top even the leading smooth-barrier approximation needs revision.

lessons.limits: One-dimensional forbidden region with χ>0. The prefactor/exponential form is leading WKB for slow variation; the chosen constant segment is locally exact but does not solve its external matching problem.

lessons.title: Use a different local solution where the wave changes character
lessons.idea: A turning point joins an oscillatory region to a decaying region; neither ordinary WKB branch works right at the join.
body: Take a simple right-hand turning point x_t where V(x_t)=E and the slope F=V′(x_t) is positive and nonzero. Nearby, replace V−E by F(x−x_t). Define the length ℓ=[ℏ²/(2mF)]^(1/3) and scaled position z=(x−x_t)/ℓ. The local Schrödinger equation becomes d²ψ/dz²=zψ.

This is the Airy equation. Its solution Ai(z) is defined as the real solution that decays for large positive z, with a conventional overall scale. We supply its leading large-distance asymptotics: for z≫1, Ai(z)≈z^(−1/4)exp[−2z^(3/2)/3]/(2√π); for u=−z≫1, Ai(−u)≈u^(−1/4)sin[2u^(3/2)/3+π/4]/√π. These are supplied asymptotic facts, not a derivation of the full special function.

Matching these forms to the WKB expressions gives a useful connection: a decaying forbidden coefficient C connects to an allowed sine coefficient 2C and a phase offset π/4. The Airy solution is finite through the turning point even though each ordinary WKB amplitude becomes singular there. Only match in an overlap region where both the local linear potential and the asymptotic form are adequate.
lessons.terms: x_t,F,m,ℓ,z: Turning point, positive potential slope, mass, local length and scaled position (m, J/m, kg, m and no unit). The prime on V is a position derivative; the double prime on ψ in the Airy equation is with respect to z. ψ,Ai,u,π: Wave, conventional decaying Airy solution, positive −z and circle constant (ψ has m^(-1/2); Ai,u,π are dimensionless before an overall physical wave scale). Ai is defined by its equation and decaying normalization convention; the listed formulas require large positive arguments. p,χ,S,C: Allowed momentum, forbidden decay momentum, forbidden action and matching coefficient (kg·m/s, kg·m/s, J·s and (kg/s)^(1/2)). The coefficient units follow from ψ=C/√momentum. S is measured from the turning point into the forbidden region; the allowed integral runs back to x_t. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: The turning-point slope sets a small length scale. Rescaling by that length gives a standard local differential equation. Its supplied asymptotics connect a decaying branch to an oscillating sine with a doubled coefficient and a quarter-π phase offset.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Let E_L=ℏ²/(2ma²), choose a=4 nm and a local slope F=8E_L/a. Then ℓ=(a³/8)^(1/3)=a/2=2 nm.

A point 8 nm to the right has z=4; a point 8 nm to the left has z=−4. The sign tells us which local branch is decaying or oscillatory; |z|=4 by itself is not a precision guarantee for a leading asymptotic formula.
If the forbidden WKB coefficient is C, the matched allowed sine coefficient is 2C, not C. The phase offset is π/4=45°. These factors follow from comparing the supplied asymptotic normalizations.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: A simple linearized turning point. The special-function asymptotics are supplied with their domain, not presented as an exact formula at z=0.

check.prompt: Keep m fixed but multiply the positive turning-point slope F by eight. How does ℓ change?
explanations: ℓ varies as F to the power −1/3.
The cube-root and inverse dependence both matter.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can this connection be applied unchanged at a flat barrier top where V′=0?
apply.answer: No. That point is not a simple nonzero-slope turning point, and two nearby turning points can merge. The linear Airy construction and separate-connection assumption break down; a different local approximation is required.

lessons.limits: Smooth isolated simple turning point, nonzero slope and a matching overlap region. The Airy equation follows from linearization; its leading asymptotics are supplied. Multiple/merged turning points, sharp discontinuities and rigorous uniform error bounds are outside this step.

lessons.title: Two smooth turning points select allowed phases
lessons.idea: A wave that decays on both sides can fit only particular accumulated phases between them.
body: Consider a bound state between two isolated smooth simple turning points x_L<x_R, with a decaying wave outside. Each Airy connection contributes a quarter-π phase shift. Requiring the two allowed-region descriptions to represent the same standing wave gives ∫_(x_L)^(x_R)p dx=(n+1/2)πℏ, with n=0,1,2,… .

The half comes from the two smooth connections, not from a rule for every boundary. An infinite hard wall has a different boundary condition; you must not attach this formula blindly to a hard-wall box.

For a harmonic potential V=mω²x²/2, the action integral is πE/ω. It can be evaluated as the area of a half ellipse in the x–p plane, or by a sine substitution. The condition therefore gives E=(n+1/2)ℏω. It happens to reproduce the exact harmonic energies, even though the ordinary WKB wave shape still fails locally at its turning points.
lessons.terms: x_L,x_R,p,ℏ: Left/right turning positions, positive local momentum and Planck action scale (m, m, kg·m/s and J·s). The integral is over one traversal between turning points, not the full closed classical orbit. n,Eₙ,m,ω,V: Nonnegative integer level label, energy, mass, angular frequency and potential (no unit, J, kg, rad/s and J). The harmonic example uses ω>0. Its oscillator length is a_osc=√[ℏ/(mω)]. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Add the allowed-region momentum over the full interval between the two smooth turning points. Matching decaying waves on both sides permits half-integer multiples of πℏ; for this harmonic potential that gives the familiar level spacing.
