example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Take ℏω=0.080 eV and n=2. The two-turning condition gives E₂=2.5×0.080 eV=0.200 eV.
The action is πE₂/ω=2.5πℏ, so the dimensionless action divided by ℏ is about 7.85398.
If a_osc=1.20 nm, the turning positions are ±√(2n+1)a_osc=±√5×1.20 nm≈±2.68328 nm. The state does not end sharply at those positions; the exterior wave decays.

check.prompt: With the same ℏω=0.080 eV, what energy does this condition give for n=3?
explanations: The smooth-turning condition includes the half term.
That would omit the correct level label/half combination.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why is the harmonic energy agreement not evidence that every ground-state WKB result is exact?
apply.answer: The harmonic oscillator is a special case. In other potentials the leading action condition has corrections, and low states need not have a broadly slow-varying region. Check assumptions and a reference rather than generalizing one successful model.

lessons.limits: Two separated smooth simple turning points, a scalar one-dimensional bound problem and leading semiclassical matching. Hard walls, singular potentials or merged turning points need different conditions; harmonic energy exactness is special.

lessons.title: A large forbidden action makes a useful leading estimate
lessons.idea: The exponential can dominate an opaque smooth barrier, but it does not excuse checking its boundaries.
body: For a smooth barrier with two separated simple turning points and a sufficiently large forbidden action S, leading WKB gives T≈exp(−2S/ℏ). Here T is the transmitted-to-incident current ratio after matching the branches, not merely a density ratio at arbitrary positions.

The approximation requires S/ℏ≫1 for an opaque barrier and valid smooth-region/matching conditions. The leading exponential does not supply every prefactor or correction. Near the barrier top the turning points approach each other and S becomes small, so separate Airy matching and the opaque estimate fail together.

For an illustrative parabolic barrier shape V(x)=V₀−mω_b²x²/2 between its turning points, let D=V₀−E>0. The forbidden momentum traces a half ellipse and its action is S=πD/ω_b. We use that local shape to calculate the exponent; outside-region and full-barrier details require their own specification.
lessons.terms: S,ℏ,T_lead: Forbidden action, reduced Planck constant and leading current transmission estimate (J·s, J·s and no unit). T_lead is not an exact formula for arbitrary barriers. Large S/ℏ is part of its regime. V,V₀,E,D,m,ω_b: Potential, barrier top, state energy, positive top deficit, mass and positive curvature frequency (energies in J, mass in kg, ω_b in rad/s). ω_b labels barrier curvature, not a bound-oscillation frequency at this unstable maximum. x_L,x_R: Two simple turning points enclosing the forbidden interval (m). They must remain separated enough for the chosen local matching construction. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Integrate the positive decay momentum across the forbidden interval, divide by ℏ and double it for the leading transmitted probability exponent. Trust this as an opaque smooth-barrier estimate only when the action and matching tests pass.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For the parabolic segment choose D=0.060 eV and ℏω_b=0.040 eV. Then S/ℏ=πD/(ℏω_b)=1.5π≈4.71239.
The leading opaque-barrier estimate is e^(−3π)≈0.0000806995. This is about 0.00807%, not an amplitude.
If the deficit rises to 0.080 eV while ℏω_b stays fixed, S/ℏ=2π and T_lead≈e^(−4π)≈0.00000348734. These are leading estimates, not certified relative-error bounds.

Its required large-action condition is disappearing, so that extrapolation is unjustified.
Approaching a barrier top does not imply a negative energy.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: How would you check a WKB prediction for an unfamiliar smooth finite barrier?
apply.answer: State the incident/outgoing normalization, solve the stationary boundary problem or evolve a suitably narrow packet, check current balance, and refine the numerical resolution. Compare the estimate only where both descriptions refer to the same potential and incident energy.

lessons.limits: One-dimensional smooth opaque barrier, separated simple turning points and elastic current matching. Leading exponential accuracy is not uniform near the top or at sharp interfaces. The parabolic action is exact for that specified segment; the transmission expression remains the stated leading estimate.

lessons.title: Keep the first small relativistic correction
lessons.idea: At low momentum, the usual kinetic energy is nearly right; the first correction makes it slightly smaller.
body: At low momentum, the usual kinetic energy is nearly right; the first correction makes it slightly smaller.

Write the small number x=p/(mc). Expanding √(1+x²) around x=0 gives 1+x²/2−x⁴/8 plus terms beginning at x⁶. The symbol O(x⁶) means the omitted error is bounded by a constant times |x|⁶ sufficiently near zero; it is not a measured error bar. Subtract the rest energy mc² to obtain the kinetic expression below.

For a bound electron, p is an operator. The supplied first perturbation is Hₖ=−p⁴/(8m³c²), and its first-order energy change is its expectation in an unperturbed state. This expansion is not a globally valid Hamiltonian for arbitrarily large momenta: its negative p⁴ term would eventually dominate.
lessons.terms: p, m, c: momentum magnitude, electron mass, light speed (kg·m/s; kg; m/s). For the operator formula p⁴=(p²)². x: small momentum ratio (1). x=p/(mc); use |x|≪1. T, Hₖ: kinetic energy and first correction (J). The correction is negative. Atomic convention: one electron of mass m and charge −e, e>0, bound to an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge +e. Set C₀=e²/(4πε₀)=αℏc, α dimensionless, a=ℏ/(mcα), and K₀=mc²α⁴ (an energy). c is light speed; ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. No reduced-mass substitution is made in these effective correction laws. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Take x=0.2. The leading kinetic energy is 0.02 mc², and the correction is −0.0002 mc².
Their sum is 0.0198 mc². The exact square root gives 0.0198039 mc², so the retained approximation is slightly low.
The small error here tests this chosen input, not all momentum distributions.

lessons.title: Include the spherical measure in a radial average
lessons.idea: A radial average counts spherical shells, not just distances along a line.
body: A radial average counts spherical shells, not just distances along a line.

Use ψ=R(r)Y(θ,φ), with angular normalization ∫|Y|²dΩ=1. Then ⟨r⁻ᵏ⟩=∫₀∞r²|R(r)|²r⁻ᵏdr. The factor r² is the shell measure. For the supplied states R₁₀=2a⁻³ᐟ²e^(−r/a) and R₂₁=(r/a)e^(−r/(2a))/(2√6 a³ᐟ²), put u=r/a to make the integral dimensionless.

The elementary integral ∫₀∞uⁿe^(−λu)du=n!/λⁿ⁺¹ follows by repeated integration by parts for integer n≥0 and λ>0; n! multiplies 1 through n, with 0!=1. It normalizes these states and evaluates their finite moments. For an s state whose R(0) is nonzero, the r⁻³ average contains a 1/r divergence at zero. Do not assign it a finite value by deleting the origin.
lessons.terms: r, a: radius and Coulomb length (m). a is positive; r runs from zero to infinity. R, Y: radial and angular wave factors (m⁻³ᐟ²; 1). Angular measure dΩ=sin θ dθ dφ. k, u, λ, n: moment power and integration variables (1). Here k denotes the inverse-radius power, not a wave number. Atomic convention: one electron of mass m and charge −e, e>0, bound to an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge +e. Set C₀=e²/(4πε₀)=αℏc, α dimensionless, a=ℏ/(mcα), and K₀=mc²α⁴ (an energy). c is light speed; ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. No reduced-mass substitution is made in these effective correction laws. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: For 2p, r²|R₂₁|²dr=u⁴e⁻ᵘdu/24. Its normalization is 4!/24=1.
Multiplying by r⁻³ leaves a⁻³u e⁻ᵘdu/24, so the average is 1/(24a³).
For 1s, the same procedure gives ⟨r⁻¹⟩=1/a and ⟨r⁻²⟩=2/a². These are different averages, not powers of one average.

It becomes one half as large

An inverse cube scales by 2⁻³.
That scaling belongs to an inverse first power.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Why can the 2p inverse-cube average converge while the 1s one diverges?
apply.answer: R₂₁ vanishes linearly at the origin, adding two powers of r to its density; R₁₀ does not. The shell measure must still be included.

lessons.limits: Only the supplied normalized low states and convergent moments are evaluated. Singular products outside their domains cannot be justified by a finite numerical grid.

lessons.title: Combine angular and radial spin-orbit factors
lessons.idea: The spin-orbit correction connects orbital angular momentum with spin, and its sign depends on their combined state.
body: The spin-orbit correction connects orbital angular momentum with spin, and its sign depends on their combined state.

Use the supplied effective law Hso=[(1/r)dV/dr] L·S/(2m²c²). Its factor 1/2 includes the Thomas correction; this lesson applies that law rather than deriving relativistic spin dynamics. For V=−C₀/r, it becomes C₀ L·S/(2m²c²r³).

For electron spin s=1/2, L·S has value ℏ²[j(j+1)−l(l+1)−3/4]/2. Here j labels total angular momentum and l labels orbital angular momentum. Multiply this angular value by the radial average. Use this separated inverse-cube formula only for l>0; an s state has zero orbital angular momentum, not an instruction to multiply zero by a divergent radial integral.
lessons.terms: l, s, j: orbital, spin and total angular labels (1). s=1/2; for l=1, j can be 1/2 or 3/2. L, S: angular momentum operators (J·s). Their dot product has units (J·s)². ΔEso: first spin-orbit shift (J). The radial and angular factors are evaluated in the unperturbed state. Atomic convention: one electron of mass m and charge −e, e>0, bound to an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge +e. Set C₀=e²/(4πε₀)=αℏc, α dimensionless, a=ℏ/(mcα), and K₀=mc²α⁴ (an energy). c is light speed; ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. No reduced-mass substitution is made in these effective correction laws. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

The positive shift refers to this j value; the other angular combination has the opposite sign.

lessons.title: Use a contact term by its integration rule
lessons.idea: A contact correction samples the density at one point; it is not an ordinary infinitely tall potential value.
body: A contact correction samples the density at one point; it is not an ordinary infinitely tall potential value.

The three-dimensional delta δ³(r) is defined by ∫δ³(r)f(r)d³r=f(0) for a suitable smooth test function. It has units m⁻³. For the point Coulomb potential, the distributional identity ∇²(−C₀/r)=4πC₀δ³(r) supplies the contact term.

Take the effective Darwin law HD=ℏ²∇²V/(8m²c²) as given. Its expectation is [πC₀ℏ²/(2m²c²)]|ψ(0)|². A continuous s-state density can be nonzero there; the delta measure evaluates its value even though a Coulomb state has a cusp. The supplied 2p wavefunction vanishes at the origin, so its contact shift is zero. No divergent inverse-cube s-state average is used.
lessons.terms: δ³(r): three-dimensional delta distribution (m⁻³). Its meaning is the stated integration rule. ∇²V: Laplacian of potential energy (J/m²). For a point source it is interpreted as a distribution. |ψ(0)|², ΔED: origin density and contact shift (m⁻³; J). The contact coefficient has units J·m³. Atomic convention: one electron of mass m and charge −e, e>0, bound to an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge +e. Set C₀=e²/(4πε₀)=αℏc, α dimensionless, a=ℏ/(mcα), and K₀=mc²α⁴ (an energy). c is light speed; ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. No reduced-mass substitution is made in these effective correction laws. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: For 1s, the origin density is 1/(πa³). The coefficient then gives ΔED=K₀/2.
With K₀=1.45 meV, the shift is +0.725 meV. It raises the level relative to the uncorrected value.
For 2s the origin density is one eighth as large, giving K₀/16=0.090625 meV at the same scale.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: If a normalized smooth density at the origin doubles, what happens to this contact expectation?
apply.answer: It doubles because the integration rule makes the expectation proportional to that density.

lessons.limits: This is a stated effective nonrelativistic correction, not a derivation of Dirac theory or finite-nucleus physics. Only well-defined contact expectations are used.

lessons.title: Add the three corrections with one mass convention
lessons.idea: Small corrections must be added using the same unperturbed atom, units and mass convention.
body: Small corrections must be added using the same unperturbed atom, units and mass convention.

For this fixed-nucleus model, the kinetic expectation is ΔEk=K₀[3−4n/(l+1/2)]/(8n⁴). It follows from p²ψ=2m(Eₙ−V)ψ and the quadratic-form value ‖p²ψ‖²=4m²⟨(Eₙ−V)²⟩ on these states, not from claiming p and V commute. The notation ‖u‖² means the inner product ⟨u|u⟩, the squared length of u. The norm-squared form is finite here; this does not assert that a Coulomb cusp state lies in the full p⁴ operator domain. Here Eₙ=−mc²α²/(2n²). The radial moments provide the finite averages.

Adding kinetic, spin-orbit and contact terms gives ΔEfs=−K₀[n/(j+1/2)−3/4]/(2n⁴). This combines only the supplied leading effective terms. The equal 2s₁/₂ and 2p₁/₂ corrections in this model are not a prediction that all real hydrogen effects leave them exactly equal.
lessons.terms: n, l, j: principal, orbital and total angular labels (1). n is a positive integer; the allowed l,j values belong to that level. ΔEk, ΔEfs, Eₙ: kinetic correction, combined correction and base energy (J). All use electron mass m with an infinitely heavy nucleus. K₀: fine-structure energy scale (J). K₀=mc²α⁴; 1.45 meV is a rounded arithmetic scale here. Atomic convention: one electron of mass m and charge −e, e>0, bound to an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge +e. Set C₀=e²/(4πε₀)=αℏc, α dimensionless, a=ℏ/(mcα), and K₀=mc²α⁴ (an energy). c is light speed; ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. No reduced-mass substitution is made in these effective correction laws. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: For 2s₁/₂: kinetic −13K₀/128, spin-orbit zero, contact +K₀/16. The sum is −5K₀/128.
For 2p₁/₂: kinetic −7K₀/384 and spin-orbit −K₀/48 sum to the same −5K₀/128. For 2p₃/₂ the sum is −K₀/128.
The 2p splitting is therefore K₀/32. At K₀=1.45 meV, it is 0.0453125 meV, with j=3/2 higher.

lessons.title: Project the magnetic moment onto total angular momentum
lessons.idea: In a sufficiently weak magnetic field, the atom’s spin and orbital motion stay coupled into a useful total j label.
body: In a sufficiently weak magnetic field, the atom’s spin and orbital motion stay coupled into a useful total j label.

For an electron, the magnetic energy is +(μB B/ℏ)(Lz+2Sz), using spin factor 2 in this model. μB=eℏ/(2m)>0; the plus sign comes from the electron’s negative charge and energy −μ·B. Projection within an isolated j multiplet gives ⟨Sz⟩/ℏ=mⱼ[j(j+1)+s(s+1)−l(l+1)]/[2j(j+1)]. Adding ⟨Jz⟩ gives the Landé factor below.

Take B along +z. The field energy scale μB|B| must be much smaller than the separation to the other coupled j multiplet, and other neglected effects must remain small. This permits first-order shifts within one multiplet; it is not a formula to extend blindly to strong fields.
lessons.terms: μB, B: positive Bohr magneton and signed z field (eV/T; T). Use rounded μB=5.788×10⁻⁵ eV/T for arithmetic. gⱼ, mⱼ, l, s, j: magnetic factor and angular labels (1). s=1/2; j>0 here; Jz has value ℏmⱼ. ΔEZ: weak-field shift (eV). Signs depend on B and mⱼ. Atomic convention: one electron of mass m and charge −e, e>0, bound to an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge +e. Set C₀=e²/(4πε₀)=αℏc, α dimensionless, a=ℏ/(mcα), and K₀=mc²α⁴ (an energy). c is light speed; ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. No reduced-mass substitution is made in these effective correction laws. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

steps: For l=1,s=1/2,j=3/2, the formula gives gⱼ=4/3.
With B=0.01 T and mⱼ=3/2, ΔEZ=2μB B=1.1576×10⁻⁶ eV.
The field scale 5.788×10⁻⁷ eV is small compared with a 4.53125×10⁻⁵ eV fine-structure gap, so this example has a useful weak-field hierarchy.

lessons.title: Use separate orbital and spin labels in the opposite limit
lessons.idea: When magnetic splitting dominates spin-orbit coupling, separate orbital and spin projections become more useful than j.
body: When magnetic splitting dominates spin-orbit coupling, separate orbital and spin projections become more useful than j.

Keep the same electron-charge convention, but use the product basis |l,mₗ⟩|s,mₛ⟩. The leading magnetic shift is μB B(mₗ+2mₛ). The spin-orbit term is now a smaller correction; strong here means strong relative to that coupling, not unlimited field strength.

At the same time, magnetic shifts and diamagnetic effects must not disrupt the assumed radial level model. A hierarchy can exist between fine splitting and much larger radial gaps. Check both sides rather than calling any large numerical B safe.
lessons.terms: mₗ, mₛ: orbital and spin z-projection labels (1). For l=1, mₗ=−1,0,1; mₛ=±1/2. μB, B: positive magnetic scale and signed field (eV/T; T). Use μB=5.788×10⁻⁵ eV/T. ΔEZ: leading decoupled magnetic shift (eV). Residual spin-orbit and quadratic magnetic terms are not included. Atomic convention: one electron of mass m and charge −e, e>0, bound to an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge +e. Set C₀=e²/(4πε₀)=αℏc, α dimensionless, a=ℏ/(mcα), and K₀=mc²α⁴ (an energy). c is light speed; ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. No reduced-mass substitution is made in these effective correction laws. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: At B=20 T, μB B=0.0011576 eV. For mₗ=1,mₛ=−1/2, the leading magnetic shift is zero.
That cancellation does not remove spin-orbit or diamagnetic corrections. For mₗ=0,mₛ=+1/2, the leading shift is +0.0011576 eV.
This scale is about 25.55 times the illustrative 4.53125×10⁻⁵ eV fine gap and still far below an eV-scale radial gap; neglected quadratic terms require their own check.

explanations: The electron convention already fixes the sign in the displayed formula.
The projection sum is −2.
Only opposite orbital and spin contributions canceled in the earlier case.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Is this formula a justification for taking B to infinity in the atom?
apply.answer: No. Eventually radial mixing, quadratic magnetic terms and other neglected physics invalidate this fixed-radial-state model.

lessons.limits: Decoupled angular limit with a separately checked radial hierarchy. No universal field boundary or precision high-field atomic spectrum.

lessons.title: Diagonalize the small block between the limits
lessons.idea: Between weak and strong fields, solve the small coupled matrix instead of choosing one limiting label too early.
body: Between weak and strong fields, solve the small coupled matrix instead of choosing one limiting label too early.

Fix l=1,s=1/2 and total projection M=1/2. Use the ordered basis |mₗ=0,mₛ=+1/2⟩ and |mₗ=1,mₛ=−1/2⟩. Write the radial-averaged spin-orbit law as ζ L·S/ℏ² and β=μB B. Angular ladder elements give the real off-diagonal ζ/√2; the diagonal entries are β and −ζ/2.

The two eigenvalues are the matrix mean plus or minus a positive square root. At β=0 they are ζ/2 and −ζ, the two j limits. At large positive β, the eigenvectors approach separate projection states. The mixing changes smoothly; an intermediate field is not exactly either limiting basis.
lessons.terms: ζ, β: spin-orbit coefficient and magnetic energy (μeV in the example). ζ>0; β=μB B may have either sign. H, E±: two-state matrix and ordered energies (μeV). The zero of energy excludes the common radial energy. M: fixed total projection (1). M=mₗ+mₛ=1/2; this block does not contain every atomic state. Atomic convention: one electron of mass m and charge −e, e>0, bound to an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge +e. Set C₀=e²/(4πε₀)=αℏc, α dimensionless, a=ℏ/(mcα), and K₀=mc²α⁴ (an energy). c is light speed; ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. No reduced-mass substitution is made in these effective correction laws. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Choose a finite illustrative block with ζ=2 μeV and β=3 μeV; these are chosen parameters, not fitted hydrogen data.
Its eigenvalues are 1±√6 μeV, approximately 3.44949 and −1.44949 μeV. Their sum is 2 μeV, matching the matrix trace.
At β=0 the same model has energies +1 and −2 μeV, so simply adding one limiting formula would miss the crossover.

check.prompt: For ζ=2 μeV and β=0, what is the level separation?
explanations: Subtract −2 from +1.
The nonzero off-diagonal coupling prevents equality here.
That is only the upper eigenvalue relative to the chosen zero.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Can an eigenvalue crossing be inferred merely because the two diagonal entries become equal?
apply.answer: No. Nonzero off-diagonal coupling splits the eigenvalues; equal diagonal entries can instead mean strongest mixing.

lessons.limits: One fixed-M block within a fixed radial/l model. This finite diagonalization does not include all atom states or neglected field corrections.

lessons.title: Let parity remove the first-order electric shift
lessons.idea: An isolated state with definite parity has no average position along z, so its first electric shift vanishes.
body: An isolated state with definite parity has no average position along z, so its first electric shift vanishes.

Parity reverses position. z changes sign, whereas the density of a definite-parity state does not; the integral for ⟨z⟩ therefore cancels. With electron charge −e and electric field ℰ along +z, scalar potential is −ℰz and the perturbation is +eℰz. The first-order shift is zero, not every order.

In a bounded two-state model, let an opposite-parity excited state lie D above the lower state and let v=eℰz₀₁ be their real coupling. The lower second-order shift is −v²/D. Writing it as −αpolℰ²/2 defines a positive polarizability αpol=2e²|z₀₁|²/D in this model. This single retained state is not the complete hydrogen polarizability.
lessons.terms: ℰ, z₀₁: electric field and dipole-position matrix element (V/m; m). The perturbation is +eℰz for an electron. D, v, ΔE: positive gap, coupling and shift (meV in the example). Require |v|≪D for the second-order estimate. αpol: two-state polarizability (C²·m²/J). It converts squared field into energy. Atomic convention: one electron of mass m and charge −e, e>0, bound to an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge +e. Set C₀=e²/(4πε₀)=αℏc, α dimensionless, a=ℏ/(mcα), and K₀=mc²α⁴ (an energy). c is light speed; ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. No reduced-mass substitution is made in these effective correction laws. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Take D=4 meV and v=0.2 meV. Then ΔE₂=−0.01 meV.
The exact lower eigenvalue of [[0,v],[v,D]] is (D−√(D²+4v²))/2=−0.00997512 meV.
The small difference checks this chosen perturbative ratio |v|/D=0.05.

check.prompt: If the field doubles with D fixed, what is the second-order estimate?
explanations: The retained excited-state denominator gives a negative lower-level shift.
v doubles and v² becomes four times larger.
That would be a linear response.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: What fails if the opposite-parity state is degenerate with the first?
apply.answer: The denominator D vanishes. Diagonalize the degenerate subspace rather than using this nondegenerate second-order expression.

lessons.limits: Isolated definite-parity state, two-state truncation and small coupling. No continuum sum or exact atomic polarizability is claimed.

lessons.title: Mix opposite parities inside a degenerate pair
lessons.idea: Opposite-parity states can mix at first order when their unperturbed energies are the same.
body: Opposite-parity states can mix at first order when their unperturbed energies are the same.

For the ideal Coulomb n=2 pair, choose real phases R₂₀=(2−r/a)e^(−r/(2a))/(2√2 a³ᐟ²), R₂₁=(r/a)e^(−r/(2a))/(2√6 a³ᐟ²), Y₀₀=1/√(4π), and Y₁₀=√(3/(4π))cos θ. Then z=r cos θ. The angular integral is 1/√3 and the radial integral ∫r³R₂₀R₂₁dr is −3√3a, so ⟨2s|z|2p₀⟩=−3a.

The diagonal dipole elements still vanish by parity. In the ordered pair (2s,2p₀), the perturbation matrix has off-diagonal −3eaℰ and zero diagonal, giving shifts ±3eaℰ as a set. The lower state for positive ℰ is the equal plus combination in this phase convention. Changing a basis state’s sign changes matrix signs but not the two energies.
lessons.terms: R₂₀, R₂₁, Y₀₀, Y₁₀: chosen radial and angular factors (m⁻³ᐟ²; angular factors dimensionless). The phases are fixed explicitly for the sign of the off-diagonal element. ℰ, a, e: field, Coulomb length and positive charge magnitude (V/m; m; C). eaℰ is an energy. ΔE: pair energy shifts (meV in the example). Both energies are measured from the common n=2 level. Atomic convention: one electron of mass m and charge −e, e>0, bound to an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge +e. Set C₀=e²/(4πε₀)=αℏc, α dimensionless, a=ℏ/(mcα), and K₀=mc²α⁴ (an energy). c is light speed; ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. No reduced-mass substitution is made in these effective correction laws. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: The radial factor uses u=r/a: (1/(8√3))∫u⁴(2−u)e⁻ᵘdu times a. Since 2·4!−5!=−72, it is −3√3a.
With eaℰ=0.004 meV, the two shifts are −0.012 and +0.012 meV.
Their separation is 0.024 meV; it scales with field magnitude rather than field squared in this degenerate model.

explanations: The upper-minus-lower gap is 6eaℰ.
That is one shift’s magnitude, not the separation.
The gap changes when the field changes.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Why should this ideal result not be used automatically at arbitrarily tiny fields in real hydrogen?
apply.answer: Fine structure and other splittings can remove the assumed degeneracy. The degenerate-pair model requires its coupling to dominate the omitted pair splitting while staying small compared with other relevant gaps.

lessons.title: Separate canonical momentum from motion momentum
lessons.idea: The momentum written as a derivative is not always the momentum associated with motion in a magnetic field.
body: The momentum written as a derivative is not always the momentum associated with motion in a magnetic field.

Introduce a scalar potential φ and a vector potential A: E=−∇φ−∂tA and B=∇×A. For signed charge q, canonical momentum is p=−iℏ∇ and kinetic momentum is π=p−qA. The spinless Hamiltonian is π²/(2m)+qφ. The order matters: in general p differentiates A as well as the wavefunction, so pA and Ap cannot simply be replaced by twice one product.

For a constant one-dimensional A, a local plane-wave factor e^(ipx/ℏ) has kinetic momentum p−qA. This local calculation is useful for checking signs; an infinite plane wave is not a normalized localized particle state. Holding the wavefunction fixed while changing A is not the complete gauge transformation taught next.
lessons.terms: q, m: signed particle charge and positive mass (C; kg). Here q is general; an electron has q=−e. A, φ: vector and scalar potentials (T·m; V). qA has momentum units; qφ has energy units. p, π: canonical and kinetic momenta (kg·m/s). p is a derivative operator; multiplication by varying A does not generally commute with it. p₀, E₀: positive reference momentum and energy (kg·m/s; J). E₀=p₀²/(2m) defines the example units. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Choose constant potentials with p=4p₀, qA=p₀ and qφ=2E₀. The kinetic momentum is 3p₀.
Its kinetic energy is 9E₀, and the total energy is 11E₀.
The vector potential alone is not an observable momentum; the state and potentials together determine π.

Squaring requires the full difference, including its cross term.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Why keep p·A+A·p when A varies in space?
apply.answer: The derivative can act on A. Preserving both ordered products retains that contribution and the Hermitian structure on a suitable domain.

lessons.limits: Nonrelativistic spinless minimal coupling with sufficiently regular potentials and stated operator domains. No spin magnetic energy is included.

lessons.title: Change the state phase together with the potentials
lessons.idea: Different potential functions can describe the same fields, but the state’s phase must change with them.
body: Different potential functions can describe the same fields, but the state’s phase must change with them.

Choose A′=A+∇χ and φ′=φ−∂tχ. The corresponding wavefunction is ψ′=e^(iqχ/ℏ)ψ. Differentiating this phase supplies exactly q∇χ, so (p−qA′)ψ′=e^(iqχ/ℏ)(p−qA)ψ. Its squared norm and physical kinetic predictions stay the same.

The time derivative also matters: iℏ∂tψ′ includes −q(∂tχ)ψ′, matching the change in qφ. Probability current is j=Re[ψ*(p−qA)ψ]/m for this spinless model. The phase factors cancel there; electric current would be qj. Omitting the state phase or the scalar time term is not a gauge transformation of the same physical solution.
lessons.terms: χ: gauge function (T·m² or J·s/C). qχ/ℏ is a dimensionless phase. ψ, ψ′: wavefunctions in two gauges (m⁻³ᐟ² in 3D). They have the same position probability density. j: probability current density (m⁻²·s⁻¹ in 3D). Re means real part; charge current is q times j. b, d: constants in χ=bx−dt (T·m; V). They shift a constant x-directed A by b and φ by d. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Use χ=bx−dt, with qb=2p₀. If p=4p₀ and qA=p₀ initially, the transformed canonical momentum is 6p₀ and qA′=3p₀.
Both gauges therefore give kinetic momentum 3p₀. If qd=0.3E₀, the plane-wave energy parameter shifts by +0.3E₀, exactly matching qφ′−qφ.
The frequency parameter can change with gauge while motion momentum and field observables do not.

visual.title: Change the state phase together with the potentials
visual.caption: Keep all potential and phase terms together so the physical current is unchanged.

check.prompt: If qb=−p₀ instead, what happens to the same initial kinetic momentum?
explanations: Changing only the potential omits the state phase.
Changing only canonical momentum omits the potential transformation.
Both canonical p and qA shift by −p₀, leaving their difference unchanged.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Can χ depend on time while φ is left unchanged?
apply.answer: Not in general. The term −∂tχ is required to describe the same electric field and transformed Schrödinger solution.

lessons.limits: Smooth single-valued local gauge changes and compatible boundary conditions. Global multiply connected boundaries require separate care; a phase cannot be silently made multivalued.

lessons.title: Compare two paths around an excluded flux
lessons.idea: Two paths can acquire a relative phase from an enclosed magnetic flux even when the field is excluded from the paths themselves.
body: Two paths can acquire a relative phase from an enclosed magnetic flux even when the field is excluded from the paths themselves.

Orient a closed loop by following path 1 forward and path 2 backward. The magnetic contribution to their relative phase is q∮A·dl/ℏ=qΦ/ℏ, where Φ is the signed flux through that oriented loop. A single-valued gauge phase cancels around it. An excluded flux tube makes the accessible region multiply connected: a loop around the hole cannot be shrunk away within that region.

For equal path amplitudes and no other relative phase, one ideal recombined output has probability P=(1+cosϕ)/2. This is an interference model, not a claim that each particle traces both drawn paths as a classical trajectory. Reversing the loop reverses the signed phase; cos alone cannot distinguish those signs in this particular output.
lessons.terms: Φ, Φ₀: oriented flux and flux period (Wb=T·m²). Φ₀ advances the phase by a full turn in magnitude. ϕ, q: relative magnetic phase and signed charge (rad; C). For an electron q=−e. P: ideal equal-amplitude output probability (1). Other path phases are set to zero in this example. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: For an electron and Φ=h/(4e), ϕ=−π/2. The output probability is 1/2.
At Φ=h/(2e), the phase is −π and this output is dark: P=0.
Adding one flux period h/e changes phase by −2π and restores the same probability.

The output uses (1+cosϕ)/2, not(1−cosϕ)/2.
An integer period gives the bright case, not this flux.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Would changing only A on one path and ignoring the rest of the loop define an observable phase?
apply.answer: No. Physical interference uses the complete relative phase with consistent endpoint and gauge conventions.

lessons.title: Turn planar magnetic motion into a shifted oscillator
lessons.idea: A uniform magnetic field makes one part of the spinless planar Hamiltonian an ordinary shifted oscillator.
body: A uniform magnetic field makes one part of the spinless planar Hamiltonian an ordinary shifted oscillator.

Choose B along z and gauge A=(0,Bx,0). With a y-dependent factor e^(iky), canonical py=ℏk. Then H=px²/(2m)+(ℏk−qBx)²/(2m), which is an oscillator centered at x₀=ℏk/(qB), with positive angular rate ωc=|qB|/m.

The oscillator energy is ℏωc(n+1/2), n=0,1,2,… . The center depends on the signed charge and field, but the spacing uses their absolute product. This lesson only establishes the planar oscillator mapping. Boundary counting, level degeneracy, edge states and Hall response are deferred, not inferred from this one factorized state.
lessons.terms: k, x₀: y wave number and oscillator center (m⁻¹; m). x₀=ℏk/(qB), with qB≠0. ωc, n: positive cyclotron rate and oscillator index (rad/s;1). ωc=|qB|/m; n is a nonnegative integer. En: planar oscillator energy (J). Spin and any free z motion are omitted. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Choose a model whose spacing ℏωc=6 meV. The first three planar energies are3,9 and 15 meV.
Doubling |B| doubles the spacing and halves x₀ for the same k and unchanged field sign.
Changing q to −q at fixed B,k reverses the center but leaves all these energies unchanged.

lessons.title: Account for a moving basis
lessons.idea: Even if a Hamiltonian is diagonal at each instant, its eigenvectors may move and mix the state’s coefficients.
body: Even if a Hamiltonian is diagonal at each instant, its eigenvectors may move and mix the state’s coefficients.

At each time choose orthonormal vectors |n(t)⟩ with H(t)|n(t)⟩=En(t)|n(t)⟩. Expand |ψ⟩=Σan(t)|n(t)⟩ without removing any phase. Differentiate both an and |n⟩, then project with ⟨m|. This gives the coefficient equation below. The derivative-coupling term is essential; simply applying separate energy phases misses it.

For a real spin basis |+⟩=(cos(θ/2),sin(θ/2)) and |−⟩=(−sin(θ/2),cos(θ/2)), the overlap ⟨−|∂t+⟩=θ̇/2. The reverse overlap has the opposite sign. Thus −iℏ⟨m|∂tn⟩ is a Hermitian matrix, consistent with norm-preserving evolution. A dot means a time derivative.
lessons.terms: an, |n(t)⟩: coefficients and instantaneous normalized basis (1). The coefficients here retain both dynamical and geometric phases. Em, ⟨m|∂tn⟩: instantaneous energy and derivative coupling (J; s⁻¹). The extra matrix term therefore has energy units. θ, θ̇: basis angle and its rate (rad; rad/s). Use the explicitly real two-component basis. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Take θ̇=0.6 rad/s. Then ⟨−|∂t+⟩=0.3 s⁻¹.
If a+=1 and a−=0 at that instant, the basis-motion contribution to ȧ− is −0.3 s⁻¹. It is an amplitude rate, not a probability.
The corresponding lower off-diagonal Hamiltonian element is −0.3iℏ/s, whose conjugate is the upper element.

Squaring a rate is not this derivative overlap.

apply.answer: No. Off-diagonal derivative couplings can transfer amplitude between those instantaneous states.

lessons.title: Compare basis motion with a nonzero gap
lessons.idea: A slowly changing Hamiltonian is easier to follow when its relevant energy levels stay well separated.
body: A slowly changing Hamiltonian is easier to follow when its relevant energy levels stay well separated.

For distinct instantaneous levels, differentiating their eigenvalue equation gives ⟨m|∂tn⟩=⟨m|Ḣ|n⟩/(En−Em). Comparing its size with the gap’s phase rate suggests ηmn=ℏ|⟨m|Ḣ|n⟩|/|En−Em|². A small η is a useful local warning check, not a universal adiabatic theorem.

Check the whole evolution: nonzero gaps, smoothness, endpoints, total duration and possible accumulation or resonance matter. A single small value at one instant does not bound every later transition. For the rotating spin basis, η=|θ̇|/(2ω) when the energy gap is ℏω.
lessons.terms: Ḣ: time derivative of the Hamiltonian (J/s). Its off-diagonal matrix element measures how strongly the change couples states. En−Em, ω: nonzero energy gap and its angular rate (J; rad/s). The gap magnitude is ℏω in the rotating example. ηmn: dimensionless local adiabatic estimate (1). Small is encouraging under further regularity assumptions, not a complete error bound. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: For ω=20 rad/s and θ̇=0.4 rad/s, η=0.01.
In a separate energy-scaled example, if the gap is 2E₀ and ℏ|⟨m|Ḣ|n⟩|=0.02E₀², η=0.005.
E₀ is any stated positive energy unit; it cancels in the ratio.

lessons.title: Separate the energy phase from the basis phase
lessons.idea: Following an instantaneous eigenstate can add two phases: one from its energy and one from how its direction changes.
body: Following an instantaneous eigenstate can add two phases: one from its energy and one from how its direction changes.

For a single isolated adiabatically followed state, write ψ(t)=e^(iδn+iγn)|n(t)⟩ up to the initial coefficient. The dynamical phase is δn=−∫En dt/ℏ. The geometric contribution in this chosen basis is γn=i∫⟨n|∂tn⟩dt. The normalized-state overlap is purely imaginary, so γn is real.

Rephase the basis by |n′⟩=e^(iβ(t))|n⟩. The geometric integral changes by −β(T)+β(0), compensating the endpoint basis phase. For a closed ray path, γn+arg⟨n(0)|n(T)⟩ is the gauge-independent loop phase modulo 2π; in a periodic basis the overlap term is zero modulo 2π. arg means the complex number’s phase angle.
lessons.terms: δn, γn, β: dynamical, geometric and basis-choice phases (rad). These are dimensionless angles, not separate probabilities. En, T: instantaneous energy and elapsed duration (J; s). Integrating energy over time gives action, divided by ℏ. i⟨n|∂tn⟩: geometric phase rate in the chosen basis (s⁻¹). A basis rephasing changes this intermediate rate. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

steps: For a smooth segment with En/ℏ=2 s⁻¹, T=0.75 s and chosen connection i⟨n|∂tn⟩=0.4 s⁻¹, δn=−1.5 rad and γn=0.3 rad.
Their phase sum in this basis is −1.2 rad. This segment is not being claimed to be a closed loop.
If β(T)−β(0)=0.2 rad, the geometric integral becomes 0.1 rad, but the endpoint eigenvector changes as well; the physical ray does not.

lessons.title: Compare slow following with an exact rotating-spin result
lessons.idea: An exact small model lets us check whether slow following is a good approximation for a chosen motion.
body: An exact small model lets us check whether slow following is a good approximation for a chosen motion.

Use H(t)=ℏω[cos(νt)σz+sin(νt)σx]/2, with ω>0 and constant ν. Start in the +z state. Define R(t)=exp(−iνtσy/2) and ψ=Rχ. The rotating Hamiltonian is Hrot=ℏ(ωσz−νσy)/2, including the −iℏR†Ṙ term. The minus sign comes from this stated frame definition.

In that frame the instantaneous lower-state probability is P−=ν² sin²(√(ω²+ν²)t/2)/(ω²+ν²). It measures failure to remain in the instantaneous upper eigenstate, not a literal spin trajectory. Its bound ν²/(ω²+ν²) becomes small for |ν|≪ω. Norm must remain one in either frame.
lessons.terms: σx, σy, σz: Pauli matrices (1). σy=[[0,−i],[i,0]]; the basis is ordered +z,−z. ω, ν, t: gap rate, signed rotation rate and time (rad/s; rad/s; s). The energy gap is ℏω. R, χ, ψ, P−: frame rotation, states and lower-state probability (1). R is unitary; χ=R†ψ. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: For ω=4 rad/s,ν=1 rad/s and t=π/√17 s, the sine reaches one. Then P−=1/17≈0.0588235.
At a slower rate ν=0.2 rad/s, its all-time bound is 1/401≈0.00249377. At ν=4 rad/s, the bound is 1/2; calling that automatically adiabatic would be wrong.
An independently refined integration of the lab-frame Schrödinger equation is compared with this exact rotating-frame solution, rather than trusting an animation alone.

lessons.title: Track a signed half-solid-angle phase
lessons.idea: A spin eigenstate taken around a closed direction loop can return to its original ray with a geometric phase.
body: A spin eigenstate taken around a closed direction loop can return to its original ray with a geometric phase.

Follow the positive eigenstate of H=ℏω n·σ/2, with ω>0, using |n+⟩=(cos(θ/2),e^(iφ)sin(θ/2)). Here θ is measured from +z and φ increases from +x toward +y. Along a cone of fixed θ, i⟨n+|∂φn+⟩=−(1−cos θ)/2.

A solid angle measures area on a unit sphere. The positively oriented cap from the north pole to this cone has Ωsolid=∫₀²πdφ∫₀θsinϑdϑ=2π(1−cos θ). Thus the positive eigenstate’s geometric phase is −Ωsolid/2 modulo 2π. Reversing the loop reverses the sign. This names the positive eigenstate, not a universal ground state.
lessons.terms: θ, φ, ϑ: polar, azimuthal and integration angles (rad). φ increases counterclockwise as seen from +z. Ωsolid: oriented solid angle (sr, dimensionless). A steradian is unit-sphere area; reversing orientation changes its sign. γ+: geometric phase of the positive eigenstate (rad). Equivalent angles differ by an integer multiple of 2π. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: At θ=π/3, the north-cap solid angle is π sr, so γ+=−π/2.
The reversed traversal gives +π/2. The two direction choices are not an arbitrary sign convention after the loop orientation is fixed.
At θ=π/2,γ+=−π, equivalent to +π modulo 2π. A common phase of an isolated state is unobservable, but comparison with a reference branch can reveal a relative geometric phase.

lessons.title: Separate a slow nuclear coordinate from electronic motion
lessons.idea: Heavy nuclei often change position more slowly than electrons, which motivates solving the electronic problem at fixed nuclear positions.
body: Heavy nuclei often change position more slowly than electrons, which motivates solving the electronic problem at fixed nuclear positions.

Use one nuclear coordinate R with mass M and let r collect the 3N spatial coordinates of N electrons. Define He(r;R) to include electronic kinetic energy, electron interactions and electron-nucleus attraction, but exclude nucleus-nucleus repulsion VNN(R). Solve Heφn=εn(R)φn with ∫|φn|²dr=1 at each fixed R. The semicolon means R is a parameter in this electronic problem.

A single-surface approximation keeps Ψ(r,R)≈χ(R)φ0(r;R). χ describes nuclear motion; the electronic factor changes as R changes, so this is not generally a product of two independent fixed states. Large M/m helps a time-scale hierarchy, but a small electronic gap or strong derivative coupling can spoil it.
lessons.terms: R, r, M, m: nuclear coordinate, electronic coordinates and masses (m; m; kg; kg). This is a one-nuclear-coordinate teaching model. He, εn, VNN: electronic operator, electronic energy and nuclear repulsion (eV in examples). VNN is excluded from He here, then added exactly once. χ, φn: nuclear and fixed-R electronic factors (χ: m⁻¹ᐟ²; φn: m^(−3N/2)). N is the number of electrons; dr is the 3N-dimensional spatial measure, with any discrete spin components summed. ∫|χ|²dR=1 and ∫|φn|²dr=1 give total normalization for this product approximation. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: If ε0(R)=−4 eV and VNN(R)=1.5 eV at a chosen position, the leading nuclear surface there is −2.5 eV.
For M/m=1600 and comparable restoring-force curvature, the oscillator rate scales as mass⁻¹ᐟ², so the nuclear/electronic rate ratio is 1/40.
The second estimate states an extra curvature assumption; the mass ratio alone does not determine a real molecule’s rates.

lessons.title: Let nuclei move near a minimum of one energy surface
lessons.idea: Once an isolated electronic surface is chosen, its energy becomes part of the potential felt by the nuclear coordinate.
body: Once an isolated electronic surface is chosen, its energy becomes part of the potential felt by the nuclear coordinate.

At leading single-surface order, use U(R)=ε0(R)+VNN(R) and solve [−ℏ²∂R²/(2M)+U(R)]χ=Eχ. Here we neglect derivative-coupling corrections and choose a locally smooth real electronic state; this approximation must be checked, not hidden in the notation.

Near a stable minimum R0, the slope vanishes and U≈U0+K(R−R0)²/2, where K>0 is the curvature. This is a harmonic oscillator with ωN=√(K/M) and energies U0+ℏωN(v+1/2). The integer v labels vibration here, not speed. A local parabola is not the entire dissociation potential.
lessons.terms: R0, U0, K: minimum position, minimum energy and curvature (m; J; N/m). N/m=J/m²; the linear term vanishes at the minimum. M, ωN, v: effective nuclear mass, vibration rate and level index (kg; rad/s;1). v=0,1,2,…; all energies use one chosen surface. E, χ: nuclear energy and normalized wave factor (J; m⁻¹ᐟ²). The one-coordinate nuclear equation omits intersurface couplings. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

Using ℏ=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s, adjacent levels are separated by 0.0131642 eV.

lessons.title: Keep the couplings that a single surface leaves out
lessons.idea: When the electronic state changes rapidly with nuclear position, motion can couple different electronic surfaces.
body: When the electronic state changes rapidly with nuclear position, motion can couple different electronic surfaces.

Expand Ψ=Σχn(R)φn(r;R) and differentiate the product twice. Define dmn=⟨φm|∂Rφn⟩ and τmn=⟨φm|∂R²φn⟩, with inner products over electronic coordinates. Projection gives the coupled nuclear equation below. The 2dmnχn′ term comes from differentiating both factors once; τmn comes from differentiating the electronic factor twice.

A useful along-path warning ratio is ηN=ℏ|Ṙ dmn|/|εn−εm|. Small gaps amplify it. In more than one nuclear coordinate, conical intersections can join surfaces and require special phase/coupling treatment; this one-coordinate example does not model their geometry. Even diagonal derivative terms and phase conventions matter in a careful one-surface theory, so dropping every derivative term is only a leading approximation.
lessons.terms: dmn, τmn: first and second electronic derivative overlaps (m⁻¹; m⁻²). Primes on χ mean derivatives with respect to R; Um=εm+VNN. Ṙ, ηN: nuclear speed along a chosen path and warning ratio (m/s;1). This estimate is not a universal error theorem. M, E, εn−εm: nuclear mass, total energy and electronic gap (kg; eV in example). The gap must be nonzero for the ratio. Units: J is joule, eV electronvolt, meV=0.001 eV, μeV=10⁻⁶ eV; m is metre when used as a unit, s second, kg kilogram, C coulomb, V volt, T tesla. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. i²=−1, * is complex conjugation and † is the adjoint; ⟨A⟩ is the mean outcome in the stated state. ℏ=h/(2π), with rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s=6.582119569×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s for conversions.

steps: For a real two-state electronic basis rotating by θ=R/L, d−+=1/(2L) and τ++=−1/(4L²). With L=1 nm=10⁻⁹ m, these are 5×10⁸ m⁻¹ and −2.5×10¹⁷ m⁻².

lessons.title: Remove the known motion first
lessons.idea: Changing coordinates can leave only the added interaction to drive the state.
body: Write the energy operator as H(t)=H₀+V(t), where H₀ is constant in time and V is the added interaction. Define U₀(t)=exp(−iH₀t/ℏ). The original state is |ψ_S⟩; the interaction-picture state is |ψ_I⟩=U₀†|ψ_S⟩. This is a reversible change of coordinates, not a physical removal of H₀. An observable changes with the same rule: A_I=U₀†A_SU₀, so its expectation is unchanged.

Differentiate the product U₀†|ψ_S⟩. Since dU₀†/dt=(i/ℏ)H₀U₀†, multiplying that derivative term by iℏ gives −H₀|ψ_I⟩. It cancels the +H₀ term from the original Schrödinger equation. The remainder is iℏ d|ψ_I⟩/dt=V_I(t)|ψ_I⟩, with V_I=U₀†VU₀. The minus sign in this cancellation matters.
lessons.terms: H₀,V,V_I: energy operators (J or a consistent energy unit). H₀ is time independent. U₀, A_S,A_I: reference evolution and observable coordinates (U₀ dimensionless; A retains its observable unit). † reverses a unitary transformation. t,ψ_S,ψ_I: time and the two state descriptions (s; dimensionless finite columns). The same physical state has different coordinates. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

At t=π/4 s, exp(iωt)=i, so (V_I)₁₀=i g and (V_I)₀₁=−i g. V_I remains Hermitian.
If V=0, |ψ_I⟩ is constant even though the original excited-state component continues to acquire phase.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Would a time-dependent H₀ generally allow the same ordinary exponential formula?
apply.answer: No. Noncommuting values at different times require a time-ordered reference evolution; this lesson assumes constant H₀.

lessons.limits: Exact coordinate change for a time-independent self-adjoint H₀ with well-defined unitary evolution. Finite matrix example; no approximation has yet been made.

lessons.title: Accumulate a small transition amplitude
lessons.idea: Small contributions add as complex amplitudes before their magnitude is squared.
body: Let |i⟩ and |f⟩ be different normalized eigenstates of H₀ with energies E_i and E_f. Begin in |i⟩ at time zero. To first order, replace the changing interaction-picture state inside its integral equation by the initial state. This keeps one use of the interaction and neglects repeated transitions.

The resulting amplitude is c_f^(1)(T)=−(i/ℏ)∫₀ᵀ V_fi(t) exp(iω_fi t) dt, where V_fi=⟨f|V|i⟩ and ω_fi=(E_f−E_i)/ℏ. The superscript (1) means first order, not a power. Probability is approximately |c_f^(1)|². Check the sum of probabilities to all other states: it must be much smaller than one. A small probability for just one channel does not guarantee this.
lessons.terms: E_i,E_f,V_fi: initial/final energies and coupling entry (J). The states use discrete normalization. ω_fi,T,t: Bohr angular frequency, duration and integration time (s⁻¹; s; s). The phase convention has +iω_fi t. c_f^(1),P: first-order amplitude and approximate probability (dimensionless). The neglected state change must remain small. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

apply.answer: No. It is a warning that the approximation has left its weak-transition regime, not a probability above certainty.

lessons.title: A finite pulse has a sinc-shaped response
lessons.idea: A shorter rectangular pulse has a broader frequency response.
body: For a constant matrix element g during 0≤t≤T and zero outside, integrate the phase in the previous lesson. Define sinc(x)=sin(x)/x when x≠0 and sinc(0)=1 by continuity. The value at zero is a removable limit, not division by zero.

The amplitude is −i(gT/ℏ) exp(iω_fi T/2) sinc(ω_fi T/2). Its central phase has magnitude one, so it drops out of the probability. At equal energies, ω_fi=0, the result is (|g|T/ℏ)². The first zeros away from resonance occur at |ω_fi|=2π/T; longer pulses distinguish closer frequencies.
lessons.terms: g,T: constant coupling and pulse duration (J; s). The pulse switches on at zero and off at T. ω_fi,x: energy-gap angular frequency and sinc argument (s⁻¹; dimensionless). x=ω_fi T/2. sinc,P: continuous sine ratio and approximate probability (dimensionless). sinc(0)=1, not zero. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

lessons.title: Keep both frequencies of a real drive
lessons.idea: A cosine drive contains two phase rotations, only one of which is slowly varying near a chosen upward transition.
body: For a real cosine drive write V_fi(t)=g cos(ω_d t), with positive drive angular frequency ω_d. Euler’s identity gives cos(ω_d t)=[exp(iω_d t)+exp(−iω_d t)]/2. After multiplication by the upward Bohr phase exp(iω_fi t), the two offsets are Δ₋=ω_fi−ω_d and Δ₊=ω_fi+ω_d.

Define F(Δ,T)=T exp(iΔT/2) sinc(ΔT/2), the time integral of exp(iΔt) from zero to T. The full first-order amplitude is −ig[F(Δ₋,T)+F(Δ₊,T)]/(2ℏ). Add these amplitudes before squaring. Near a positive upward resonance, Δ₋ is small while Δ₊ oscillates rapidly. Neglecting the latter requires a scale argument, not just a convenient label.

Δ₋,Δ₊,F: frequency offsets and phase integral (s⁻¹; s⁻¹; s). F has units of time. T,c_f^(1): duration and transition amplitude (s; dimensionless). Both pieces use the same declared phase convention. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

apply.answer: No. The cosine contributes g/2 to that rotating piece. Omitting the factor of two changes the predicted weak probability by four.

lessons.title: Test a dipole element rather than guessing
lessons.idea: Symmetry can force a dipole matrix element to vanish before any radial integral is done.
body: An electric dipole couples through position. In one dimension, x changes sign under x→−x. If both wavefunctions have the same definite parity (both even or both odd), the integrand ψ_f* x ψ_i is odd on a symmetric domain and integrates to zero. Opposite parity removes this obstruction but does not guarantee a nonzero answer.

For central-potential states, the azimuthal factor is exp(imφ). The z component has no φ phase, so ∫₀²π exp[i(m_i−m_f)φ] dφ is zero unless m_f=m_i. Components x±iy add exp(±iφ), giving m_f=m_i±1. These are component tests, not a derivation of every angular-momentum selection rule. As an explicit low-state angular example, Y₀₀=1/√(4π) and Y₁₀=√(3/(4π)) cosθ give ∫Y₁₀* cosθ Y₀₀ dΩ=1/√3; the same integral with Y₀₀ on both sides is zero.
lessons.terms: ψ_i,ψ_f,x: one-dimensional wavefunctions and position (m⁻¹ᐟ²; m⁻¹ᐟ²; m). A normalized position matrix element has metres as its unit. m_i,m_f,φ,θ: integer magnetic labels and spherical angles (dimensionless; radians). m here is a label, not mass; dΩ=sinθ dθ dφ. Y₀₀,Y₁₀,dΩ: normalized angular functions and solid-angle measure (dimensionless). Their angular factors multiply a separate radial integral. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

apply.text: Can opposite parity alone establish an allowed transition with a known strength?
apply.answer: No. Other angular cancellations or a zero radial integral can still suppress it; strength requires the complete matrix element.

lessons.title: Know when the weak-pulse answer stops working
lessons.idea: An exact two-state model oscillates; its small-time approximation keeps growing.
body: Consider an already specified constant effective two-state Hamiltonian H_eff=gσ_x with real g. Here σ_x swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩. Starting in |0⟩ gives |ψ(T)⟩=cos(gT/ℏ)|0⟩−i sin(gT/ℏ)|1⟩. The transition probability is sin²(gT/ℏ). This is exact for this effective Hamiltonian, not automatically for the original cosine-driven laboratory Hamiltonian.

For the dimensionless angle a=gT/ℏ much smaller than one, sin a≈a, so first order predicts P≈a². At larger angles the exact model transfers probability back and forth while a² keeps growing. Check the approximation at the duration of interest, not just the smallness of g in isolation.

T,a: pulse duration and accumulated angle (s; dimensionless). a includes both strength and duration. P_exact,P_weak: exact effective-model and approximate probabilities (dimensionless). Exact here refers only to H_eff. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. lessons.title: Count final states per unit energy
lessons.idea: A density of states converts a count over closely spaced levels into an energy integral.
body: Put a free, spinless particle in a large periodic cube of volume V_b. Allowed wavevectors form a grid with one point per volume (2π)³/V_b in wavevector space. A thin spherical shell has volume 4πk²dk, so its state count is dN=V_b k²dk/(2π²). This includes all directions and counts no spin degeneracy. It is a large-box continuum approximation, not an exact count of a tiny shell.

For kinetic energy E=ℏ²k²/(2m)>0, dE/dk=ℏ²k/m. Changing the integration variable therefore gives ρ_E(E)=dN/dE=V_b m k/(2π²ℏ²). This derivative factor is the Jacobian: it changes the size of an interval when the variable changes. Thus ∑_f F(E_f)≈∫ρ_E(E)F(E)dE. Box-normalized matrix elements have energy units. For a localized source feeding extended final states, their squared magnitudes typically scale as 1/V_b, canceling the volume in ρ_E; one must not change normalization in only one factor.

Periodic cube; positive k. m,E,ρ_E: mass, kinetic energy and density per energy (kg; J; J⁻¹). ρ_E dE is a dimensionless number of states. N,F: state count and a quantity summed over final states (count; units appropriate to F). No spin multiplicity is included. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. apply.text: If instead using density per angular frequency ω=E/ℏ, what is the conversion?

lessons.title: A long pulse still needs a short-enough observation
lessons.idea: The rate limit uses a pulse long enough to resolve energies but short enough not to empty the initial state.
body: Use the angular-frequency convention A_T(ω)=∫₀ᵀ exp(iωt)dt; the inverse Fourier transform carries 1/(2π). Then |A_T|²=T² sinc²(ωT/2), and integrating over all angular frequencies gives ∫₋∞∞ |A_T(ω)|²dω=2πT. Consequently W_T=|A_T|²/(2πT) has unit area. Its central width shrinks as 1/T, but its integral does not vanish.

Calling W_T “delta-like” means that its integral against a sufficiently smooth frequency function approaches that function’s value at zero. A delta is a rule inside an integral, not an ordinary infinite-height number. For a finite weakly coupled spectrum, a useful rate window requires ℏ/ΔE_s≪T≪ℏ/δE and ΓT≪1. Here ΔE_s is the energy scale over which the coupling-weighted density changes, δE is nearby level spacing, and Γ is the candidate rate. The first inequality gives resolution; the second avoids resolving individual levels; the last avoids large depletion.

They are different scales. Γ: candidate transition rate (s⁻¹). ΓT must be small for first-order total probability. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

check.prompt: In the same model, why is T=100 s not an acceptable weak-continuum window?
options: Its probability must be exactly zero
It resolves the level-spacing scale and gives ΓT=2
A longer pulse always improves all approximations
explanations: Failure of an approximation does not imply zero physical probability.
Both the discrete-level and weak-depletion conditions fail; longer is not automatically better.
Improving resolution can simultaneously violate discreteness and depletion conditions.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Can the literal limit T→∞ be taken while retaining ΓT≪1 at a fixed positive Γ?
apply.answer: No. The rate formula is useful in an intermediate window or a controlled weak-coupling limit, not as an unlimited first-order probability.

lessons.limits: The full-line window identity is exact. Applying it to a physical spectrum needs smoothness around an interior resonant energy; thresholds and sharp spectral features need separate treatment.

lessons.title: Turn weak continuum transfer into a rate
lessons.idea: A golden-rule rate combines a squared coupling with the number of accessible states per energy.
body: For a weak constant perturbation, sum the finite-pulse probabilities over densely spaced final levels. Near an interior resonant energy E_f=E_i, replace the smooth product |M_fi|²ρ_E by its local value. The frequency-window area then gives Γ=(2π/ℏ)|M_fi|²ρ_E(E_i), and total transition probability is approximately ΓT inside the window just established.

M_fi is a box-normalized energy matrix element and ρ_E is a density per energy with matching normalization. Their units give J²×J⁻¹/(J·s)=s⁻¹. For absorption from a cosine drive, evaluate the final density at E_i+ℏω_d and use the rotating component M=g/2, not the full cosine amplitude g. State the available channels and add their rates only when the final states are distinct.
lessons.terms: M_fi,ρ_E,E_res: coupling, density per energy and resonant final energy (J; J⁻¹; J). Use consistent state normalization. Γ,T: rate and observation duration (s⁻¹; s). P≈ΓT only when ΓT is small. g,ω_d: cosine amplitude and drive angular frequency (J; s⁻¹). For the selected absorption term M=g/2. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

At T=100 ps, ΓT≈0.0152736. If the independently known resolution and discreteness scales are 1 ps and 10000 ps, respectively, all three window conditions can be compatible.
The inverse rate is approximately 6547.24 ps. Treating that as an exponential lifetime requires an additional rate-model assumption, not this first-order calculation alone.

check.prompt: If the same smooth density doubles while M and all validity conditions stay fixed, what happens to Γ?
explanations: Fourfold growth would follow from doubling the coupling magnitude, not the density.
There are twice as many available states per energy, so the summed rate changes.
The density enters linearly; it is the coupling magnitude that is squared.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: How does a coupling magnitude increased by three change the weak rate?
apply.answer: It multiplies Γ by nine. The shorter depletion time may shrink or remove the previously valid time window.

lessons.limits: Weak coupling to a smooth dense set of distinct final states, compatible intermediate time window and consistent normalization. No irreversible rate for an arbitrary isolated discrete pair is implied.

lessons.title: A threshold changes the available phase space
lessons.idea: In a simple three-dimensional continuum, the number of nearby final states shrinks to zero at threshold.
body: Let the final energy be E=E_th+ℏ²k²/(2m), where E_th is the lowest energy of this channel. Define excess energy ε=E−E_th. Counting free three-dimensional states gives ρ_E=C√ε for ε>0, with C=V_b(2m)^(3/2)/(4π²ℏ³). There are no propagating states in this channel for ε<0. The factor √ε comes from the shell area and the energy Jacobian together.

If the transition matrix element approaches a nonzero constant near threshold, the simple golden-rule rate also scales as √ε. This square-root law is not universal: angular momentum, a vanishing coupling or interactions can change it. Very near threshold, the finite pulse samples the edge rather than a smooth interior density; do not blindly use the long-time replacement there.
lessons.equation: ρ_E=C√ε for ε>0; ε=E−E_th; Γ∝√ε for a smooth nonzero coupling
lessons.terms: E,E_th,ε: final, threshold and excess energies (J). ε must be positive for this free outgoing channel. C,V_b,m: density coefficient, box volume and mass (J⁻³ᐟ²; m³; kg). No spin degeneracy; same normalization as before. k,Γ: outgoing wavevector magnitude and rate (m⁻¹; s⁻¹). The scaling assumes a nonzero smooth coupling. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. steps: Suppose a specified model has Γ=0.03 ns⁻¹ at excess energy 0.04 eV, and its coupling is constant across the tested range.
At excess energy 0.09 eV the ratio is √(0.09/0.04)=1.5, so Γ=0.045 ns⁻¹.
Below threshold the energy-conserving propagating channel is closed. A finite-pulse transient is not described by simply extending the square root to a negative energy.

check.prompt: Under the same square-root model, change excess energy from 0.04 eV to 0.01 eV. What is Γ?
explanations: The excess energy is one quarter as large, so its square root and the rate are halved.
That would be linear scaling with excess energy; this model has square-root scaling.
Lower positive excess energy reduces, rather than increases, this rate.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: If the coupling magnitude itself is proportional to k near threshold, how does the rate scale?
apply.answer: Its square contributes k²∝ε. Multiplying by the density √ε gives ε^(3/2), rather than √ε.

lessons.limits: One nonrelativistic, spinless, free three-dimensional final channel. The threshold scaling concerns an energy-conserving continuum regime; finite bandwidth and threshold singularities can invalidate a local rate approximation.

lessons.title: Three time regimes need not share one law
lessons.idea: Quadratic early survival and exponential intermediate decay belong to different approximations.
body: For a normalized state under a time-independent Hamiltonian with finite energy variance, expanding its survival amplitude gives S(t)=1−(ΔH)²t²/ℏ² plus higher-order terms. Here (ΔH)²=⟨H²⟩−⟨H⟩². The initial loss is quadratic, not linear. A continuum rate approximation cannot replace this exact very-short-time behavior all the way down to zero.

A separate memoryless population model uses dS/dt=−ΓS and gives S=exp(−Γt). Memoryless means the current rate depends on the present population rather than its detailed history. This can be useful over an intermediate range after the reservoir’s short memory has become unimportant. Finite discrete systems can recur; spectral edges can also spoil exponential behavior at very long times.
lessons.equation: S(t)=1−(ΔH)²t²/ℏ²+… near zero; S_rate(t)=e^(−Γt) in a stated rate regime
lessons.terms: S,t: survival probability and elapsed time (dimensionless; s). Survival means return probability to the initial state in the closed-system expression. ΔH,Γ: energy standard deviation and effective decay rate (J; s⁻¹). The variance must be finite for the stated quadratic expansion. …: higher-order omitted terms (same units as S). Their neglect needs a sufficiently short time. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

Quadratic loss becomes one quarter as large: 4×0.005²=0.0001.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Can a measured intermediate decay rate establish exact exponential behavior for all later times?
apply.answer: No. The model must be checked against the spectrum, reservoir memory and observation window; a fitted rate is not a universal lifetime law.

lessons.title: A dipole sees nearly the same field across the system
lessons.idea: The electric-dipole approximation neglects spatial variation of the driving field over a small system.
body: For a plane wave, the phase changes by about ka across a system of size a, where k=2π/λ and λ is wavelength. If ka≪1, use a nearly uniform electric field over the system. In the stated length-gauge model, the interaction is V(t)=−d·E(t), with dipole operator d=q r for a single charge q measured from the chosen origin.

For polarization unit vector e and field E(t)=e E₀ cos(ω_d t), the coupling entry is g=−E₀ e·d_fi, where d_fi=⟨f|d|i⟩. A dipole entry has coulomb-metres, and multiplying by volts per metre gives joules. The spatial smallness condition is separate from weak excitation: even a spatially uniform field can drive large coherent population transfer over enough time.
lessons.terms: a,λ,k: system size, wavelength and wave number (m; m; m⁻¹). ka is dimensionless. d,q,r,d_fi: dipole, signed charge, position and dipole entry (C·m; C; m; C·m). The charge sign belongs in d. E₀,e,g: field amplitude, polarization direction and cosine coupling (V/m; dimensionless; J). The resonant rotating amplitude is g/2. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units.
