The spatial phase variation depends on wavelength.
ka is inversely proportional to wavelength; reducing λ by ten increases ka by ten.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Does ka≪1 alone justify first-order transition probabilities?
apply.answer: No. It justifies the spatial approximation. Coupling strength, duration, accessible channels and total transferred probability still determine perturbative validity.

lessons.limits: Specified electric-dipole length-gauge model for a small localized system, prescribed classical field and chosen polarization. No laser engineering, arbitrary strong-field, gauge-truncation equivalence or spontaneous-emission derivation is claimed.

lessons.title: Use a supplied spontaneous rate honestly
lessons.idea: A spontaneous-emission rate can be an explicit physical input without pretending it came from a classical drive.
body: Take A>0 as a supplied spontaneous population-decay rate for one excited level. With no pumping, no competing channels and no reabsorption, the effective population equation is dN_e/dt=−A N_e. It predicts N_e(t)=N₀ exp(−At), lifetime τ=1/A and mean emitted count N₀−N_e(t). Counts are expected averages, not a deterministic schedule of individual photons.

This lesson does not derive A. A classical prescribed drive set to zero has zero dipole drive coupling; that does not derive or remove spontaneous emission. Obtaining the physical rate from electromagnetic vacuum modes needs a quantized-field model and additional approximations outside this example.
lessons.terms: A,τ,t: supplied decay rate, lifetime and time (s⁻¹; s; s). The model is applied over its assumed valid range. N₀,N_e: initial and mean surviving populations (counts). A mean count need not be an integer. e^(−At): survival fraction (dimensionless). At=1 gives 1/e, not one half. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

steps: Let A=0.4 ns⁻¹ and N₀=500 independently prepared excitations. The lifetime is 2.5 ns.
After 5 ns, the survival fraction is exp(−2)≈0.135335. The expected surviving count is about 67.6676 and the emitted count about 432.332.
Half-life is ln(2)/A≈1.73287 ns, shorter than the 1/e lifetime. Here ln is the natural logarithm.

check.prompt: With the same A, what survival fraction does the model predict after one lifetime?
explanations: At=Aτ=1, so survival is exp(−1). Lifetime does not mean every excitation has decayed.
One half defines half-life, not the exponential 1/e lifetime.
An exponential population does not become identically zero at one finite lifetime.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: If detection efficiency is 0.60 with no background, how many detections are expected from the 5 ns example?
apply.answer: Multiply the emitted mean by efficiency: 0.60×432.332≈259.399 detections. Efficiency is a separate measurement input.

lessons.title: A balanced two-level drive does not create steady inversion
lessons.idea: Equal upward and downward stimulated rates cap a two-level steady population at one half.
body: Let p be the excited fraction in a closed two-level population model. A prescribed incoherent field gives equal stimulated upward and downward rates W≥0; spontaneous downward decay adds A≥0. Upward flow is W(1−p), downward flow is (W+A)p. Their difference gives dp/dt=W−(2W+A)p. For 2W+A>0, p tends to p_ss=W/(2W+A), at most one half. Inversion means p>1/2.

A separate three-level pumping picture can avoid this balance: an auxiliary level is pumped and rapidly feeds the upper lasing level, with negligible reverse flow in the assumed idealization. After eliminating that fast auxiliary population, a one-way effective pump rate R gives dp/dt=R(1−p)−Ap and p_ss=R/(R+A). This is a different supplied population model, not a consequence of driving the same closed two-level transition coherently.
lessons.terms: p,p_ss: excited fraction and steady fraction (dimensionless). Inversion is relative to the other level in the specified effective pair. W,A,R: stimulated rate each way, decay and effective one-way pump (s⁻¹). All are nonnegative; R belongs to a different model. t: time (s). Constant rates are assumed. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

At t=2 ns this gives p≈0.299289, still below the steady value and below one half.
In the separate one-way-pump model, R=0.6 ns⁻¹ and A=0.2 ns⁻¹ give p_ss=0.75. The altered pathway, not the same symmetric drive, permits inversion.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: If R=A>0 in the one-way-pump model, is the steady pair inverted?
apply.answer: No. R/(R+A)=1/2. In this idealized model inversion requires R>A; it does not by itself establish a functioning laser.

If all relevant rates vanish, the initial population stays fixed and the displayed steady-state quotient is undefined.

lessons.title: An environment can hide local phase information
lessons.idea: A unitary change of a larger system can reduce the coherence visible in one part.
body: Use basis |0⟩,|1⟩ for the system and a separate environment initially in |0_E⟩. Define a controlled unitary U=|0⟩⟨0|⊗I_E+|1⟩⟨1|⊗R(θ), where R(θ)=[[cosθ,−sinθ],[sinθ,cosθ]]. It leaves the environment alone when the system is 0 and rotates it when the system is 1. This real rotation is unitary because its columns are orthonormal.

For initial system a|0⟩+b|1⟩, the joint result is a|0⟩|0_E⟩+b|1⟩(cosθ|0_E⟩+sinθ|1_E⟩). Tracing out the unobserved environment gives ρ_S=[[|a|²,ab* cosθ],[a*b cosθ,|b|²]]. The populations do not change; the off-diagonal entries, which encode phase-sensitive interference, shrink when |cosθ|<1. The total state remains pure and its evolution reversible.
lessons.terms: a,b,ρ_S: initial amplitudes and reduced system state (dimensionless). |a|²+|b|²=1; trace means sum over unobserved environment labels. θ,R,U: rotation angle, environment rotation and joint unitary (radians; dimensionless matrices). ⊗ acts on the ordered system/environment spaces. I_E,cosθ: environment identity and record overlap (dimensionless). The overlap controls the local off-diagonal factor. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

Its eigenvalues are 0.75 and 0.25, so it is positive with trace one. Its purity tr(ρ_S²)=0.625 is below one.

A normalized finite density matrix cannot have zero purity.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Can reversing this exact joint unitary restore the initial interference?
apply.answer: Yes, if both parts remain accessible and the controlled unitary can actually be reversed. The reduced description alone does not imply fundamental destruction of the joint state.

lessons.limits: Initially uncorrelated system/environment and this explicitly defined finite unitary. It does not produce universal monotonic decay or a memoryless bath; repeated joint dynamics can restore coherence.

lessons.title: A Kraus sum works on an attached system too
lessons.idea: Complete positivity asks whether a local map remains positive when another system is attached.
body: A channel can be written Φ(ρ)=∑_r K_rρK_r†. Each K_r is a matrix called a Kraus operator; r labels the terms, not an observed outcome unless a measurement interpretation is separately supplied. The identity ∑_r K_r†K_r=I preserves trace. For phase flips, use K₀=√(1−q)I and K₁=√q Z, with Z=diag(1,−1) and 0≤q≤1. Then populations stay fixed and coherence is multiplied by 1−2q.

Positivity means a valid input state stays positive. Complete positivity makes the stronger demand for every larger composite: (Φ⊗identity)(ρ_AB) must also stay positive. A Kraus representation ensures this because each term (K_r⊗I)ρ_AB(K_r†⊗I) has nonnegative expectation in every vector, and so does their sum. Checking the eigenvalues of one output is only an example, not that general proof. In contrast, matrix transpose preserves positivity of a single matrix but its action on one side of a Bell state gives an eigenvalue −1/2; it is not completely positive.
lessons.equation: Φ(ρ)=∑_r K_rρK_r†; ∑_r K_r†K_r=I; K₀=√(1−q)I, K₁=√q Z
lessons.terms: ρ,Φ,K_r: state, channel and Kraus matrices (dimensionless). The map is linear and applied to initially valid density matrices. q,Z,I: phase-flip probability, sign matrix and identity (dimensionless). q lies from zero to one. ρ_AB,⊗identity: joint state and local extension (dimensionless). The identity map leaves the second system unchanged. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: With q=0.20 and input |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2, the output is [[0.5,0.3],[0.3,0.5]], with eigenvalues 0.8 and 0.2.
For the Bell input |Φ+⟩=(|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 in order 00,01,10,11, applying the map only to A gives 0.8|Φ+⟩⟨Φ+|+0.2|Φ−⟩⟨Φ−|, where |Φ−⟩=(|00⟩−|11⟩)/√2.
The joint eigenvalues are 0.8,0.2,0,0 and trace is one. By comparison, partial transpose of the original Bell projector has eigenvalues 0.5,0.5,0.5,−0.5.

check.prompt: In the phase-flip channel, which q completely removes an input off-diagonal entry?
explanations: The coherence multiplier 1−2q vanishes at one half. At q=1 the operation is the reversible sign flip Z.
q=1 applies Z deterministically and preserves coherence magnitude.
q=0 is the identity channel and does not erase coherence.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: If a numerical test shows positivity for ten selected states, has it proved complete positivity?
apply.answer: No. The Kraus construction provides a general composite argument; a finite sample is only a diagnostic check.

lessons.limits: Specified finite-dimensional channel with 0≤q≤1 and a full Kraus completeness identity. A system initially correlated with its environment need not admit the same state-independent channel on every possible input.

lessons.title: Amplitude damping moves population and reduces coherence
lessons.idea: One simple channel transfers excited population into the ground state without adding an arbitrary normalization step.
body: Choose ground state |0⟩ and excited state |1⟩. For decay probability 0≤p≤1, use K₀=[[1,0],[0,√(1−p)]] and K₁=[[0,√p],[0,0]]. The first term keeps the ground amplitude and reduces the excited amplitude; the second moves the lost excited population to the ground entry. Their adjoint products add to I.

For ρ=[[a,c],[c*,b]], where a+b=1, the output is [[a+pb,√(1−p)c],[√(1−p)c*,(1−p)b]]. Its trace is automatically one. This is not simply deleting amplitude and renormalizing a vector: it sums two alternatives into a density matrix. At p=1 every input becomes |0⟩⟨0|; at p=0 the map is the identity. The Kraus form also proves complete positivity on a composite.
lessons.terms: a,b,c: ground population, excited population and coherence (dimensionless). a,b≥0; a+b=1 and |c|²≤ab for a valid state. p,K₀,K₁: decay probability and two Kraus matrices (dimensionless). 0≤p≤1; matrix order is ground then excited. ρ,ρ′: input and output state (dimensionless). The channel is trace preserving without a normalization repair. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Apply the channel to half of |Φ+⟩. What happens to the other half’s unconditioned reduced state?
apply.answer: It remains I/2 because the operation is local and trace preserving. Conditioning on a recorded decay event would be a different, normalized subensemble.

lessons.limits: Ideal two-level downward amplitude-damping channel, not a universal finite-temperature model or literal trajectory. Decay-event interpretations require an explicit record; the unconditional map sums all terms.

lessons.title: Two relaxation times come from different terms
lessons.idea: In this constant-rate qubit model, population decay and phase loss combine to set the coherence time.
body: Assume a memoryless, time-homogeneous two-level model: the same constant nonnegative rates apply at every time. Work in an interaction picture with no remaining coherent Hamiltonian. Define σ₋=|0⟩⟨1|, σ₊=σ₋† and Z=diag(1,−1). The equation is dρ/dt=γ₁(σ₋ρσ₊−{σ₊σ₋,ρ}/2)+(γφ/2)(ZρZ−ρ). The braces mean {A,B}=AB+BA. The first term transfers excited population downward; the second changes phase without changing populations.

Read its entries: db/dt=−γ₁b for b=ρ₁₁, and dc/dt=−(γ₁/2+γφ)c for c=ρ₀₁. Thus b(t)=b(0)exp(−γ₁t) and c(t)=c(0)exp[−(γ₁/2+γφ)t]. For positive decay rates, T₁=1/γ₁ and T₂=1/(γ₁/2+γφ), so T₂≤2T₁. A zero denominator means no decay of that quantity, conventionally an infinite time. The channel is amplitude damping with p=1−exp(−γ₁t), followed by phase flipping with q=[1−exp(−γφt)]/2, which verifies complete positivity for t≥0.
lessons.terms: γ₁,γφ: downward population and pure-dephasing rates (s⁻¹). Both are constant and nonnegative. T₁,T₂,t: population time, coherence time and time (s). The time inequality is specific to this model. b,c,σ₋,σ₊,Z: excited population, coherence and stated matrices (dimensionless). Ground population is 1−b; {A,B}=AB+BA. Finite-basis amplitudes and density-matrix entries are dimensionless. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate and † conjugate transpose. ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π, with energy×time units. Matrix lists give rows and act on columns. Angles in exponentials are dimensionless radians. Bare-number substitutions use the explicitly stated units; probabilities have no units.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: Can a negative γφ be inserted into this time-homogeneous model just to obtain a longer T₂?
apply.answer: Not as the stated nonnegative-rate Markov model. Negative coefficients require a different, carefully checked dynamical description; positive eigenvalues for one initial state would not establish a valid channel for all composites.

lessons.limits: Time-homogeneous Markovian downward-decay and pure-dephasing model, initially valid state and t≥0. No upward thermal excitation, universal bath law or general non-Markovian T₁/T₂ bound is claimed.

practice.reasoning: Explain why complete positivity is a statement about every composite input, not just these three entries. Enter decimal or scientific-notation numbers, not expressions. Entry tolerance allows rounding; it is not physical measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: A cross section turns a beam flux into an event rate
lessons.idea: The area unit describes how strongly a target scatters, not necessarily its geometric size.
body: Number density n tells us how many incident particles occupy a volume. If a uniform beam moves with speed v, its incident number flux is j_in=nv: the number crossing one square metre each second. For a monochromatic nonrelativistic beam, v=ℏk/m, where k>0 is the incident wave number and m is the particle mass.

A scattering cross section σ has units of area. In a dilute thin sample with N_t independent targets, the expected scattering rate is R=N_t j_in σ. This assumes the flux is essentially unchanged through the sample and scattered particles are not counted repeatedly. It is a mean rate, not a promise of evenly spaced events.

To connect this to the wave calculation, write the physical incident wave as Φ_in=√n exp(ikz). Its density is n and its current is nℏk/m in the +z direction. Later we use the dimensionless shape ψ=Φ/√n; setting that shape’s incoming amplitude to one does not set a dimensional number density to one.
lessons.terms: n,v,j_in: Incident number density, speed and number flux (m⁻³, m/s and m⁻²·s⁻¹). The beam is uniform over the target area in this model. m,k,ℏ: Incident particle mass, positive wave number and reduced Planck constant (kg, m⁻¹ and J·s). v=ℏk/m is the nonrelativistic free-particle relation. N_t,σ,R: Number of independent targets, cross section and expected count rate (count, m² and s⁻¹). Counts are pure numbers; rate has inverse-time units. Φ_in,ψ,z: Physical density-amplitude, normalized incident shape and beam-axis coordinate (m^(-3/2), no unit and m). Φ=√n ψ fixes the dimensional normalization used throughout this scattering block. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Multiply number per volume by speed to obtain number per area per time. Multiply that flux by the cross section of each independent target and by the target count to obtain the expected event rate.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Take j_in=5×10¹⁴ m⁻²·s⁻¹, N_t=2×10⁸ and σ=3×10⁻²⁴ m². Then R=(2×10⁸)(5×10¹⁴)(3×10⁻²⁴) s⁻¹=0.30 s⁻¹.
In ten seconds the expected count is 3, not a guarantee that exactly three events occur.
For beam area A_beam=10⁻¹⁰ m², the thin-sample scattering fraction is N_tσ/A_beam=6×10⁻⁶. The incident rate j_in A_beam=5×10⁴ s⁻¹ times that fraction also gives 0.30 s⁻¹.

check.prompt: Double the incident flux while keeping the same dilute sample and cross section. What is the new expected rate?
explanations: Doubling flux does not halve the rate.
The number arriving per area per time has changed.
Correct. The rate is proportional to flux in this thin-sample model.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If a detector records only 60% of these events, what is its mean recorded rate before background?
apply.answer: Multiply the ideal 0.30 s⁻¹ by efficiency 0.60 to obtain 0.18 s⁻¹. This efficiency changes recorded counts, not the underlying target cross section. A real extraction of cross section must account for efficiency and uncertainty.

lessons.limits: Uniform dilute independent targets, negligible beam depletion/multiple scattering, nonrelativistic elastic beam normalization and stated counting efficiency if used. Cross section is not automatically a literal target radius.

lessons.title: The far wave tells us how likely each direction is
lessons.idea: The scattered wave’s inverse-distance falloff turns into a probability per solid angle.
body: For a localized short-range scatterer and an incident beam along +z, choose time dependence exp(−iEt/ℏ). Far away, write the dimensionless stationary shape as ψ≈exp(ikz)+f(θ,φ)exp(ikr)/r. The first term is incoming plane-wave shape; the second is an outgoing spherical wave. The amplitude f has units of length because ψ has no units.

The physical wave is Φ=√n ψ, as defined in the previous step. The outgoing radial contribution to current is approximately n(ℏk/m)|f|²/r². An area patch on a sphere is r²dΩ, so the r² cancels when comparing scattered rate in that angular patch with incident flux.

Therefore dσ/dΩ=|f|² in this normalization. This is differential cross section: area per solid angle, not a dimensionless probability by itself. The incident–scattered interference near the forward direction still matters for global flux conservation; the optical theorem later keeps that interference account.
lessons.terms: ψ,Φ,n: Dimensionless wave shape, physical wave and incident number density (no unit, m^(-3/2) and m⁻³). The relation is Φ=√n ψ; the incident shape amplitude equals one. r,z,θ,φ,k: Radius, beam coordinate, polar/azimuthal angles and incident wave number (m, m, rad, rad and m⁻¹). Elastic scattering has the same positive outgoing wave number; θ=0 is forward. f,dσ/dΩ,dΩ: Scattering amplitude, differential cross section and solid-angle element (m, m²/sr and sr). Steradian is dimensionless in SI but marks angular measure. The current derivation is a far-field leading statement. E,t,ℏ: Energy, time and reduced Planck constant in the phase convention (J, s and J·s). With exp(−iEt/ℏ), exp(+ikr)/r is outgoing. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: The angular amplitude is the coefficient of the outgoing inverse-distance wave. Its magnitude square gives the cross section per unit solid angle, after the radial area and flux factors cancel.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For an isotropic example at k=1 nm⁻¹, let f=(0.5+0.5i) nm. Its magnitude square is (0.5²+0.5²) nm²=0.50 nm².
Thus dσ/dΩ=0.50 nm²/sr in every direction for this example. The complex amplitude is not itself a probability.
At r=100 nm, the scattered-only density relative to n is |f|²/r²=0.50/10000=0.00005. Multiplying its outward flux by spherical area removes this inverse-square falloff.

check.prompt: For a separate allowed isotropic amplitude f=i nm at the same k, what is dσ/dΩ?
explanations: Correct. |i nm|²=1 nm².
The magnitude square of i is positive one.
A cross section is real and nonnegative.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can a value of 2 nm²/sr be rejected simply because it exceeds one?
apply.answer: No. It is not a unit-free probability. Multiply by a solid-angle acceptance and combine with incident flux and target count to predict events. The unit-free probability additionally depends on the beam/sample geometry.

lessons.limits: Elastic single-channel nonrelativistic scattering from a localized short-range potential, far from the interaction region, with the declared incoming amplitude/time convention. Coulomb long-range asymptotics need modification.

lessons.title: Add over directions with the correct angular area
lessons.idea: Equal changes in polar angle do not cover equal patches near a pole and near the equator.
body: Solid angle measures a patch of directions. On a sphere of radius r, divide the patch area by r² to obtain dΩ=sinθ dθ dφ. A complete sphere has solid angle 4π steradians. The factor sinθ shrinks a band near the polar axis.

The total cross section is the integral of dσ/dΩ over the accepted directions. For an azimuthally symmetric distribution, the φ integration gives 2π. It is incorrect to integrate over θ with no sinθ factor, or to multiply one sampled direction by 4π unless the distribution is isotropic.

For an illustrative nonnegative measured angular fit, let dσ/dΩ=A(1+b cos²θ), with A>0 and b≥0. Integrating gives σ=4πA(1+b/3). This fit specifies count distribution only; it does not by itself identify a complex scattering amplitude or an underlying potential.
lessons.equation: dΩ=sinθ dθ dφ;  σ=∫|f|²dΩ;  A(1+b cos²θ) ⇒ σ=4πA(1+b/3)

A steradian is the unit of solid angle. f,σ,A,b: Complex amplitude, total cross section, fit scale and shape coefficient (m, m², m²/sr and no unit). The illustrative fit gives a differential cross section, not the phase of f. ∫,sinθ,cosθ: Angular integration and trigonometric weights (the trig factors have no unit). The integral shown covers the full sphere unless an acceptance range is explicitly stated. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Weight each direction by its actual solid-angle patch before adding. The same angular density contributes less to a narrow polar band than to an equal-width equatorial band.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If a detector covers only a small solid angle ΔΩ around a direction, when can you use (dσ/dΩ)ΔΩ?
apply.answer: When the angular distribution changes little across that acceptance, the product is a useful approximation. Otherwise integrate the distribution and detector efficiency over the actual accepted directions.

lessons.limits: Correct solid-angle integration with declared angular ranges. The A,b form is a simple fitted distribution, not proof of a particular central potential; incomplete acceptance and varying efficiency require explicit integration.

lessons.title: Build a wave from localized responses
lessons.idea: A Green function is the response used to assemble a solution from many small source contributions.
body: Outside an interaction, the stationary equation can be written using L=∇²+k². A Green function supplies the response to a localized unit source. We choose G₊(r)=exp(ikr)/(4πr), which obeys LG₊=−δ³(r) with an outgoing condition and the time convention exp(−iEt/ℏ). The plus label means outgoing, not the sign of the delta source.

The delta distribution is defined by integration: ∫δ³(r)h(r)d³r=h(0) for a suitable smooth test function h. It is not an ordinary function whose height can be plugged into arithmetic. Away from r=0, direct radial differentiation gives LG₊=0.

The minus sign at the origin follows by integrating over a tiny sphere. The leading G₊≈1/(4πr) has outward derivative −1/(4πr²), so its surface derivative flux tends to −1. The volume integral of k²G₊ tends to zero. This fixes the distribution normalization used in the next integral equation.
lessons.terms: G₊,r,k: Outgoing Green kernel, source separation and positive wave number (m⁻¹, m and m⁻¹). The kernel depends on |r−r′| when source and observation points differ. ∇²,δ³,h,d³r: Laplacian, three-dimensional delta distribution, test function and volume element (m⁻² as an operator; δ³ has m⁻³; d³r has m³). The Laplacian sums the second spatial derivatives. The test-function integral defines the delta normalization. L,E,t,ℏ: Free Helmholtz operator, energy, time and Planck action scale (L has m⁻²; E in J, t in s, ℏ in J·s). The outgoing sign is paired with exp(−iEt/ℏ). Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: The outgoing spherical kernel solves the free wave equation everywhere except at its localized source. Its tiny-sphere derivative flux fixes the source sign and magnitude.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Choose r=2 nm and k=π/(2 nm), so kr=π. Then G₊=−1/(8π nm)≈−0.0397887 nm⁻¹.
At r=4 nm with the same k, kr=2π and G₊=+1/(16π nm)≈0.0198944 nm⁻¹. The magnitude halves while the complex phase changes.
For a sphere of small radius ε, the leading radial derivative is −1/(4πε²). Multiplying by area 4πε² gives −1, independent of the shrinking radius.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: A mathematical response kernel, not a literal particle emitted by a physical point source in this calculation.

check.prompt: At a separation where kr=π/2, what is the phase factor in this outgoing kernel?
explanations: That would correspond to the opposite exponential at this phase.
That is exp(iπ), not exp(iπ/2).
Correct. exp(iπ/2)=i in the stated convention.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Could you replace exp(+ikr) by exp(−ikr) without changing the physical boundary condition?
apply.answer: No. With the same exp(−iEt/ℏ) time convention, that selects an incoming spherical response instead. Source signs and boundary conditions must be tracked together rather than treating either kernel as interchangeable.

lessons.limits: Free three-dimensional Helmholtz kernel at positive real k with an outgoing radiation condition. Its singularity is distributional. Long-range interactions, evanescent energies and rigorous limiting-absorption analysis need further care.

lessons.title: The unknown wave also acts as its own scattering source
lessons.idea: The exact integral equation is not solved merely by writing it down.
body: The stationary Schrödinger equation gives (∇²+k²)ψ=(2m/ℏ²)Vψ for E=ℏ²k²/(2m). Combine this with the outgoing kernel whose operator gives −δ³. The result is ψ(r)=exp(ikz)−(2m/ℏ²)∫G₊(r−r′)V(r′)ψ(r′)d³r′.

The minus sign comes from that kernel convention. The incident term is the chosen free plane-wave shape, and the integral adds the outgoing response to the potential times the wave inside it. The unknown ψ appears on both sides, so this is an exact reformulation, not yet an approximate answer.

Evaluating the right-hand side with a guessed interior wave gives one iteration. Replacing it by the free incident wave everywhere produces the first Born approximation later. Either way, check convergence or a justified weak-potential regime before calling the output accurate.
lessons.terms: ψ,r,r′,z: Dimensionless wave shape, observation/source position vectors and beam-axis coordinate (ψ has no unit; coordinates in m). The prime labels integration position, not a derivative. The incident beam points along +z. G₊,V,2m/ℏ²: Outgoing kernel, potential energy and conversion factor (m⁻¹, J and (J·m²)⁻¹). Multiplying kernel, potential and d³r′ gives J·m², so the correction is dimensionless. m,ℏ,k,d³r′: Mass, Planck action scale, incident wave number and source volume element (kg, J·s, m⁻¹ and m³). The energy reference has V tending to zero at infinity; E=ℏ²k²/(2m). Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Add the incident wave to the outgoing response produced by the potential acting on the full wave. Because the full wave is unknown inside the integral, approximation or numerical solution still requires a separate step.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: To check a small quadrature contribution, define E_L=ℏ²/(2ma²). At a sampled source cell suppose G₊=(0.02+0.01i)/a, V=0.50E_L, ψ=1 and cell volume Δ𝒱=0.10a³.
The integral contribution times 2m/ℏ² is (0.02+0.01i)×0.50×0.10=0.001+0.0005i. All length/energy units cancel.

With the displayed minus sign, that cell contributes −0.001−0.0005i to ψ. This is illustrative sampled-cell arithmetic, not a converged full scattering solution or proof that the guessed interior wave is correct.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: The kernel integrates sources in configuration space. A cell sum needs quadrature refinement and a self-consistent wave, not just visually smooth output.

items.label: One guessed evaluation
items.value: An iteration, not a solution proof

check.prompt: Hold all sampled cell values fixed except reverse the sign of V. What happens to this one cell contribution?
options: The entire exact cross section must reverse sign
explanations: Correct. At fixed sampled ψ, this contribution is linear in V.
The integral equation adds complex amplitudes, not their magnitude squares.
Cross sections remain nonnegative; the exact wave also depends on V.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why does the one-cell sign test not prove that the full wave is linear in potential strength?
apply.answer: In the exact equation, ψ inside the integral changes when V changes. Only a fixed-ψ iteration is linear in the sampled V values. Multiple scattering within the potential appears through the self-consistent dependence.

lessons.limits: Elastic nonrelativistic short-range scattering with declared outgoing convention. The integral equation is formal unless appropriate domains/boundaries are controlled; its numerical evaluation requires convergence, not a single coarse cell estimate.

lessons.title: A stationary answer can approximate a narrow beam of energies
lessons.idea: Check what is narrow and which weighting describes the measured rate.
body: A stationary scattering solution has one exact energy and extends indefinitely. A physical localized packet contains a range of momenta and energies. A single-energy cross section can approximate its response only if the relevant scattering amplitude changes little across the packet’s band.

For a narrow Gaussian momentum distribution with mean k₀>0 and standard deviation σ_k, the relative free-energy spread is approximately σ_E/E₀≈2σ_k/k₀, from E=ℏ²k²/(2m). This first-order spread estimate needs σ_k≪k₀. It does not say the cross section is smooth near every threshold or resonance.

For a separate incoherent beam with several energy groups, rates use incoming flux weights: if group i supplies flux j_i and cross section σ_i, the total one-target rate is Σ_i j_iσ_i. Do not use equal weights merely because there are two energy labels, or substitute number-density weights when speeds differ.
lessons.equation: σ_E/E₀≈2σ_k/k₀;  R_one=Σ_i j_iσ_i;  σ_eff=Σ_i w_iσ_i,  w_i=j_i/(Σ_j j_j)
lessons.terms: k₀,σ_k,E₀,σ_E: Mean wave number, its standard deviation, mean-energy reference and leading energy spread (m⁻¹, m⁻¹, J and J). E₀=ℏ²k₀²/(2m); using it as the mean energy is a narrow-band approximation. i,j_i,σ_i,w_i: Energy-group label, group flux, group cross section and flux fraction (label has no unit; m⁻²·s⁻¹, m² and no unit). The weights sum to one when the total incident flux is positive. R_one,σ_eff,Σ: One-target expected rate, effective cross section and sum (s⁻¹, m² and a summation operation). The symbol σ with a k/E subscript marks spread; with a group/eff subscript it marks cross section. These are different quantities. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: First check the packet’s fractional energy width. For a beam rate with distinct incoherent groups, weight each cross section by its fraction of incoming flux, not by an arbitrary average of labels.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For k₀=2 nm⁻¹ and σ_k=0.050 nm⁻¹, the wave-number spread is 2.5% and the leading energy spread is approximately 5%.
Separately, let 40% of an incoherent incoming flux have cross section 2 nm² and 60% have cross section 5 nm². Then σ_eff=0.4×2+0.6×5=3.8 nm².
If the total flux is 10¹⁴ m⁻²·s⁻¹, the one-target mean rate is (10¹⁴)(3.8×10⁻¹⁸) s⁻¹=0.00038 s⁻¹. This uses 1 nm²=10⁻¹⁸ m².

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: The incoherent two-group rate example is distinct from coherent packet interference. No infinite plane wave is being normalized as a bound state.

check.prompt: Change only the two flux fractions to 50% and 50%, retaining cross sections 2 and 5 nm². What is σ_eff?
explanations: The weights must sum to one, not two.
Correct. The equal-flux average is (2+5)/2=3.5 nm².
That was the previous unequal-flux average.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Could a 1% energy spread still matter strongly near a sharp scattering resonance?
apply.answer: Yes. Narrowness relative to the mean energy does not guarantee narrowness relative to a much smaller resonance width. Compare the whole amplitude or cross section across the actual bandwidth before using one central-energy value.

lessons.limits: Elastic short-range single-channel stationary reference and a sufficiently narrow incident packet for central-energy use. The two-group example is explicitly incoherent and flux-weighted; thresholds, inelastic channels, long-range tails and sharp resonances need separate treatment.

practice.prompt: Use separate cases: a dilute sample with N_t=10⁶, j=2×10¹⁵ m⁻²·s⁻¹ and σ=4×10⁻²⁴ m²; an isotropic angular density 0.20 nm²/sr; and a narrow free packet with k₀=4 nm⁻¹ and σ_k=0.040 nm⁻¹.

parts.label: Expected dilute-sample event rate
parts.feedback: Multiply target count, flux and cross section.

parts.label: One nm² expressed in m²
parts.feedback: Square the length conversion 10⁻⁹ m per nm.

practice.reasoning: State which quantities are densities, rates, areas or dimensionless spreads, and why one model’s numbers must not be inserted into another. Enter decimal or scientific-notation numbers, not fractions or expressions. Entry tolerances allow rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: Separate the angular pattern from the radial wave
lessons.idea: A central potential lets us organize a scattering wave into angular pieces with known free radial behavior.
body: For a potential depending only on radius and a beam along z, use u=cosθ. The Legendre polynomials begin P₀(u)=1, P₁(u)=u and P₂(u)=(3u²−1)/2. Their higher members follow (l+1)P_(l+1)=(2l+1)uP_l−lP_(l−1). Here l is a nonnegative integer, not a length.

The angular identity ∫₋₁¹P_l(u)P_j(u)du=2δ_lj/(2l+1) says different angular pieces have zero integrated overlap. The symbol δ_lj is the Kronecker delta: one when the indices match and zero otherwise. It is not the three-dimensional delta distribution used for the Green function.

The free radial functions are spherical Bessel functions j_l(x) and n_l(x), with x=kr. For l=0, j₀(x)=sin x/x and n₀(x)=−cos x/x. Their large-x behavior is j_l≈sin(x−lπ/2)/x and n_l≈−cos(x−lπ/2)/x. These supplied functions solve the free radial equation; the phase shift later changes their mixture, not their definitions. Higher members can be obtained from q_(l+1)=(2l+1)q_l/x−q_(l−1), for q=j or n, using j₁=sin x/x²−cos x/x and n₁=−cos x/x²−sin x/x.
lessons.terms: u,θ,l,j,δ_lj,P_l: Cosine of angle, polar angle, integer labels, Kronecker delta and Legendre polynomial (all unit-free except θ shown in rad). The j label in δ_lj is an index, distinct from the named radial function j_l. x,k,r,j_l,n_l: Scaled radius kr, wave number, radius and two free radial functions (x,j_l,n_l have no unit; k in m⁻¹ and r in m). The l=0 formulas have removable j₀(0)=1 but n₀ is singular at the origin; not every free solution is an allowed interior solution. q,≈: Either radial-function family and leading asymptotic equality (no unit). The higher-l asymptotics require large positive x; the recurrence is an identity away from x=0. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: The Legendre functions provide orthogonal angular patterns; the spherical Bessel pair provides free radial waves. Keeping those two roles separate makes the later partial-wave sum easier to follow.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: The overlap of P₀=1 with P₁=u is ∫₋₁¹u du=0. The squared norm of P₁ is ∫₋₁¹u²du=2/3.
At u=1/2, P₂=(3/4−1)/2=−1/8. A negative polynomial value is an amplitude pattern value, not a negative probability.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: The special-function identities are supplied and explicitly defined here. These angular patterns are wave amplitudes, not trajectories.

items.label: Orthogonality
items.value: Different angular pieces cancel on integration

check.prompt: What is P₂ at θ=π/2, where u=0?
explanations: Substitute into the whole formula, including its constant term.
That is P₀ everywhere, not P₂ at u=0.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can the singular n₀ function alone describe a regular free wave at the origin?
apply.answer: No. Interior boundary conditions must be checked. The n_l family is useful for exterior scattering combinations where the origin is outside that exterior region, but regular-origin solutions select the appropriate nonsingular behavior.

lessons.limits: Central scalar potential, axial incoming direction, integer orbital l and the stated free radial-function conventions. The supplied orthogonality/recurrence identities do not constitute a full special-function proof.

lessons.title: An elastic central potential changes a radial phase
lessons.idea: Compare the outgoing radial wave with the free reference before interpreting its phase.
body: Outside a short-range real central potential, a radial solution can be written as a combination cosδ_l j_l(kr)−sinδ_l n_l(kr). Far away this is proportional to sin(kr−lπ/2+δ_l)/(kr). The real angle δ_l is the phase shift for that orbital angular channel.

Splitting that sine into incoming and outgoing exponentials shows that their magnitudes are equal. Define S_l=e^(2iδ_l) as the outgoing/incoming ratio relative to the free radial reference, including its fixed sign and angular phase. It is not the raw ratio of the two sine coefficients, which contains an extra minus sign.

For a real potential with only this elastic channel open, |S_l|=1 expresses flux conservation. A phase shift can still change the angular scattering strongly. Shifting δ_l by π leaves S_l unchanged; choose a consistent continuous branch when following energy dependence.
lessons.terms: R_l,j_l,n_l: Exterior radial factor and the specified free radial pair (R_l,j_l,n_l are dimensionless in the declared scattering shape). Only the relative combination matters for δ_l here. δ_l,S_l,l: Phase shift, free-reference scattering factor and orbital label (rad, no unit and nonnegative integer). S_l is defined relative to the free radial reference, not as the unadjusted sine coefficient ratio. k,r: Positive free wave number and radius (m⁻¹ and m). The asymptotic sine form requires large kr outside the potential range. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: The potential selects a mixture of the two free radial functions. In a purely elastic channel it changes their relative phase while preserving equal incoming and outgoing flux magnitudes.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: At δ₀=π/6, S₀=exp(iπ/3)=1/2+i√3/2.
Its magnitude square is 1/4+3/4=1, consistent with elastic flux conservation.
Changing δ₀ to δ₀+π multiplies S₀ by exp(2iπ)=1, so the same elastic scattering factor is obtained.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: A phase shift is a stationary radial-wave comparison. It is not an extra spatial turn taken by a particle.

items.label: |S_l|=1
items.value: No net loss from this channel

check.prompt: What is S_l for a changed phase shift δ_l=π/4?
explanations: Correct. The exponent is 2iδ_l=iπ/2.
That corresponds to δ_l=π/2 modulo π.
That is neither the complex phase nor a unit-magnitude S_l here.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would |S_l|<1 be compatible with this purely elastic single-channel assumption?
apply.answer: Not for an exactly solved real single-channel model. It would signal missing outgoing channels, absorption in an effective description, or a numerical/normalization problem. Those alternatives must be identified before applying the elastic formulas.

lessons.limits: Real short-range central potential, one elastic channel and the declared free radial convention. Absorption, coupled/inelastic channels and long-range Coulomb phases require different bookkeeping.

lessons.title: Add the angular amplitudes before squaring
lessons.idea: Different angular channels can reinforce or cancel in one direction.
body: For the declared central-potential convention, the scattering amplitude is f(θ)=k⁻¹Σ_l(2l+1)e^(iδ_l)sinδ_l P_l(cosθ). The factor 2l+1 counts the angular multiplicity entering this axial expansion. Each term has length units because k⁻¹ is a length.

The complex terms must be added before taking |f|² for a direction. Squaring each term separately would discard angular interference. Later, integrating over the whole sphere uses orthogonality to remove those cross terms; that is a different operation.

A zero phase shift modulo π contributes no scattering in that channel. A finite partial-wave truncation is justified only when omitted channels are negligible for the potential range and energy; merely writing two terms does not establish that fact.
lessons.terms: f,k,θ,δ_l: Amplitude, positive free wave number, angle and phase shifts (m, m⁻¹, rad and rad). Each phase is supplied at the chosen energy; changing energy generally changes the phases too. l,P_l,2l+1,Σ: Orbital integer, Legendre pattern, angular weight and sum (no unit). The illustrative s-plus-p case explicitly sets all higher contributions to zero. dσ/dΩ: Angular cross section (m²/sr). Cross terms survive at a specified angle even when they vanish after full angular integration. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). equationGuide.meaning: Build one complex angular amplitude by adding the phase-shift contributions. Then square the magnitude of that complete amplitude to obtain the differential cross section.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Use a stipulated s-plus-p sample with k=2 nm⁻¹, δ₀=π/2 and δ₁=π/4. Then f(θ)=[i+1.5(1+i)cosθ]/(2 nm⁻¹).
Forward, f(0)=(0.75+1.25i) nm, giving dσ/dΩ=2.125 nm²/sr.
Sideways, cosθ=0, so f=i(0.50 nm) and the angular cross section is 0.25 nm²/sr. Backward it is (−0.75−0.25i) nm, giving 0.625 nm²/sr.

visual.title: See angular interference while checking the total area
visual.caption: Stipulated elastic distinguishable-particle central-potential phase data with only l=0 and l=1 retained. The amplitude is f(θ)=[exp(iδ₀)sinδ₀+3exp(iδ₁)sinδ₁ cosθ]/k. Angle sliders display degrees and calculations convert to radians. k is in nm⁻¹, so f is in nm and |f|² is in nm²/sr. The full-sphere total is 4π[sin²δ₀+3sin²δ₁]/k² and equals (4π/k) Im f(0) for these real elastic phases. The curve adds amplitudes before squaring; its vertical scale adjusts to the selected phase data and remains finite when all scattering vanishes. Changing k while holding phases compares stipulated samples, not automatically one fixed potential at different energies. This is not the identical-pair hemisphere/event formula.

check.prompt: In a separate stipulated parameter sample, keep those phases but use k=4 nm⁻¹. What is the forward angular cross section?
explanations: The amplitude halves, so its magnitude square drops by four, not two.
Correct. The factor 1/k halves f, giving 2.125/4=0.53125 nm²/sr.
The explicit 1/k scale changed.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does doubling the energy of one fixed potential necessarily leave δ₀ and δ₁ unchanged as in that parameter comparison?
apply.answer: No. The phase shifts are themselves energy-dependent. The changed-case exercise isolates the explicit k factor using stipulated phases; predicting a fixed potential at a new energy also requires recalculating its phases.

lessons.limits: Elastic real central short-range model with a complete convergent partial-wave expansion, or an explicitly justified truncation. The worked two-phase sample is illustrative; no general omission-error bound is inferred.

lessons.title: Angular integration removes the cross terms
lessons.idea: The total elastic cross section is a sum of partial contributions even though a directional cross section is not.
body: Insert the partial-wave amplitude into the full-sphere integral. The Legendre orthogonality relation makes terms with different l vanish after angular integration. The result is σ=4πk⁻²Σ_l(2l+1)sin²δ_l.
The l contribution is σ_l=4π(2l+1)sin²δ_l/k². Since sin²δ_l≤1 for real elastic phases, each channel has an upper limit 4π(2l+1)/k². This is an elastic partial-wave unitarity limit.

The per-channel bound is not a universal bound on the sum over all infinitely many l. The number of important channels depends on energy and interaction range. Keep a directional amplitude sum distinct from an integrated probability/area sum.
lessons.terms: σ,σ_l,k: Total/partial elastic cross sections and positive wave number (m², m² and m⁻¹). These areas integrate over the full sphere for distinguishable scattering outcomes. l,δ_l,π: Orbital integer, elastic phase and circle constant (no unit, rad and no unit). The upper limit follows from real δ_l and sin²δ_l≤1. Σ_l,≤: Sum and upper-bound relation (no unit). A total bound would additionally need control of how many channels contribute. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For k=1 nm⁻¹, δ₀=π/6 and δ₁=π/2 with higher phases zero, σ₀=4π×1/4 nm²=π nm².
The p contribution is σ₁=4π×3 nm²=12π nm², at that channel’s elastic maximum.
The full total is 13π nm²≈40.8407 nm². This sum is justified after angular integration, not by ignoring interference in each direction.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: The bound is specific to each elastic partial wave. It is not a geometric hard-sphere radius or an all-energy total bound.

check.prompt: Use a separate sample with the same stipulated phases but k=2 nm⁻¹. What is its total cross section?
explanations: The explicit k⁻² scale has changed.
Doubling k divides the area by four.
Correct. With phases fixed in this comparison, the total is 13π/4 nm².

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: At δ_l=π, is that partial-wave contribution maximal because the phase is large?
apply.answer: No. sin²π=0, so that channel contributes zero scattering at that energy in this convention. The relevant periodic phase combination, not the size of an angle label alone, controls the result.

lessons.limits: Elastic real central short-range scattering and full-sphere integration. The unitarity bound is channel-by-channel; inelasticity or identical-event counting changes the appropriate formulas.

lessons.title: The forward phase carries the total flux account
lessons.idea: A complex forward amplitude contains information that its magnitude alone does not show.
body: At θ=0 every Legendre polynomial has P_l(1)=1. Also Im[e^(iδ_l)sinδ_l]=sin²δ_l for real δ_l. Therefore the imaginary part of the forward partial-wave amplitude is k⁻¹Σ_l(2l+1)sin²δ_l.

Comparing this with the total elastic cross section gives σ=(4π/k)Im f(0) in our outgoing-wave convention. This is the optical theorem for the stated purely elastic case. It is the global flux consequence of interference between the incident and scattered wave, including the forward region.

If other reaction channels are present, the analogous total includes the corresponding loss from the incident channel, not just the elastic angular integral. We keep the current example elastic. A real first-order weak-potential amplitude will later need a careful order-by-order discussion rather than a claim of exact unitarity.
lessons.terms: σ_el,k,f(0),Im: Total elastic cross section, positive wave number, forward amplitude and imaginary-part operation (m², m⁻¹, m and an operation). Im f is the real coefficient of i in the complex amplitude, not its magnitude square. δ_l,P_l: Real elastic phase and angular polynomial (rad and no unit). The derivation uses P_l(1)=1 and real phases to obtain the same positive sum as the total cross section. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Multiply the forward amplitude’s imaginary part by 4π/k to recover the total elastic area in this single-channel real-potential model. The sign follows the stated outgoing/time convention.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For a pure s-wave sample at k=0.50 nm⁻¹ and δ₀=π/3, f=(√3/2+1.5i) nm.
The isotropic angular value is |f|²=(3/4+2.25) nm²=3 nm², giving σ_el=12π nm².
The forward relation gives (4π/(0.50 nm⁻¹))(1.5 nm)=12π nm² as well. Both routes have area units.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: This theorem is a wave-interference conservation relation. It does not mean all scattering events occur in the forward direction.

check.prompt: If all phase shifts vanish in the stated model, what do both sides predict?
options: A nonzero cross section despite f=0
explanations: Correct. Every sinδ_l is zero, so both f and σ_el vanish.
With no partial-wave amplitude there is no scattered contribution.
The conserved elastic cross section is nonnegative.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: What should you do if a numerical elastic calculation gives a total angular cross section inconsistent with its forward imaginary amplitude?
apply.answer: Check partial-wave truncation, boundary conditions, phase/sign conventions and numerical resolution. Agreement is a useful conservation test, not an optional cosmetic property of an exact elastic solution.

lessons.limits: Purely elastic short-range scalar central potential with the specified exp(−iEt/ℏ) and outgoing exp(+ikr) conventions. General optical theorems include reaction channels; Coulomb long-range forward singularities require modified treatment.

lessons.title: Low-energy scattering can be summarized by a signed length
lessons.idea: The length is an extrapolation of a radial wave, not a literal size that must stay positive.
body: Take an attractive spherical well V=−U for r<a and V=0 outside, with U>0. In the zero-energy s-wave limit the regular interior reduced radial wave u(r)=rR(r), with R dimensionless and u in units of length in our scattering-shape convention, is proportional to sin(κr), where κ=√(2mU)/ℏ. Outside, the zero-energy form is proportional to r−a_s. Its extrapolated zero defines the scattering length a_s.

Matching u and its derivative at r=a gives κcot(κa)=1/(a−a_s), hence a_s=a−tan(κa)/κ. The result can be negative even for an attractive potential. Near κa=(n+1/2)π, with n=0,1,2,…, it diverges, signaling a threshold bound-state condition rather than an infinitely large geometric object.

At sufficiently low k, the leading amplitude is f₀≈−a_s/(1+ika_s) when effective-range corrections are negligible. Only when k|a_s|≪1 does σ₀≈4πa_s² follow. Near a divergent a_s, retain finite-k unitarity and effective-range checks instead of reporting an unlimited finite-energy cross section.
lessons.equation: a_s=a[1−tan q/q],  q=κa;  f₀≈−a_s/(1+ika_s);  σ₀≈4πa_s² when k|a_s|≪1
lessons.terms: a,U,κ,q: Well radius, positive depth, interior zero-energy wave number and scaled depth (m, J, m⁻¹ and no unit). q=κa>0 for this attractive well; tangent poles mark threshold conditions. u,R,a_s: Reduced radial wave, ordinary radial factor and scattering length (u in m, R dimensionless and a_s in m). The exterior zero-energy form u∝r−a_s defines a_s; it is not a positive physical radius. k,f₀,σ₀: Small positive exterior wave number, s-wave amplitude and cross section (m⁻¹, m and m²). The amplitude retains its unitary denominator; the constant-area limit needs k|a_s| much less than one. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Choose a=2 nm and q=π/4, so tan q=1. Then a_s=2 nm×(1−4/π)≈−0.54647909 nm.
The negative sign means the extrapolated zero lies at negative r; it does not imply a negative cross section.

For k small enough that both range corrections and k|a_s| are negligible, the cross section tends to 4πa_s². At a nonzero k near a threshold pole this constant-area shortcut must be replaced by the finite-k expression.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: Zero-energy s-wave matching for one specified short-range well. A negative or divergent scattering length is not a literal target dimension.

check.prompt: For a changed well with q=π and the same radius a, what is a_s?
explanations: The tangent term is zero, leaving a rather than zero.
Correct. tanπ=0, so a_s=a.
The tangent poles occur at half-integer multiples of π.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why can the finite-k s-wave area not simply diverge when a_s becomes very large?
apply.answer: The unitary low-energy amplitude retains 1+ika_s in its denominator. At fixed nonzero k, its magnitude approaches 1/k rather than infinity, so σ₀ approaches 4π/k² within that approximation. Effective-range and threshold limits still need separate checks.

lessons.limits: Attractive finite spherical square well, zero-energy s-wave matching and low-energy short-range effective description. The leading scattering-length amplitude assumes effective-range terms are negligible; threshold and zero-energy limits cannot be interchanged without care.

lessons.title: A resonance has a finite width, not an infinite probability
lessons.idea: A rapid phase change can bring one elastic channel close to its allowed maximum over a small energy interval.
body: For an isolated elastic resonance, use the explicitly specified model S_l(E)=(E−E_r−iΓ/2)/(E−E_r+iΓ/2), with Γ>0 and no background phase. Its numerator and denominator are conjugates for real E, so |S_l|=1. This is a model of one narrow resonance, not a universal formula for every potential.
The resulting sin²δ_l is (Γ/2)²/[(E−E_r)²+(Γ/2)²]. It reaches one at E_r and one-half at E_r±Γ/2. Thus Γ is the full width at half maximum of this phase-factor peak.

The cross section includes the additional factor 4π(2l+1)/k(E)². If Γ is much smaller than E_r and the threshold is far away, k varies little across the narrow window and may be replaced by k_r for a simple Lorentzian area profile. Otherwise retain its energy dependence. Background phases can change the line shape.
lessons.terms: E,E_r,Γ: Incident energy, resonance energy and positive full-width parameter (meV in this example). A narrow isolated resonance away from threshold is assumed; Γ is not a probability or an angular rate. S_l,l,δ_l: Elastic scattering factor, orbital label and phase (no unit, integer and rad). A continuous phase branch may be chosen; S_l itself is single-valued in this model. k,k_r,σ_l: Energy-dependent wave number, value at the center and channel cross section (nm⁻¹, nm⁻¹ and nm² here). Treating k as constant is an explicitly narrow-window approximation. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: The resonance ratio changes phase while keeping elastic flux magnitude one. Its energy width determines how quickly the partial cross section rises and falls around the center, subject to the separate wave-number factor.

symbols.description: A narrow isolated resonance away from threshold is assumed; Γ is not a probability or an angular rate.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Use an s-wave resonance with E_r=100 meV, Γ=2 meV and k_r=1 nm⁻¹. In the narrow-window approximation, the peak cross section is 4π nm².
At 99 or 101 meV, |E−E_r|=Γ/2, so the model area is approximately 2π nm².
At 102 meV the phase-factor ratio is 1/(4+1)=1/5, giving approximately 0.8π nm². Small k variation is deliberately omitted in these displayed area values.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: An explicitly supplied elastic resonance model. The finite peak is controlled by channel unitarity, not an infinite event probability.

check.prompt: In this same narrow-window model, change the offset to E−E_r=3Γ/2. What fraction of the peak phase factor remains?
explanations: This nonnegative peak-normalized factor never exceeds one.
That was the smaller offset Γ/2 in the worked example.
Correct. The denominator is 9(Γ/2)²+(Γ/2)², so the ratio is 1/10.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would a resonance located almost at the zero-energy threshold necessarily have this symmetric constant-k cross-section shape?
apply.answer: No. The k⁻² factor and threshold dependence of physical widths/backgrounds can vary strongly there. State the actual energy-dependent model instead of extending this isolated narrow-window approximation into a different regime.

lessons.limits: Supplied isolated single-channel elastic resonance, positive width, zero background and a specified energy window. Constant-k displayed areas additionally assume Γ≪E_r and distance from threshold. This is not a complete resonance theory.

lessons.title: Count an indistinguishable pair only once
lessons.idea: Exchanging the two final directions can describe the same event, so amplitudes and counting conventions both matter.
body: Work in the center-of-mass frame of an elastic collision of two identical equal-mass particles under a central interaction. A final pair leaves in opposite directions. If the two alternatives cannot be distinguished, add the direct amplitude f(θ) and exchanged amplitude f(π−θ), using plus for a symmetric spatial state and minus for an antisymmetric one.

For an event cross section, choose one hemisphere of final directions and integrate |f(θ)±f(π−θ)|² there. Equivalently integrate over the full sphere and divide by two. Without that factor the same unlabelled outgoing pair is counted twice. Counting individual detector hits instead of pair events is a different convention and must be named.

For two identical spin-one-half fermions with a spin-independent interaction, the antisymmetric spin singlet has symmetric spatial scattering, while the symmetric triplet has antisymmetric spatial scattering. For an unpolarized incoherent spin preparation the weights are 1/4 and 3/4; average those cross sections, not their amplitudes. Spinless bosons use the symmetric spatial case.
lessons.terms: f,F_±,θ: Distinguishable-reference amplitude, symmetry-combined amplitude and center-of-mass polar angle (m, m and rad). The reference amplitude is defined using the relative-coordinate problem; the two outgoing momenta are opposite. σ_event,dΩ: Pair-event cross section and angular element (m² and sr). Use one hemisphere or half the full sphere, not an unqualified full-sphere event integral. ±,singlet,triplet: Spatial symmetry sign and two-spin sectors (no unit). For spin-independent scattering, unpolarized fermions use an incoherent 1/4 symmetric-spatial plus 3/4 antisymmetric-spatial area average. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Add the indistinguishable direct and exchange amplitudes with the required spatial symmetry, then count each final pair once. Spin preparation determines which spatial symmetry contributes for fermions.

symbols.name: Distinguishable-reference amplitude, symmetry-combined amplitude and center-of-mass polar angle
symbols.description: The reference amplitude is defined using the relative-coordinate problem; the two outgoing momenta are opposite.

symbols.name: Pair-event cross section and angular element
symbols.description: Use one hemisphere or half the full sphere, not an unqualified full-sphere event integral.

symbols.name: Spatial symmetry sign and two-spin sectors

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: In the pure s-wave limit take f₀=(0.5+0.5i) nm, so |f₀|²=0.50 nm². The symmetric amplitude is 2f₀ and the antisymmetric amplitude is zero.
A spinless-boson or pure fermion-singlet pair-event area is (2π)(4|f₀|²)=4π nm². The triplet s-wave area is zero.
An unpolarized identical-fermion preparation then has event cross section (1/4)(4π nm²)+(3/4)(0)=π nm². A distinguishable full-sphere area for this f₀ would instead be 2π nm².

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: Center-of-mass pair-event convention. These formulas do not count two opposite detector hits as two separate collisions.

items.label: Pair event
items.value: Half-sphere counting or half of full sphere

check.prompt: Change the spin mixture to 60% singlet and 40% triplet, keeping the same s-wave amplitude. What is the pair-event area?
explanations: Correct. The singlet area is 4π nm² and the triplet s-wave area is zero, so 0.60×4π=2.4π nm².
That assigns all preparation weight to the singlet, not the stated 60%.
The nonzero s-wave contribution belongs to the 60% singlet group.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why do only even l survive for a symmetric spatial amplitude of a central potential?
apply.answer: Because P_l(−cosθ)=(−1)^lP_l(cosθ). Adding the exchanged amplitude cancels odd-l terms, while subtracting it cancels even-l terms. This is spatial exchange symmetry; the complete fermion state also includes spin.

lessons.limits: Elastic central-interaction scattering of identical equal-mass particles, center-of-mass frame, indistinguishable final alternatives and stated event-counting/spin convention. Spin-dependent interactions, polarization correlations, distinguishable species and detector-hit counting require their own treatment.

practice.prompt: Keep separate models distinct: an attractive square well with a=3 nm and κa=π; an elastic pure s wave with δ₀=π/2 at k=2 nm⁻¹; and identical pairs using that latter s-wave amplitude.

parts.label: Square-well zero-energy constant-area limit
parts.feedback: 4πa_s²=36π nm², only in its stated low-k limit.

parts.label: Separate distinguishable s-wave area
parts.feedback: 4π/k²=π nm² at the unitary s-wave maximum.

parts.label: Separate spinless-boson pair-event area
parts.feedback: The symmetric identical event area is twice the distinguishable pure-s result.

parts.label: Separate unpolarized fermion pair-event area
parts.feedback: One-quarter of the symmetric pair area remains when the triplet s wave vanishes.

practice.reasoning: Explain why the first well’s zero-energy limit and the separate unitary finite-k sample are not one unchanged physical potential. Enter decimal or scientific-notation numbers, not fractions or expressions. Entry tolerances allow rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: Use the free wave once to estimate weak scattering
lessons.idea: The first Born approximation replaces the unknown interior wave by a stated simple input.
body: In the exact outgoing integral equation, the wave inside the potential is unknown. The first Born step replaces that interior wave by the incident plane wave exp(ik_in·r). This is one approximation step, not an exact solution for every weak-sounding potential.

Far from the potential, the outgoing kernel contributes exp(ikr)exp(−ik_out·r′)/(4πr). Combining its source phase with the incident phase gives exp(−iq·r′), where q=k_out−k_in. Therefore f_B(q)=−m/(2πℏ²)∫exp(−iq·r)V(r)d³r.

This uses the explicitly unnormalized Fourier transform of V: no extra (2π)^(−3/2) factor is hidden in the integral. A different transform convention changes the coefficient. The forward value q=0 adds the signed potential over volume; it is not an absolute-value integral.
lessons.terms: f_B,q,k_in,k_out: First Born amplitude, momentum-transfer wave vector and incoming/outgoing wave vectors (m; all wave vectors in m⁻¹). Actual momentum transfer is ℏq. Elastic magnitudes satisfy |k_in|=|k_out|=k. V,r,d³r,m,ℏ: Potential, position vector, volume element, mass and Planck action scale (J, m, m³, kg and J·s). The integral has J·m³, while m/ℏ² has (J·m²)⁻¹, leaving a length. i,exp,2π: Imaginary unit, Fourier phase and normalization constant (no unit). The unnormalized transform convention is part of the formula; no other Fourier factors are implicit. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Take the spatial Fourier transform of the potential in the declared convention, then multiply by the energy-to-length factor. The approximation comes from using the undistorted incoming wave inside that transform.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For a weak positive spherical barrier of radius a, take V₀=0.060E_L, where E_L=ℏ²/(2ma²). At q=0 the potential integral is V₀(4πa³/3).
Substitution gives f_B(0)=−(V₀/E_L)a/3=−0.020a. For a=2 nm this is −0.040 nm.
The forward differential cross section from this approximation is |f_B(0)|²=0.0016 nm²/sr. This is a forward value, not the full angular integral at an unspecified k.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: Weak-potential scattering amplitude estimate. The example is not a claim of exact flux conservation from a first-order truncation.

check.prompt: Reverse the sign of this weak barrier into a well with the same magnitude and radius. What happens to its first Born forward amplitude?
explanations: The potential integral changed sign.
Correct. This first-order amplitude is linear in the signed potential.
An amplitude may have either sign; its magnitude square remains nonnegative.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would equal leading cross sections for opposite weak potentials prove their exact scattering is identical?
apply.answer: No. The first amplitudes differ by a sign, which disappears in their squared magnitudes, but higher-order distortion and possible bound-state/resonance structure need not agree. The approximation order matters.

lessons.limits: First Born approximation for elastic nonrelativistic short-range scattering with explicit outgoing/Fourier conventions. Its validity requires weak wave distortion in the relevant regime, not just a small numerical label on V.

lessons.title: A spherical potential reduces the transform to one radial integral
lessons.idea: The scattering angle selects how quickly the Fourier phase varies across the potential.
body: For a central V(r), orient the polar axis of the source integration along q. Integrating exp(−iqr cosθ′) over that source angle gives 4π sin(qr)/(qr). This source-integration angle θ′ is distinct from the observed scattering angle θ.
The resulting amplitude is f_B(q)=−(2m/ℏ²)∫₀∞r²V(r)sinc(qr)dr, where sinc y=sin y/y for y≠0 and sinc 0=1. Writing the continuous sinc form avoids dividing by q at forward scattering.

Elastic geometry gives q=2k sin(θ/2): subtract two vectors of equal length k separated by angle θ. Thus forward scattering has q=0 and backward scattering has q=2k. The physical momentum-transfer magnitude is ℏq.
lessons.terms: r,q,k,θ,θ′: Source radius, transfer wave-number magnitude, incident magnitude, observation angle and source-integration angle (r in m; q,k in m⁻¹; angles in rad). The two angles play different roles. Elastic k is the same before and after scattering. sinc(y),y,V,f_B: Continuous sin(y)/y function, unit-free argument, potential and Born amplitude (sinc,y have no unit; V in J and f_B in m). Define sinc(0)=1 by the limit, not by evaluating 0/0. m,ℏ,∫₀∞: Particle mass, action scale and radial integral (kg, J·s and an integration operation). A central short-range potential is required for this reduction. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: Average the Fourier phase over source directions to obtain a radial sinc weight. The observed angle fixes q; small q samples the signed potential with little phase cancellation.
