example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For k=2 nm⁻¹ and observed θ=π/3, q=2(2 nm⁻¹)sin(π/6)=2 nm⁻¹.
For a separate constant spherical barrier, integrating its radial sine weight gives f_B=−(V₀/E_L)a[sin Q−Qcos Q]/Q³, where Q=qa and E_L=ℏ²/(2ma²). The continuous Q=0 limit is −(V₀/E_L)a/3.
At Q=π, V₀/E_L=0.060 and a=2 nm, the value is −0.120 nm/π²≈−0.0121585 nm. Oscillatory source phases have reduced it relative to its −0.040 nm forward value.

visual.title: Keep the roles separate
visual.caption: A central-potential transform calculation. The stipulated Q example is separate from the first geometry sample.

check.prompt: For k=1 nm⁻¹ and a changed observation angle θ=π/2, what is q?
explanations: The half-angle sine is √2/2, multiplied by 2k.
That is the backward θ=π transfer.
Correct. 2×1×sin(π/4)=√2 nm⁻¹.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does substituting q=0 into a version written with sin(qr)/q mean the forward amplitude is undefined?
apply.answer: No. Rewrite using the continuous sinc form or take the limit before numerical evaluation. The radial integral can be finite even though an algebraically rearranged formula displays a removable 0/0.

lessons.limits: Central short-range potential, elastic geometry and the first Born replacement. Radial convergence and the forward limit must be checked; the formula does not apply unchanged to an unscreened long-range Coulomb tail.

lessons.title: A broad smooth potential produces a narrow angular pattern
lessons.idea: The potential’s spatial width controls how rapidly its Fourier transform falls with transferred momentum.
body: Choose V(r)=V₀exp(−r²/a²), with a>0 and signed energy scale V₀. The three Cartesian Gaussian integrals factor, giving ∫exp(−iq·r)V(r)d³r=V₀π^(3/2)a³exp(−q²a²/4). This is a transform of a potential, not a normalized quantum state.
With E_L=ℏ²/(2ma²), the Born amplitude is f_B(q)=−(√π/4)(V₀/E_L)a exp(−q²a²/4). Its differential cross section relative to its forward value is exp(−q²a²/2). Squaring doubles the exponent.

The half-height angular point satisfies qa=√(2 ln2). Using q=2k sin(θ/2), θ_half=2arcsin[√(2 ln2)/(2ka)] if that argument is at most one. Here ln is the natural logarithm and arcsin returns the angle with the given sine in [−π/2,π/2]. If the required q exceeds 2k, no half-height point occurs before backward scattering.
lessons.terms: V₀,a,E_L,m,ℏ: Signed potential scale, positive width, ℏ²/(2ma²), mass and action scale (J, m, J, kg and J·s). The potential width a is fixed by its explicit exponential, not a probability standard deviation. q,k,f_B,θ_half: Transfer/incident wave numbers, amplitude and half-height polar angle (m⁻¹, m⁻¹, m and rad). The angle is measured from forward scattering; its existence requires √(2 ln2)≤2ka. ln,arcsin,exp: Natural logarithm, inverse sine and exponential (functions of unit-free arguments). The formula assumes a nonzero forward amplitude; at V₀=0 the scattering is zero and relative width is undefined. example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Choose V₀/E_L=0.080 and a=2 nm. The forward amplitude is −0.040√π nm≈−0.0708982 nm, with forward differential value 0.0016π nm²/sr≈0.00502655 nm²/sr.
At qa=2 the amplitude is multiplied by e⁻¹ and its magnitude square by e⁻²≈0.135335. The angular value is then about 0.000680269 nm²/sr.
For a separate chosen incident value ka=2, the half-height angle is approximately 0.597556 rad, or 34.2374°. At this angle the cross section is half the forward value, not half the amplitude.

check.prompt: Change the transfer to qa=√(4 ln2). What is the differential cross section divided by its forward value?
explanations: Correct. The cross-section ratio is exp[−(4 ln2)/2]=1/4; the amplitude ratio is 1/2.
That is the amplitude ratio at this new transfer, not its magnitude square.
The exponent for the cross section is doubled relative to the amplitude.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If ka is so small that √(2 ln2)/(2ka)>1, should a numerical program return a complex half-height angle?
apply.answer: No. The physical angle lies between zero and π, where q≤2k. The correct report is that this angular distribution never reaches half its forward value in the accessible angular range. Complex inverse-sine output is not a physical direction here.

lessons.limits: First Born approximation for a short-range Gaussian potential, nonzero V₀ when quoting a relative angular width, and the stated accessible-angle condition. A smooth profile alone does not prove weak-distortion validity.

lessons.title: Keep the screening length when evaluating a long-tailed model
lessons.idea: Removing the screen can change the class of scattering problem, not just one parameter value.
body: Use V(r)=g_Y exp(−μr)/r with μ>0. The coefficient g_Y has energy-times-length units, and 1/μ is the screening length. The exponential makes the tail short range even though the potential behaves as 1/r near the origin.

The central Born integral uses ∫₀∞exp(−μr)sin(qr)dr=q/(μ²+q²). This follows by taking the imaginary part of ∫₀∞exp[−(μ−iq)r]dr=1/(μ−iq), whose convergence requires μ>0. The result is f_B=−2mg_Y/[ℏ²(q²+μ²)].

As μ tends to zero at fixed g_Y, the forward amplitude diverges. The unscreened Coulomb tail no longer satisfies the short-range asymptotic assumptions used here. Do not treat that limit as a complete Coulomb scattering derivation, particularly in the forward direction or optical-theorem discussion.
lessons.terms: g_Y,μ,r,V: Signed coupling, positive inverse screening length, radius and potential (J·m, m⁻¹, m and J). The subscript Y is a label; g_Y is not an angular frequency. q,f_B,m,ℏ: Transfer wave number, Born amplitude, mass and action scale (m⁻¹, m, kg and J·s). The displayed amplitude remains a first-order approximation, not an exact solution for a strong screened potential. i,∫,μ−iq: Imaginary unit, convergent half-line integral and complex inverse-length coefficient (i unit-free; μ−iq in m⁻¹). Its positive real part μ makes the exponential integral converge. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). steps: Let μ=1/a and g_Y=0.040E_La, where E_L=ℏ²/(2ma²). Then f_B=−0.040a/[1+(qa)²].
For a=2 nm, the forward amplitude is −0.080 nm. At qa=1 it is −0.040 nm, so that angular cross section is one-quarter of the forward value.
At qa=3, it is −0.008 nm, one-tenth of the forward amplitude and one-hundredth of its magnitude square. The screening scale remains finite throughout.

Correct. Doubling μ multiplies its squared denominator by four.
Stronger screening reduces this forward amplitude at fixed coupling.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why must the potential coefficient’s units be checked before using a quoted screened formula?
apply.answer: Some conventions put an energy-times-length coupling in the numerator, while others factor a reference length into an energy scale. Substituting one convention’s numerical coefficient into another can introduce a length error even if the algebra looks similar.

lessons.limits: μ>0 screened central potential, convergent transform and weak-distortion Born regime. The singular short-distance potential still needs the usual operator/validity care; μ→0 is not a uniform short-range limit.

lessons.title: A first-order amplitude needs an order-by-order conservation check
lessons.idea: The cross section starts at second order, even when the amplitude starts at first order.
body: For a weak attractive spherical well, let q_d=κa with κ=√(2mU)/ℏ. The exact zero-energy scattering length is a_s=a[1−tan q_d/q_d]. Its leading small-depth term is a_s,B=−a q_d²/3, which follows from the first Born forward amplitude. The subscript d distinguishes this depth parameter from momentum transfer q.

Comparing these lengths tests an actual weak-well limit. A small dimensionless depth such as q_d² helps here, but Born validity in a general potential also depends on energy, range and resonances. A potential that supports a near-threshold state can defeat a naive weak-looking estimate.

For a real potential, the first Born forward amplitude is real. The angular cross section from |f_B|² is of second order in potential strength, while the corresponding imaginary forward term first appears at second amplitude order. Thus a first-order amplitude cannot satisfy the optical theorem through second order by itself. This is a missing-order issue, not permission for an exact elastic solution to violate conservation.
lessons.equation: a_s,B=−a q_d²/3;  a_s=a[1−tan q_d/q_d];  Im f^(2)(0) supplies the order-V² flux account
lessons.terms: a,q_d,κ,U,a_s,a_s,B: Well radius, scaled depth, interior wave number, positive depth and exact/leading scattering lengths (m, no unit, m⁻¹, J, m and m). q_d is not the transfer wave number q used in the Fourier formula. f^(2),V,Im: Second amplitude-order contribution, potential and imaginary-part operation (amplitude in m; V in J). The superscript labels perturbative order, not an amplitude square. The phrase order-V² refers to scaling when a unit-free strength multiplies a fixed potential. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). check.prompt: If a first-order real forward amplitude gives Im f_B(0)=0 but |f_B|² is nonzero, which conclusion is sound?

explanations: The exact conservation relation still holds in its stated regime.
A vanishing first-order imaginary component does not make the second-order area vanish.
Correct. The squared first-order amplitude and forward imaginary part arise at different amplitude orders.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: What evidence would support a Born estimate for a new short-range potential?
apply.answer: State a dimensionless strength/range/energy regime, compare with a controlled exact or numerically converged reference where possible, and test limiting behavior and flux at consistent order. A smooth graph or a small potential written in arbitrary units is insufficient.

lessons.limits: Weak short-range first Born scattering, explicitly separated from the exact elastic result. The square-well length comparison is a low-energy limit; generic Born convergence, higher-order resummation and resonance methods are not established by it.

practice.prompt: Use separate weak models: a spherical well with a=2 nm and q_d=0.20; a Gaussian with V₀/E_L=0.040 and a=1 nm; geometry with k=1 nm⁻¹ and θ=π/3; and a screened model with f_B=−0.040a/[1+(qa)²], a=1 nm and qa=1.

lessons.title: Choose the approximation from the actual obstacle
lessons.idea: A small coupling, a tied subspace, a restricted trial family and a smooth turning point are different problems.
body: Begin by naming what is known and what is small. An isolated reference level with small coupling-to-gap ratios suggests nondegenerate perturbation. A nearly tied block instead needs the internal mixing kept together. A variational trial supplies an upper energy bound without requiring weak coupling.

WKB answers a different question: whether a stationary wave changes slowly over its local scale and whether its turning-point connections are appropriate. Smoothness, a nonzero gap and a good trial shape are not interchangeable assumptions. A method should be chosen for a reason visible in the actual model.

After calculating, report the type of result: an expansion estimate, a block eigenvalue, an upper bound or a leading semiclassical value. Compare against an exact or refined numerical reference when available, and do not turn a finite successful comparison into a theorem about every potential.
lessons.terms: g,Δ,E₂: Actual two-level coupling, positive gap and second-order lower-energy estimate (eV). The reference lower energy is zero for this displayed estimate; it is not a generic formula for every level. η,E_trial,E_ground: Coupling ratio, allowed trial expectation and true ground energy (no unit, eV and eV). A variational upper bound requires a normalized allowed finite-energy trial, not weak mixing. k,k′,ε_WKB: Local positive wave number, its position derivative and local variation ratio (m⁻¹, m⁻² and no unit). The WKB diagnostic is only one part of a smooth-wave approximation check. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For the two-level reference gap Δ=5 eV and real coupling g=0.20 eV, η=0.04 and E₂=−0.008 eV. The exact block energy is [5−√(25+0.16)]/2 eV≈−0.00798724 eV.

In a separate exact spectrum 1,4,10 eV, a trial orthogonal to the ground state with excited weights 0.90 and 0.10 has energy 4.6 eV. That is an upper bound on the first excited energy, not an exact new level.
For a separate smooth harmonic well with ℏω=0.060 eV and n=2, the two-turning action condition gives 0.150 eV. Replacing its smooth boundaries by hard walls would change the boundary rule.

check.prompt: A new pair has Δ=0.020 eV and |g|=0.020 eV. Which next step is best justified?
options: Retain and diagonalize the mixed pair as a block
Trust the isolated-level second-order shift without checking
Call the coupling weak solely because its eV value is small
explanations: Correct. The internal coupling is as large as the reference gap.
The ratio is one, not a small perturbation parameter.
Smallness must be compared with the relevant gap, not a unit-dependent decimal.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: What would make a short approximation report useful to another learner?
apply.answer: State the Hamiltonian and units, the retained states or trial family, the relevant smallness/domain conditions, what kind of result was obtained, and one comparison or failure test. An unexplained final number hides the very choices the method was meant to control.

lessons.limits: A synthesis of the earlier finite-model, variational and semiclassical assumptions, not a new universal approximation theorem. Supplied effective atomic corrections and broader many-body/relativistic methods retain their separate scope limits.

practice.prompt: Keep three cases separate: reference energies 0 and 6 eV coupled by g=0.30 eV; an excited-state trial orthogonal to a known ground with weights 0.80 and 0.20 on energies 4 and 10 eV; and a smooth harmonic well with n=1 and ℏω=0.120 eV.
practice.reasoning: For each answer, name the result type and one condition that would make its use invalid. Enter decimal or scientific-notation numbers, not fractions or expressions. Entry tolerances allow rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: Keep coherent oscillation, transition rate and decay separate
lessons.idea: Similar-looking probabilities may come from different physical assumptions.
body: For a closed two-state system with H=(ℏΩ/2)σ_x and initial |0⟩, the exact transfer is P₁=sin²(Ωt/2). The weak-pulse expression (Ωt/2)² is its short-time expansion, not a probability formula to continue past one. Ω is a positive angular rate here, not an energy.

A continuum transition rate Γ gives P≈Γt only within the stated rate window and before appreciable depletion. A separate amplitude-damping model with decay rate γ gives excited population p₁(t)=exp(−γt) from an initially excited state. With no extra pure dephasing, a general state’s coherence is multiplied by exp(−γt/2).

These are three different preparations/models: closed coherent transfer, weak continuum transfer and an explicitly open decay channel. The density matrix of a trace-preserving open model keeps trace one; lost excited population moves to the ground population, not outside total probability. Combining drive and decay requires solving a combined equation, not adding these separate formulas.
lessons.terms: Ω,t,P₁,P_weak: Closed-system angular rate, time and exact/short-time transfer probabilities (rad/s, s and no unit). The Hamiltonian is explicitly ℏΩσ_x/2 and the initial state is |0⟩. Γ,P_rate: Weak continuum transition rate and leading transferred probability (s⁻¹ and no unit). Use the separately established continuum resolution/weak-depletion window; Γt must remain small. γ,p₁,decay,ρ: Open-channel population-decay rate, excited population and density matrix (s⁻¹ and no unit). The initial excited population is one in this example. Coherence decay γ/2 assumes no additional pure dephasing. ℏ,σ_x,H: Reduced Planck constant, Pauli-x matrix and Hamiltonian (J·s, no unit and J). σ_x=[[0,1],[1,0]] in the stated zero/one basis. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.

equationGuide.meaning: The closed system oscillates coherently. A weak-pulse approximation keeps only the initial quadratic rise. A continuum rate is approximately linear over its valid window, while a stated open decay channel gives an exponential population decrease.

check.prompt: A weak-pulse calculation gives (Ωt/2)²=1.44. What should be concluded?
options: The short-time approximation is outside its useful probability regime
Always clip it to one and call that exact
explanations: A probability cannot exceed one.
Correct. Use the full model and check its assumptions rather than extending the weak expansion blindly.
Clipping does not recover the coherent oscillation or a controlled error.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: How can an open-system density matrix lose coherence while retaining total probability?
apply.answer: The off-diagonal elements can decrease while populations remain nonnegative and sum to one. In the stated channels this follows from the complete-positive trace-preserving map; it is different from simply deleting norm from a state vector.

lessons.limits: Declared closed two-state Hamiltonian, separately valid weak-continuum rate and separately specified Markov amplitude-damping channel. No extra pure dephasing in the quoted coherence factor. These formulas do not solve arbitrary drive-plus-bath dynamics.

lessons.title: Audit the answer as well as the number
lessons.idea: A useful result includes its units, normalization, approximation order and a check that could reveal a mistake.
body: For scattering, record the incoming density/flux convention, potential range, elastic versus inelastic channels and whether events are distinguishable. A directional cross section is |f|²; a total requires angular integration. Identical pair-event counting additionally needs the stated hemisphere convention.

Check a central elastic calculation in two ways: sum its partial areas and compute the forward-imaginary-amplitude expression. Agreement is a conservation test. For a first Born truncation, keep the optical-theorem order discussion consistent rather than demanding a missing second-order amplitude from a first-order formula.

For numerical work, report a refinement comparison and a physical identity such as flux, norm or trace preservation. For approximation work, name the smallness, isolation, continuum or slow-change condition. Passing the course checks gives practice with these bounded models, not a certification of every advanced method or experimental skill.

The equalities use the short-range real central single-channel and outgoing-wave conventions established earlier. R,N_t,j_in,σ: Expected event rate, target count, incident flux and the appropriate event cross section (s⁻¹, count, m⁻²·s⁻¹ and m²). For identical collisions, use the correct event area rather than double-counting outgoing hits. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); meV means millielectronvolt (10⁻³ eV). example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Take a stipulated distinguishable s-plus-p elastic sample with k=1.5 nm⁻¹, δ₀=π/6 and δ₁=π/3. The partial sum gives σ_el=(4π/2.25)(0.25+3×0.75) nm²=40π/9 nm².
Its forward amplitude is f(0)=[√3+2.5i]/(1.5 nm⁻¹), so Im f(0)=5/3 nm. The optical expression gives the same 40π/9 nm²≈13.9626 nm².

If a numerical result disagreed between those two routes, examine angular resolution, omitted l values, phase conventions and boundary matching before interpreting a new physical effect. A first-order Born result would instead require its explicit order-limited comparison.

check.prompt: Two opposite detectors identify 30 coincident pairs from 30 identical-particle collisions. In the declared pair-event convention, how many events should enter the rate?
options: 60 because there were two hits per collision
explanations: That counts the same final pair twice.
Using a hemisphere avoids duplication; it does not discard half the known coincidence events.
Correct. One collision gives one pair event even if both particles are detected.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: What remains beyond this introductory course even after every local check is solved?
apply.answer: Rigorous operator/asymptotic theorems, full relativistic/QED and molecular dynamics, general non-Markovian channels, coupled or long-range scattering, interacting many-body theory and laboratory analysis remain separate study. The value of these steps is a clearly defined foundation for checking models, not a claim that all quantum research is finished.

lessons.limits: All earlier assumptions remain attached to their respective methods. The displayed elastic equalities are not a shortcut for Coulomb, inelastic, strongly truncated or inconsistently normalized calculations; event rates additionally need a dilute calibrated geometry.

modules.title: A bounded introduction to open systems
Choose, test and report an approximation

statusNote: This defined introductory course contains 84 micro-lessons and 68 numerical practice parts. It teaches nondegenerate/degenerate perturbation, variational bounds, WKB with explicit turning-point bridges, supplied effective atomic corrections, external fields/gauge choices, adiabatic and Born–Oppenheimer models, weak transitions and continuum rates, bounded light/open-channel examples, and elastic partial-wave/Born scattering. Source-level science and plain-language review is complete; completion marks do not certify independent mastery. Each supplied effective law, approximation domain and numerical check is distinguished from a full derivation or general theorem. Relativistic/QED, full molecular/bath dynamics, general long-range/inelastic scattering, many-body methods and laboratory expertise remain outside this finite course or in later paths. It is not all quantum physics.
deferred: Full derivations of Dirac theory, radiative/Lamb, hyperfine, recoil and finite-nucleus corrections; only named effective low-order atomic corrections are taught here.
Rigorous asymptotic error theorems, all turning-point/Stokes or uniform WKB methods, functional-analysis proofs and convergent perturbation classifications.
